Within a package an edit only adds and comes out with any release of the line, and a breaking edit is a new package, `v2`, and a new line of `spec`, so a breaking edit of a contract does not come out as a patch. `api` holds the current and the previous major package — a window, as for the format from v1.
- **What changes the format version.** The rule is one for everything the format sets: what a module contains and how it is checked, built into a package and an index, and executed — the check kinds and normalization, the generator and the derivation of seeds, the templates, the open view. Normatively, the [format text](../format/README.md), in its rule on versions.
  - **A minor version** is an addition. After it, every module of the previous version passes the check and on the same inputs — module, seed, read value — gives the same verdict, open view and numbers, and a package and an index built by the previous version read as before. Such are an optional field — a new field is closed until it is opened explicitly —, a new check kind or canvas kind, a tool, a value of a list, a parameter whose default value is the previous behaviour, and a new place of randomness that does not shift the numbers of the previous ones. A module that takes an addition names the new minor version.
  - **A major version** is everything else: a field removed, renamed or made required; what was correct became incorrect; on the same inputs another verdict, open view or other numbers are possible. So are changed the behaviour of a check kind, the numbers of an existing place of randomness or the templates, and so is opened a field that was closed.
  - **The check.** How the verdict of an item is made up of the verdicts of its slots, and the step limit of a predicate, are behaviour of the check: changing them is a major version.
  - **The generator and the derivation of seeds** have no version of their own: they are a part of the format version and cover all the places of randomness of the platform, and `engine` and `sim` take them from the format version their release reads. In each format version the generator is one for the whole platform, and the numbers of a module's template and widget depend only on the format version of its manifest. Major — the constants, the output, FNV-1a, the text of a place of randomness, any function and how many integers it takes. Minor — a new function and a new reserved first name of a module's places. What a place takes and in what order is decided by its owner, the template. The cost: from v1 a major edit of the generator means two generators in `module-kit`, one for each major version in the window.
  - **Task templates.** Major — the meaning of template expressions, the order of combinations, how the instance of an attempt is chosen and the names of its place, the placeholder and a lowered limit of combinations. Minor — a new construct of an expression, a raised limit, parameters of an item and a new place of a template. Templates enter v1 only if a module of the first slice takes them (the [format text](../format/README.md), in its rule on templates).
  - **The canonical view and the package digest** depend only on the module's files and the format version of its manifest, without the version of `module-kit` and the time. The members of the canonical view, its canonical text, the list of the device part, the inventory and the rule of the digest are a part of the format version: a new member or a new entry of the list is a minor version, the rest a major one. A package is read by the version its inventory names.
  - **The module index** holds the records of all format versions, so its members keep their place and meaning in all versions, while the format is v0 too, like `module_format_version` in the manifest. A new version may add only an optional member of a record or a withdrawal reason, and this is minor. A reader skips a record whose format version it does not read, rather than rejecting the index.
  - **Starlark and the package.** The version of go.starlark.net is a part of the format: raising it is a new format version, a major one. The places of the package that version comparison reads hold in all versions, v0 too, as the members of the index do.
  - **The vocabulary of the shared taxonomy** enters the format version. A new anchor skill and the mark `deprecated` are a minor version, the removal of an anchor skill and a change of its meaning a major one, and a skill with a new meaning gets a new ID; other words of the same meaning in the description are an editorial change, and the ID of an anchor skill is not reused.
  - **The eval set format** does not enter the format version: a sample of `eval/` is the message `Sample` of the contract `novatrail.eval.v1`, versioned as a contract.
  - **A SHOULD without a rule** requires no version: the format rules are only MUST (the [format text](../format/README.md), in its format rules), and a SHOULD does not change the verdict, the open view or the numbers.
  - **While the format is v0,** compatibility is not promised beyond the places kept in every version — `module_format_version` in the manifest, the members of the index, the places of the package that version comparison reads —, and any change of the format is the next version 0.y.
  - **The number of a released version does not go back** and is not reused: reverting a change is a new version too.
  - **An error of `module-kit`** that the test vectors catch is not a change of the format: an implementation that does not pass them does not conform to the format.
- **A module is executed by the version of its manifest.** `module-kit` checks, builds and executes a module by the format version its manifest names.
  - A module takes only what its version has. A module of a version newer than those the release of `module-kit` knows is rejected with a reason.
  - A new format version changes neither the verdict, nor the open view, nor the numbers of a published module until the author moves the module to it. The move is a new version of the module: its manifest changed. Which version part of the module it raises, the semver rules of `module-kit` decide.
  - Since the canonical view and the package digest depend only on the module's sources and the format version in its manifest, the verdict, the open view and the numbers are decided by the package digest, not by the version the server chose.
  - Within a major version the implementation is one — minor versions only add —, and `module-kit` holds no more than two: of the current major version and of the previous one.
- **Which versions the platform reads is the window.**
  - While the format is v0, only the current version 0.y. The official modules move to a new one in one pull request of `modules`, and there are no third-party modules before v1.
  - From v1, version v0 leaves the window. After that the window is the current major version with all its minor ones and the previous major one. The previous one leaves when the next major one comes out — by count, not by time.
  - The window is a rule for everyone who reads modules and packages. That is `module-kit` — in CI of `modules`, in `api`, in the eval runner of `tutor` and in CI of `canvas`; `sim`, which reads packages by the types of the canonical view; `app` and `canvas`, which get the open view by the types from the releases of `spec`. A module of a version outside the window is rejected with a reason.
  - The types are a package for each major version in the window, named by it: `types/formatv0`, whose types a minor version changes but not its path; from v1, `formatv1` stands beside it.
  - How a new version passes through the repositories, `docs/repositories.md` says with the flows between them.
- **The attempt and the replay of a verdict.**
  - The attempt also keeps the version of `module-kit`, as the engine choice keeps the versions of `engine` and `learner-model`. A fixed error of `module-kit` changes the verdict on the same inputs although the format is the same, and an exact replay takes the release that delivered the verdict.
  - An attempt begun on a version that has left the window, `api` no longer checks in its process. What to do with it, the detailing of `api` decides. The recommendation is as for a withdrawn version: "unchecked" and a neutral phrase, since this is not the learner's error.
  - A replay of the verdict for such an attempt goes outside `api` — by the release of `module-kit` that checked it.
- **The first version and v1.**
  - The first version is 0.1, numbered in `format/VERSION` before the first schema. It came out with v0.3.0, the first release of line 0.3, where the schemas are files for code: the code of other repositories takes them only from there. Before it, 0.1 was a draft, which the tasks of epic E2 edited without raising the number and the code of other repositories did not take. The rules of the number apply from that release, so the implementation knows only the released 0.1, and the number in code has one meaning: a module written by the draft is checked by the released version. From line 0.3 one line has one format.
  - The format becomes v1 by the author's decision — a record in this log —, when both modules of the first slice have passed through the platform without subject code in the core, and the success criteria of the first slice in `docs/product.md` are met. v1.0 is the last version 0.y without what no module of the first slice took.
- **The versions released.** The [format text](../format/README.md) lists each and what it holds, with its rule on versions.
  - **0.2** came out with v0.6.0, the first release of line 0.6. Without `canvas.digit_height` the digit height in it is 24 px, and besides it 0.2 holds only a guide for authors about the page of a workbook, without a rule, in the format text's rule on the task. A module 0.1 without the field was read at 32 px; moved to 0.2, it is read at 24 px unless it sets 32. Its vectors pin what the text already says and do not change the version: the case `previous-minor` of `manifest.format-version` — a reader 0.2 rejects a module 0.1, since while the format is v0 the platform reads only the current version; the case `next-minor` moves to 0.3 — and the vector of the index `earlier-format-version`, whose previous index was built by 0.1 and keeps its records 0.1 while both modules moved to 0.2 with new versions and records naming 0.2, as the first release of `modules` after a new format version looks.
  - **0.3** came out with v0.9.0, the first release of line 0.9: line 0.7 was opened by the package and the tag of the contracts, line 0.8 by the admission table, and their releases carry format 0.2. It holds the version of go.starlark.net and one dialect of Starlark and the rules of version comparison.
  - **0.4** came out with v0.10.0, the first release of line 0.10, in one pull request of the branch `e6`: the tasks of epic E6 went on it one by one, and the last raised `format/VERSION` and `RELEASE_LINE`. It holds what the three modules of the first slice and `module-kit` asked of the format.
- **A new canvas kind or check kind** is platform code and an addition, that is, a minor version.
  - In v0 a kind may enter even without a module that takes it, as the check kind "predicate", `predicate`, did.
  - Only what the modules of the first slice took enters v1. The text canvas and the check kinds "text", "edit" and "predicate", if no module of the slice takes them, do not enter v1.
  - After v1 a new kind enters together with the module that needs it first.
  - A kind can be fixed later by a new kind or a parameter — a minor version, and the previous behaviour leaves with the next major one —, or by a major version.
- **What this entry does not decide:**
  - the version of the widget protocol — epic E5;
  - which format versions the publication of third-party modules accepts — the publication rules (О-9; epic E5).

— *Why:* the link with the line of `spec`, the execution by the version of the manifest, the rules of v0, the path of a new kind and the version of `module-kit` in the attempt are the plan's proposal. All sources were read 2026-10-22.
- **Two versions.** The tag of `spec` grows with every edit of a document: 21 releases, v0.2.0–v0.2.20, came out from 2026-10-19 to 2026-10-22, and not one has a schema. A format version equal to the tag would change without the format. One line for everything does not do either: neither the contracts of E3 nor the widget protocol of E5 could raise it without giving the format a new version. So in Kubernetes too: "The API versioning and software versioning are indirectly related" ([Kubernetes, API Overview](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/#api-versioning)).
- **The link with the line** gives whoever takes `spec` one rule: within a line the format is the same. The same holds for each other part with a version of its own, and a breaking edit of a contract does not come out as a patch.
- **Without a patch** — as in OpenAPI: "The `major`.`minor` portion of the version string (for example `3.1`) SHALL designate the OAS feature set. `.patch` versions address errors in, or provide clarifications to, this document, not the feature set" and "The patch version SHOULD NOT be considered by tooling" ([OpenAPI Specification v3.1.1, Versions](https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.1.1.html#versions)). An editorial change of `spec` is named by the tag anyway.
- **The execution by the version of the manifest** — as for a Go module by its `go` line: "A `go` directive indicates that a module was written assuming the semantics of a given version of Go", "Go toolchains refuse to use modules declaring newer Go versions" and "the compiler rejects use of language features introduced after the version specified by the `go` directive" ([Go Modules Reference](https://go.dev/ref/mod#go-mod-file-go)). So Go 1.22 changed the meaning of loop variables: "the new semantics will only apply in packages contained in modules that declare `go 1.22` or later in their `go.mod` files", and "Old code will continue to mean exactly what it means today: the fix only applies to new or updated code" ([Fixing For Loops in Go 1.22](https://go.dev/blog/loopvar-preview), David Chase and Russ Cox, 2023-09-19).
  - The format is stricter than Go: Go changes meaning in a minor version too, and the format only in a major one. So `module-kit` has one implementation per major version.
  - The verdict is held by the package digest, not the server's choice, and an edit of behaviour reaches the learner through the module's CI — its check and eval set.
- **v0 without promises** — by semver: "Major version zero (0.y.z) is for initial development. Anything MAY change at any time. The public API SHOULD NOT be considered stable", and "Version 1.0.0 defines the public API" ([Semantic Versioning 2.0.0](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html), items 4 and 5). A window in v0 would be a cost without benefit: the official modules lie in one repository so that an edit of the format is one for all, and there are no third-party ones before v1. "Nothing is promised" is narrowed for the places kept in every version: the index holds the records of all versions, and version comparison reads a package of an earlier one.
- **Version 0.2:**
  - two edits of the format in a row would give two lines of `spec` and two moves of each repository, and the cross-repository plan leads them by one move to line 0.6; the other edits were not ready for the version and waited for their epics;
  - the SHOULD that `canvas` asked for — an opaque light background of a picture — does not wait for a format version and may come with any release, and the rows of one letter of `canvas` are recorded together;
  - the modules are written in 0.2 at once, and the first release of `module-kit` with code must reject 0.1, not read it by the schemas of 0.2: the vector `previous-minor` holds this. The vector of an index of two versions checks that the build takes a previous index of another version rather than rejecting it.
- **Version 0.4 in one pull request:** in one line there is one format, and a rule of 0.4 on `main` would earlier have come out as a patch of line 0.9.
- **Only what is tested in v1:** an abstraction without a consumer bends to the first one, and a kind can be fixed after v1 only by a new version.
- **The version of `module-kit` in the attempt:** without it a replay of the verdict would not tell a fixed error of `module-kit` from a change of the format.

— *Rejected:*
- one version, the line of `spec`: the format would take the line, and a breaking edit of a contract of E3 would come out as a patch;
- two independent versions, and the line at discretion: a breaking edit of the format could come out as a patch, and the line would not show whether the format changed;
- a patch for the format version: the tag of `spec` names an editorial change;
- execution by the newest version within its major one, with the version in the attempt: the verdict of the same module of the same version would change without its CI and eval set, and `module-kit` would keep the behaviour of every minor version for the replay;
- the window "current and previous" already in v0: `module-kit`, `sim` and the types of the open view would hold two versions each while the format changes most often, and there is nobody to move one by one;
- preliminary kinds — with a mark that a module takes explicitly, and outside the promise of compatibility, like the alpha versions of an API in Kubernetes: "Built-in alpha API versions are disabled by default and must be explicitly enabled in the `kube-apiserver` configuration to be used" and "The API may change in incompatible ways in a later software release without notice" (Kubernetes, API Overview). The mark would go into the schema and into `module-kit`, and a replay of the verdict would require behaviour for every minor version. The format already has a preliminary stage — v0;
- all of v0 into v1: a kind without a module would set untested;
- the SHOULD of the opaque background in 0.2, in one edit with the version: the row would leave its letter, and it needs no version;
- for 0.2, only replacing 0.1 with 0.2, without new vectors: until the next version no vector would pin that a reader 0.2 rejects 0.1 and that the index holds records of two versions; only the case `previous-minor`.

— *Consequence:* `docs/concepts.md`; `docs/architecture.md`; `docs/repositories.md`; `docs/decisions.md`; `format/README.md` and `format/VERSION`; `RELEASE_LINE` in `.github/workflows/release.yml`; `tools/release/` — `format-line.mjs` and the filters of the other parts; `types/formatv0`.

## The module format: JSON Schema and conventions

**R45. The module format is JSON Schema 2020-12, and the author writes a module in YAML 1.2.2 with restrictions. The format text, the schemas, the examples and the test vectors lie in `format/` and are written by one set of conventions.** Normatively the conventions are written in English in the format text, [format/README.md](../format/README.md), in its parts from the files of `format/` to the test vectors, and here is what is decided, why, and what is rejected.
- **The schemas** are JSON Schema 2020-12, JSON files `format/schemas/<term>.schema.json`. The term is the English term of the part from the glossary of `docs/concepts.md`, in kebab-case; the common definitions of the parts lie in `common.schema.json` — the parts of the task statement, the canvas and the rectangle of the sheet among them —, and the schema of a part does not reference the schema of another part.
  - `$id` is `https://altnovatrail.github.io/spec/format/`, the number from `format/VERSION`, a slash and the file name. References between schemas are relative, in one of three forms: `#/$defs/<name>`, `<file>.schema.json` or `<file>.schema.json#/$defs/<name>`. An absolute reference to this prefix is forbidden: it would silently tie the schema to one version; so would `../0.1/common.schema.json`, which `ajv` allows, so a ban on the prefix alone is not enough.
  - The keywords of a schema are only the list of the [format text](../format/README.md), in its rules on writing a schema: the keywords of 2020-12 and `x-open`, and `$schema` and `$id` only at the root. The strict mode of `ajv` does not hold this: it lets through `nullable`, `definitions` and `dependencies`, which 2020-12 does not have. Of 2020-12, the list leaves out:
    - `$anchor`, `$dynamicRef`, `$dynamicAnchor` and `$vocabulary` — a reference names only `$defs`;
    - `minContains` and `maxContains` — `ajv` names their error `contains` (`dist/vocabularies/applicator/contains.js`, 8.20.0), and an invalid example would name a keyword the specification does not name;
    - `unevaluatedItems` — the test runner of `ajv` skips the cases of the JSON Schema suite where it meets `contains` (`spec/json-schema.spec.ts`, v8.20.0), and an array has enough with `items` and `maxItems`;
    - `dependentSchemas` — see the item on `ajv` below;
    - the content vocabulary — the format does not need it.
  - The root of a schema has `title` and `description`; `description` is at the subschema of each field, there too where it has only `$ref`: under `properties` and `patternProperties` and at the schema of the values of a dictionary. A condition — what `if` and `not` hold — does not need it. All in English, as every normative text for authors.
  - **Closing is by place.** An object is closed by `unevaluatedProperties: false` in the schema that describes it whole in its place: only the schema at the object's place closes it. A schema that another takes and extends — through `allOf` or through `$ref` beside its own `properties` — is open: closed, it would reject the fields of the extension.
    - A place is the root of a schema or a subschema directly under `properties`, `patternProperties`, `additionalProperties`, `items`, `prefixItems` or `contains`, outside a condition. The entries of `$defs`, the targets of `$ref` and the branches of `allOf`, `anyOf`, `oneOf`, `if`, `then`, `else`, `not` and `dependentSchemas` are parts of the place.
    - If the parts of a place describe an object, the place has `unevaluatedProperties: false`. `unevaluatedProperties` stands only at a place and only as `false`, and beside a `$ref` to an object there is the line `"unevaluatedProperties": false`. A dictionary whose keys are data is set and closed by `additionalProperties` with a schema and `propertyNames`.
    - `additionalProperties: false` is not used: it does not see properties declared through `$ref` and `allOf`.
    - **A name from `if` or `not`** is declared also by a part of the place that always applies: the place itself or where its `$ref` and `allOf` lead. By 2020-12 a subschema that failed gives no annotations, while `ajv` counts a field of a failed `if` as evaluated when there is an `else`. The test runner of `ajv` skips this case of the suite: "unevaluatedProperties with if/then/else, then not defined" — "when if is false and has unevaluated properties" (`spec/json-schema.spec.ts`, v8.20.0). Without the rule, `spec` would let through a value that the validator of `module-kit` rejects by 2020-12.
  - **`ajv`'s two errors.** A schema of the format does not take `dependentSchemas` and does not put `$ref` beside `oneOf` or `anyOf` in one subschema, and `format-check` rejects both forms and names the cause and its workaround: `allOf` with `if: {required: [<key>]}` and `then` instead of `dependentSchemas`, and `$ref` or the branches in `allOf`. Beside `unevaluatedProperties: false`, `ajv` counts the fields of the place as unevaluated when the object lacks the key of `dependentSchemas` or when, at `$ref` together with `oneOf` or `anyOf`, a branch other than the first passes; it rejects a value valid by 2020-12, and its error names `unevaluatedProperties`, not the cause. The workarounds `ajv` checks correctly, and the test of `format-check` that pins both errors checks the workarounds too. The ban is no new version: no schema of format 0.3 and of the admission table took either form, so neither a module, nor a package, nor an index changes by it, only how `spec` writes its schemas. The check of the conventions and the open view still go through the branches of `dependentSchemas`, so what stands in them is checked too; a change of this entry lifts the ban when `ajv` fixes the errors and the test says so.
  - A module is checked by the schemas of exactly its MAJOR.MINOR. So an unknown field is an error, and a module does not take a field of a version newer than its own.
  - The check does not rest on `format`. The subschema `false` stands only at `unevaluatedProperties`.
  - **`pattern`** — and the keys of `patternProperties` — is written only from the tokens that 2020-12 advises, without `\d`, `\w` and `\s`, and beyond them so that Go and JavaScript, into which `ajv` compiles a pattern in mode `u`, read alike:
    - in a class `[` and `]` are escaped, `-` is first, last or between the ends of a range, a range is ascending, there is no empty class. Go reads `[]a]` as a class of `]` and `a` — "] and - are okay as first char in class" (`parseClass`) — and rejects `[^]`, while JavaScript rejects `[]a]` and accepts `[^]`;
    - outside a class `{`, `}` and `]` only in a quantifier or escaped: Go reads them as letters, while JavaScript rejects them;
    - a count has no leading zeros — "Disallow leading zeros" (`parseInt`): `a{01}` in Go is letters, and in JavaScript `a{1}`;
    - neither a count nor the product of nested counts is greater than 1000, and Go counts them so: `{x}` and `{x,y}` by the largest, `{x,}` by `x`, and `{0,}` as 1: "Implementation restriction: The counting forms x{n,m}, x{n,}, and x{n} reject forms that create a minimum or maximum repetition count above 1000" (`doc.go`; `repeatIsValid` in `parse.go`).

    Go — `src/regexp/syntax`, commit fb3c20e; JavaScript — `new RegExp(pattern, "u")` in Node 24 of the devcontainer.
  - Marks of our own carry the prefix `x-`, and the format text lists them. For now there is one mark — `x-open`.
  - **Schemas without a part.** `format/schemas/` also holds schemas that describe no part of a module, each named by its term of the glossary or by the vectors it describes:
    - the vocabulary of the shared taxonomy, `shared-taxonomy.schema.json`, which the parts reference as they do `common.schema.json`;
    - of the package, `canonical-view.schema.json` and `inventory.schema.json`; the schema of the canonical view references the schemas of the parts, and the rule that the schema of a part does not reference the schema of another part does not concern it;
    - of the module index, `module-index.schema.json`;
    - of the vectors, below: `verdict-vector.schema.json`, `leak-vector.schema.json` and `template-vector.schema.json`, which reference the schema of a task, `random-vector.schema.json`, which references no other, `tier-vector.schema.json`, `package-vector.schema.json` and `index-vector.schema.json`.

    Of them only the inventory and the module index have examples of their own.
- **The names** of fields and of the values of enumerations are the English terms of the glossary in snake_case: `answer_slots`, `trap_advice`. A field without a term — `id`, `title`, `version` — is a plain English word. An array is in the plural, but for a field that names by a verb how its element is linked with others: `replaced_by` of a retired skill is the skills that replaced it, and `teaches` of a skill is an array too, so the name reads as a link, not as an object. A new term first enters the glossary, as did the fields of traps, leaks and lessons — `trap_advice`, `trap_values`, `rung_templates`, `simpler_case`, `leak_phrases`, `givens`, `unknown`, `exit_condition`, `segments`, `explanation`, `worked_example`, `demo` and `area`. A module writes the format version number as a string: `"0.1"`.
  - `teaches` of an index record is a string in the form of an anchor skill's ID, not a `$ref` to the vocabulary: the record lives longer than the version of the vocabulary.
  - The integers `from` and `to` of a template's range and the width and height of a picture have the bounds ±(2^53−1): an integer written with an exponent, `1e20`, passed `type: integer` and `yaml.json-scalars`.
  - The schema of the deployment configuration file, `deployment/schemas/deployment.schema.json`, keeps the field names that `app` reads in camelCase — the keys of the Firebase configuration object; its other conventions are the same, and its vector's schema keeps them all. The check of the conventions lifts the snake_case rule from this schema alone.
- **The author's YAML** is YAML 1.2.2 with the Core schema, and rules beyond it, each with an ID `yaml.<name>`:
  - UTF-8 without BOM; one document, `---` allowed at the start; without directives, anchors, aliases `*` and tags;
  - keys are strings: quoted or plain by the rule below, but not `null`, `true`, `false` and not a number. After escapes are processed they do not repeat;
  - the plain scalars `null`, `true`, `false` and JSON numbers are these values. A number fits in a double, an integer lies within ±(2^53−1), and `-0` is an error. By `yaml.json-scalars` an integer is a number written without a fraction and an exponent, as go-yaml divides int and float. Any number is finite as a double, and precision is not a criterion: otherwise `0.1` would be a violation too. There is no negative zero in any notation, as there is no negative number that a double rounds to zero, such as `-1e-400`: it reads as the same −0;
  - any other plain scalar is a string. It is not empty, does not start with a digit, `+`, `-`, `.`, `~`, `<` or `=`, and is not equal, case-insensitively, to `y`, `n`, `yes`, `no`, `on`, `off`, `true`, `false` or `null`. Such a string is quoted;
  - strings hold no surrogates and no Unicode noncharacters, and no escape `\/`. By `yaml.characters` an escaped surrogate is forbidden both in a pair and in the form `\U`: `yaml` joins a pair into one character, while go-yaml rejects any such escape: "found invalid Unicode character escape code" (`internal/libyaml/scanner.go`, commit 32734c3). Escapes are read from left to right, and `\\/` is a backslash and a slash;
  - a character outside the printable set of [YAML 1.2.2](https://yaml.org/spec/1.2.2/), section 5.1, even in a comment, is not YAML. `yaml` lets through the C0 control characters and U+FFFE, while go-yaml rejects them: "control characters are not allowed" (`internal/libyaml/reader.go`, commit 32734c3). In quotes too it is refused by the rule `yaml.printable`.

  Comments, block strings and flow collections are allowed. The order of keys carries no meaning, and the reader does not normalize Unicode. A file in JSON syntax is read by the same rules.
- **An open field** is marked by `x-open: true` in the subschema of a property under `properties`, `patternProperties` or `additionalProperties`, beside `$ref` if there is one.
  - A place in a module is open when its parent is open and it itself is an element of an array or is marked; the root of a part is open.
  - A mark counts only if its subschema applies and passes, in the branches of `allOf`, `anyOf`, `oneOf`, `if`/`then`/`else` and `dependentSchemas` too: JSON Schema 2020-12 collects an annotation only at a subschema that passes. Under `if`, `not`, `contains` and `propertyNames` the mark opens nothing, and `format-check` does not let it through there.
  - The field by which an open object chooses a branch of `oneOf` or of `if`/`then` is open.
  - Without the mark a field is closed, so a new field is closed until it is opened explicitly. The key or the predicate, the solution, the traps — the trap values, the trap catalog and the traps of a task — and the leak phrases are never opened: the tutor does not name the answer.
  - Opening a closed field is a major format version, and a new field open at once is a minor one.
- **A format rule** is what a schema does not express: a graph without cycles, references, keys, and also the rules of YAML.
  - A rule has an ID `<part>.<name>` in kebab-case, where the part is the one in which the violation is reported, and a statement with the word MUST. The ID is not reused.
  - The rule is checked by `module-kit`, and its refusal names the ID. A new rule or one stricter than before is a major version.
  - The rules of a part are listed in the [format text](../format/README.md) as a table whose first column is the ID, like the YAML rules in its part on writing a module. By the tables, `just format-check` matches the rules with their vectors.
  - `format-check` checks itself, by a second implementation beside `module-kit`, the rules of YAML, the rules of the whole module `module.*` and `manifest.format-version`, and `lesson.no-leaks`, together with the leak check: on its vectors, on the valid modules and on the module vectors of other rules.
  - The rules of the module index, `module-index.<name>`, reject the build of an index, not a module.
- **The test vectors** are normative. `format-check` computes each kind by a second implementation beside `module-kit` and compares.
  - The vectors of a rule lie in `format/vectors/rules/<ID>/`. A case is a file, and if the rule links several files, a folder laid out as a module. It passes the schema of its part and breaks only this rule; a vector of a YAML rule breaks only its YAML rule. CI of `spec` checks both, and CI of `module-kit` that the case is rejected with the rule's ID. The vectors of a rule of the index are refusals among the index vectors, `format/vectors/indexes/`, not folders of `vectors/rules/`.
  - The valid examples meet the format rules that are checked within a part too, and CI of `module-kit` runs them as well. So each rule also has cases that it lets pass. A rule between parts is checked on examples laid out as a whole module.
  - The vectors of the open view are folders `format/vectors/open-view/<part>/<case>/`: `part.yaml` — a part that passes its schema, and `open-view.yaml` — its open view. This is a kind of folder of its own, not laid out as a module. `format-check` builds the open view and compares it with the vector without regard to the order of keys. The placeholder `<id>` in the layout is a name in the form of a local ID before the extension of the last name: `tasks/<id>.yaml`; `format-check` checks the form of the name by the definition `local_id` from `common.schema.json`, not by a copy of its pattern.
  - The verdict vectors lie in `format/vectors/verdicts/<kind>/<case>.yaml`; `tools/format-check/verdicts.mjs` computes them, for a predicate only "blank" and "not in notation", since `spec` has no Starlark.
  - The leak vectors lie in `format/vectors/leaks/<case>.yaml`; `tools/format-check/leaks.mjs` computes them. They hold no templates: a leak of a template is looked for by its instances.
  - The generator vectors lie in `format/vectors/random/<case>.yaml`. The 64-bit integers in them are strings of decimal digits: a YAML number holds an integer of no more than 53 bits. `tools/format-check/random.mjs` computes them, and it is checked against the references of Go and RFC 9923.
  - The template vectors lie in `format/vectors/templates/<case>.yaml`: a template, the number of its instances, and attempts — the seed, the numbers of the instance and the instance itself. `expressions.mjs` and `templates.mjs` compute them, and `format-check` checks the rules of a task and `lesson.no-leaks`, which it implements, on each instance.
  - The tier vectors and the package vectors are decided with the module package, the index vectors with the module index.
- **The examples** are `format/examples/<term>/valid/<case>.yaml` and `…/invalid/<case>.yaml`; an example of a whole module is a folder `format/examples/module/valid/<case>/`. A valid one passes its schema. An invalid one breaks one thing and names in its first line the error it must give: `# error: <keyword> at <place>`.
  - The place is a JSON Pointer in a URI fragment: `#` is the whole file, `#/answer_slots/0` an element. It is the place where the schema with this keyword applies. For `required`, `additionalProperties`, `unevaluatedProperties` and other keywords about an object the place is the object, for keywords about an array the array, for `type`, `enum`, `const`, `pattern` and other keywords about a value the value.
  - `$ref`, `allOf`, `properties`, `items` and `if`/`then`/`else` are not named: the keyword that failed inside is named. `oneOf` and `anyOf` are named when no branch passed.
  - The check looks for this pair among all errors of the validator, not for the text of the message: validators have different texts.
  - The examples show the format and check the schemas, but add no rules.
- **The folder `format/`:** `README.md` — the format text, in English, with normative words by BCP 14 and numbered sections; `VERSION` — the version number; `schemas/`, `examples/` and `vectors/`, laid out by the [format text](../format/README.md), in its part on files.
- **The packages and the open view in the contract.** The packages for code come out of `spec`'s releases — each normative part with a version of its own as a release file `<part>-<version>.tar.gz`, the Go module `github.com/altnovatrail/spec` and the npm package `@altnovatrail/spec`. The open view goes into the contract `app` ↔ `api` as `OpenView`: the bytes of the format's JSON with `module_format_version` beside them, not protobuf messages of its own.

— *Why:* the format of the modules, the version of JSON Schema, `$id`, the mark of an open field, the error of an example, YAML and the style of names are the plan's recommendations. The rest — the rules for `$ref`, the closing of objects, `pattern`, the format rules and the vectors — is the plan's proposal after an independent review of the draft. Where the check `just format-check` needs an exact reading, the format text gives it, together with the limits of Go for `pattern`; a review of the plan's draft by an independent agent found where the draft diverged from 2020-12, from `ajv` and from Go, and this was checked against the primary sources. All sources were read 2026-10-22, unless another date is named.
- **JSON Schema 2020-12.** "The current version is 2020-12!" ([JSON Schema, Specification](https://json-schema.org/specification)). It is implemented by validators in both languages of the platform — `spec`, `canvas` and `app` are written in TypeScript, `module-kit` in Go:
  - ajv 8.20.0 under MIT: "Supports JSON Schema draft-04/06/07/2019-09/2020-12" ([ajv-validator/ajv](https://github.com/ajv-validator/ajv), README);
  - santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema 6.0.3 under Apache-2.0, whose README marks 2020-12 with a Bowtie badge ([santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema](https://github.com/santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema)).

  In draft-07 a mark beside `$ref` would be lost: "All other properties in a "$ref" object MUST be ignored" ([JSON Schema draft-07 core](https://json-schema.org/draft-07/draft-handrews-json-schema-01), §8.3). The author writes data, not API messages: JSON Schema checks the author's YAML directly and expresses enumerations, string patterns and conditions.
- **`$id`.** "Note that this URI is an identifier and not necessarily a network locator" ([JSON Schema 2020-12 core](https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/json-schema-core), §8.2.1). The address of a project on GitHub Pages is "http(s)://<owner>.github.io/<repositoryname>" ([GitHub Docs, About GitHub Pages](https://docs.github.com/en/pages/getting-started-with-github-pages/about-github-pages)): this is the organization's space, nobody else will take it. The address is hierarchical, so the references between schemas are relative, and the version number stands only in `$id`.
- **`x-open`.** "Unknown keywords SHOULD be treated as annotations, where the value of the keyword is the value of the annotation" (2020-12 core, §4.3.1). The next version of JSON Schema will not allow unknown keywords, and for user marks "the prefix `x-` has been selected" ([json-schema-spec, ADR 2023-04-sva-prefix](https://github.com/json-schema-org/json-schema-spec/blob/main/adr/2023-04-sva-prefix.md), accepted 2023-04-04). A mark in the schema itself will not diverge from the schema, as a separate list would. That it counts only where its subschema passes: "Schema objects that produce a false assertion result MUST NOT produce any annotation results" ([2020-12 core](https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/json-schema-core), §7.7.1.2, read 2026-10-26).
- **The error of an example.** The output unit of 2020-12 names the keyword and the place: "The JSON key for this information is `keywordLocation`" and likewise "`instanceLocation`" (2020-12 core, §12.3). So the comparison does not depend on the texts of messages. The whole document in a URI fragment is `#` ([RFC 6901](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6901), §6).
- **YAML.**
  - YAML 1.2 was conceived as a superset of JSON: "Its primary focus was making YAML a strict superset of JSON" ([YAML 1.2.2](https://yaml.org/spec/1.2.2/), §1.2). Keys in it are unique: "each of the keys is unique" (ibid., §3.2.1.1). The Core schema is "the recommended default schema": a plain scalar that resembles nothing it reads as a string, while the JSON schema counts such a scalar an error, and then the whole text would have to be quoted (ibid., chapter 10).
  - Parsers read the same thing differently. `go-yaml`, which the YAML organization maintains, "Supports octals encoded and decoded as `0777` per YAML 1.1, rather than `0o777` as specified in YAML 1.2" and "Supports YAML 1.1 bools (`yes`/`no`, `on`/`off`) as long as they are being decoded into a typed bool value" ([yaml/go-yaml](https://github.com/yaml/go-yaml), README, commit 32734c3), while the Core schema reads `0777` as 777. So the format leaves plain only the scalars that all read alike, and the others are quoted.
  - Characters, numbers and repeated keys follow I-JSON ([RFC 7493](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7493), §2.1–2.3):
    - strings "MUST NOT include code points that identify Surrogates or Noncharacters";
    - numbers no larger than a double allows, and integers in "[-(2**53)+1, (2**53)-1]";
    - repeated names are counted "after processing any escaped characters".

    Then Go and TypeScript get the same JSON value from a file.
- **snake_case** — as the content of standalone, which is carried over into `modules`, writes: `grade_level`, `correct_answer`, `builds_on` ([standalone@42b4408](https://github.com/mathtrail/mathtrail-standalone/tree/42b4408)). And as the fields of protobuf: "Use snake_case for field names, including extensions. Use pluralized names for repeated fields" ([Protocol Buffers Style Guide](https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/style/)). An array named by a verb without the plural: the plan's proposal.
- **The normative words** follow BCP 14: they are normative "when, and only when, they appear in all capitals" ([RFC 8174](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8174)).
- **`ajv`'s two errors:** the ban and its workarounds keep `ajv`, change no schema in force, and tell the author of a schema the cause at once. There is no release of `ajv` newer than 8.20.0 (npm, read 2026-11-04).
- **README.md names no version:** the version has one home, `format/VERSION`, and which release brought which version the format text lists among its versions.

— *Rejected:*
- protobuf for the modules too — one format for everything: the author would write the text format of protobuf or its JSON, and protobuf does not itself express enumerations, string patterns and conditions;
- draft-07: without `unevaluatedProperties` and `$defs`, and keys beside `$ref` do not act in it;
- `$id` on a domain of our own: there is no domain, and the purchase waits for О-16. If a domain appears before v1, `$id` moves to it with the next 0.y;
- `$id` as a URN: there are no relative references, and the version number would stand in every reference;
- a separate list of open fields — it is edited apart from the schema and can diverge from it;
- a JSON Schema vocabulary of our own with its own metaschema — it would have to be written and released together with the format;
- a file of expectations at the invalid examples — a second place that can diverge from the example;
- one keyword without the place — an example could fail not where it was meant to;
- YAML 1.2.2 Core without restrictions: numbers and booleans would depend on the parser, and anchors and aliases make a file not a tree;
- JSON only: without comments and multiline strings it is harder for authors to write, and `modules` already plans to write YAML;
- camelCase: standalone and `tutor` write in snake_case, and carrying the tasks over would rename every field;
- `additionalProperties: false` for closing an object — it does not see properties declared through `$ref` and `allOf`;
- the rule of "extensible" subschemas from the draft: the branches of `allOf`, the targets of `$ref` beside their own fields and the branches at a schema with its own fields are open, and the other objects closed. It let through an open object — `if`, `then` and `else` without fields of their own — and rejected a lawful one — a common base with `oneOf` —, and an edit of the base in one file pulled edits of places in others;
- a dynamic probe — an unknown field in each object of the valid examples: it sees only what is in the examples;
- the strict mode of `ajv` instead of the list of keywords;
- an integer by value: then `1e300` too would be an integer out of bounds;
- snake_case for the values of `enum` too: they hold `"0.1"`, SPDX identifiers and BCP 47 tags;
- to leave the text as it is and put what is disputed into an open question: the check and the text would say different things;
- for `ajv`'s two errors: to report them to `ajv` — not now, it is an action outside the repository; another validator of 2020-12 — a new dependency, its license to be checked, and the headers of the errors of the invalid examples would have to be checked again; to do nothing — the author of a schema would learn of the form only when their valid example failed, and not for that reason.

— *Consequence:*
- `format/README.md`; `tools/format-check/` — `schemas.mjs` and its tests, and the second implementations; `deployment/README.md` — the camelCase of its schema;
- `docs/decisions.md`;
- `CLAUDE.md` and `docs/repositories.md` name the format text and the version number, `README.md` the format text alone; `docs/repositories.md` — the vectors of the rules too;
- `docs/concepts.md` — snake_case in the schemas; the terms "open field", "format example", "test vector" and "format rule", and with them "solution" and "leak phrase", which the format text names; "open view" — at any part of a module. `docs/architecture.md` — the open view by `x-open`, YAML with restrictions and the format rules by ID.

## Module manifest and layout

**R46. A module is a folder: the manifest `manifest.yaml`, the files of its parts, `media/`, `eval/`, a required `LICENSE` and an optional `NOTICE`. The module ID is `<publisher>/<name>`, skills, tasks, traps, techniques and lessons have a local ID, and the module version is semver `X.Y.Z`. A module has one explanation language.** Normatively it is written in English in the [format text](../format/README.md), in its parts on a module and on the manifest, and in the schemas `common.schema.json` and `manifest.schema.json`; here is what was decided, why, and what was rejected.
- **Identifiers.**
  - The module ID is `<publisher>/<name>`, both in kebab-case starting with a letter: `novatrail/olympiad-math`. A publisher owns the namespace of its modules, so the module IDs of two authors will not coincide.
  - A skill, a task, a trap, a technique and a lesson are each an "entry" of the module in the format text, not an "item": an "item" is an item of a task. An entry has a local ID: kebab-case starting with a letter, no longer than 64 characters, unique within its kind inside the module. The module's files name its parts only so. A published ID of a trap, like that of a skill, never names another trap: the learner's progress counts traps by their full IDs.
  - The full ID is the module, the kind and the local ID joined by `/`: `novatrail/olympiad-math/skill/counting-gaps`. The kinds are `skill`, `task`, `trap`, `technique` and `lesson`. The learner model, the engine and progress know a part of a module by its full ID, and the module's files do not hold it.
  - An anchor skill of the shared taxonomy has the ID `core.<name>`. It is not part of a module and has no full ID: outside a module the same ID names it.
  - Neither the publisher and the name in the module ID nor a local ID is ever the name of a Windows device — `con`, `prn`, `aux`, `nul`, `com1`–`com9`, `lpt1`–`lpt9`: a local ID becomes a file name, and a module ID may become a folder path.
- **The module version** is semver `X.Y.Z`, as a quoted string, with no pre-releases and no build metadata. To allow them later is to widen the pattern, and that is a minor format version.
- **The layout.** A module is a folder, and what lies in it is set by the table of the format text: the path, the part the schema checks, and what is in the file. Each part's row comes with the decision on that part.
  - `manifest.yaml` is the manifest; `media/` holds pictures and sound.
  - `eval/` is the eval set. The format of its samples is the eval protocol, not the module format: which files of `eval/` are samples and what is in them is said by the eval protocol of the [contracts text](../contracts/README.md). A sample is every file under `eval/` whose name ends in `.json`. The layout `eval/<path>` stands, and the [format text](../format/README.md) says this in words. The eval set is not part of the package.
  - `LICENSE` is required: the text of the license the manifest names. `NOTICE` holds the license notices and is optional. Both are UTF-8 without a BOM, and their lines end with a single LF. Both go into the package byte for byte, in the device part, and the notices the licenses require stand only in `NOTICE`: comments of the module's files do not get into the package.
  - A part of which a module has one is a file in the root: `skill-graph.yaml`, `traps.yaml`, `techniques.yaml` and `solving-steps.yaml`. The solving steps and the skill graph are named by their term, and a catalog by the entries it holds, in the plural.
  - Parts of which a module has many — tasks and lessons — lie in a folder, a file for each, `tasks/<id>.yaml` and `lessons/<id>.yaml`: the file is named by its local ID and carries it in the field `id`. So the open view and the canonical view get the ID from the part itself.
  - Names are compared exactly as the folder lists them, case-sensitive. Files and folders starting with `.` are not part of the module, a folder without files holds nothing, there are no symbolic links, and the order of files carries no meaning.
  - Where the module's folder lies and what it is called, the format does not say: `modules` decides that.
- **The manifest** is `manifest.yaml` by the schema `manifest.schema.json`, and all its fields are open:
  - `module_format_version` — the format version, as a string: `"0.1"`. It stands in the root of the manifest in every format version, and the schema gives it the pattern MAJOR.MINOR, not a single value. A version the reader does not read is rejected by the rule `manifest.format-version`;
  - `id` and `version`; `title` — in the explanation language;
  - `subject` — the subject code: `mathematics`, `physics` or `writing`. `physics` is for the manifest of a third-party module, as in the physics illustration of `docs/concepts.md`. A new code is a new value of the list, that is, a minor version, and v1 will hold only the codes of the modules of the first slice;
  - `audience.age_categories` — a non-empty list without repeats of the age category codes: `under_13`, `from_13_to_consent`, `from_consent_to_18` and `adult`. The platform offers the module only to learners of these categories;
  - `audience.grades` — the grade as a label of the module; the starting point by grade comes with the difficulty bands `bands`;
  - `languages.explanation` — the explanation language, and `languages.target` — the target language, only in a language module. A language is a BCP 47 tag of the language, the script and the region, and the script and the region are optional. The case of letters is as in the registry: `en`, `zh-Hans`, `pt-BR`, `es-419`. The schema checks the form of the tag, but not that it is in the registry;
  - `authors` — a non-empty list of `{ name }`;
  - `license` — an SPDX identifier: letters, digits, `.` and `-`; the official modules have `Apache-2.0`. Whether it is in the SPDX list, the schema does not check;
  - `dependencies` — a non-empty list without repeats of the anchor skills on which the module's skills rest: exactly those that the skill graph names as prerequisites, by the rule `manifest.dependencies`;
  - the difficulty bands `bands`, with the rule `manifest.bands`, and the digit height on the crop `canvas.digit_height`; the rung templates `rung_templates`, with the rule `manifest.rung-templates`.
- **One explanation language per module** in v0. All the module's texts are in it, except the material of a language module: that is in the target language. There are no translations in format v0, and the same content in another explanation language is another module, with its own ID and its own progress. Translations later are most likely files by language on top of the module's texts. That is an addition, a minor version, and earlier modules do not change.
- **Media files** are PNG, JPEG, WebP and MP3, with one extension for each format: `.png`, `.jpg`, `.webp` and `.mp3`. A part refers to a file by its path from `media/`: names in kebab-case joined by `/` and an extension, no longer than 128 characters — `pictures/ladder.png` (`media_path` in `common.schema.json`).
- **Rules.** The rules of the whole module have the part `module`, and it has no schema of its own:
  - `module.manifest` — the module's folder has `manifest.yaml`;
  - `module.layout` — every file stands at a path of the layout table, and the module holds nothing but files and folders;
  - `module.file-ids` — a file at a path with `<id>` carries that name in the field `id`;
  - `module.media` — a file in `media/` stands at a path of the form `media_path` and begins with the signature of its format;
  - `module.license` and `module.plain-text` — of `LICENSE` and `NOTICE`.

  A module may break more than one rule — `Manifest.yaml` instead of `manifest.yaml` breaks both `module.manifest` and `module.layout` —, but each vector breaks exactly one. The rules `module.manifest`, `module.layout`, `module.file-ids` and `module.media` and the manifest's rule `manifest.format-version` `just format-check` checks itself, like the YAML rules, and it reads the layout table from the format text.
- **Examples and vectors.**
  - An example of a whole module is a folder `format/examples/module/valid/<case>/`, laid out as a module: the files with a part pass their schemas, and the module breaks no rule. There are no invalid examples of a whole module: a module that breaks a rule is a vector of that rule.
  - A vector of a rule that links files is a folder laid out as a module. A vector of a rule of the whole module breaks only that rule, and a vector of a part's rule passes the rules of the whole module and holds the file of its part.
  - The manifest in an example and a vector names the version from `format/VERSION`, except the vectors of `manifest.format-version`: they name a version outside the window of the reader of this version. One names `"0.0"`, which the format never had, the other the next minor version.
- **Common definitions** are `common.schema.json`: the format version, the module ID and version, the local ID and, on it, the ID of a skill, a task, a trap, a technique and a lesson, the language tag, the license, the age category, the subject, the media file path, and text — a non-empty string. The patterns are of the format's `pattern` subset: with classes, without `\d` and `(?:`.
- **What this entry does not decide:**
  - translations — and what they will have to cover: leak phrases, the keys of text answers, the open view, the types of `app` and `canvas`;
  - the presentation style — О-23;
  - who may publish under which publisher — the publication rules (О-9) — and which licenses third-party modules carry (О-10);
  - SPDX expressions such as `MIT OR Apache-2.0` and BCP 47 tags with variants and extensions: to widen the pattern later is a minor version.

— *Why:* the form of the ID, a module as a folder, one explanation language, the presentation style outside the manifest, and `dependencies` and `module.media` left to the decisions on the taxonomy and on tasks are the plan's recommendations. The rest — the manifest's fields, the rules and the layout of the vectors — is the plan's proposal after an independent check of the draft. All sources were read 2026-10-22.
- **A local ID, and the full ID outside the module.** A module's file does not repeat its module's ID in every reference, and renaming the module does not touch its files. The full ID is needed where parts of different modules lie side by side: in the learner model, the engine and progress.
- **A folder, not one file.** The olympiad maths module has 603 tasks ([standalone@42b4408](https://github.com/mathtrail/mathtrail-standalone/tree/42b4408)). In one file an edit of a task is an edit of the whole module, and in a folder of one file, and a pull request of `modules` shows it separately. A file per task, not per topic as in standalone ([standalone@42b4408](https://github.com/mathtrail/mathtrail-standalone/tree/42b4408)): a topic is a label of the task, and a task that changes its topic does not move.
- **The format version as a pattern.** A single value, `const`, would reject the manifests of the earlier version already in the schema of the next minor version, though a minor version only adds. A refusal by version is a rule with its own vectors, and the reader names its ID.
- **The case of language tags.** BCP 47 compares tags without case: "language tags and their subtags, including private use and extensions, are to be treated as case insensitive", but "The format of subtags in the registry is RECOMMENDED as the form to use in language tags" ([RFC 5646](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5646), §2.1.1). The format takes the registry's form, and one tag is always written as one string.
- **semver:** "A normal version number MUST take the form X.Y.Z where X, Y, and Z are non-negative integers, and MUST NOT contain leading zeroes" ([Semantic Versioning 2.0.0](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html), item 2). The regular expression of its FAQ writes `\d` and `(?:`, which the format's `pattern` subset lacks, so the pattern is written with classes.
- **SPDX.** An identifier is "idstring = 1*(ALPHA / DIGIT / "-" / "." )" ([SPDX License Expressions](https://spdx.github.io/spdx-spec/v3.0.1/annexes/spdx-license-expressions/)); the list is SPDX License List 3.29.0 of 2026-09-16 ([spdx.org/licenses](https://spdx.org/licenses/)).
- **The media formats** are those every browser shows ([MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/), mdn/content, `main` 8bc3252):
  - PNG, JPEG and WebP — "All versions of Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Opera, and Safari" ([Image file type and format guide](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Media/Guides/Formats/Image_types));
  - MP3 — "MP3 (MPEG-1 Audio Layer III) is supported by all major browsers" ([Web audio codec guide](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Media/Guides/Formats/Audio_codecs)).
- **The names of Windows devices** — "Do not use the following reserved names for the name of a file: CON, PRN, AUX, NUL, COM1, …, LPT9 … Also avoid these names followed immediately by an extension; for example, NUL.txt and NUL.tar.gz are both equivalent to NUL", and also "Do not assume case sensitivity" ([Microsoft, Naming Files, Paths, and Namespaces](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/naming-a-file), revision of 2024-08-28). Hence IDs and names in lowercase only, and names compared by the folder's listing.
- **`NOTICE`** is for the notices that licenses require to be kept. Apache-2.0: "If the Work includes a "NOTICE" text file as part of its distribution, then any Derivative Works that You distribute must include a readable copy of the attribution notices contained within such NOTICE file" ([Apache License 2.0](https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0), section 4(d)), and the recipient gets a copy of the license too: "You must give any other recipients of the Work or Derivative Works a copy of this License" ([Apache License 2.0](https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0), section 4(a)). MIT: "The above copyright notice and this permission notice shall be included in all copies or substantial portions of the Software" ([MIT License](https://opensource.org/license/mit)). standalone's tasks are under MIT, and whether to keep their notice or to re-release the content under Apache-2.0, `modules` decides.

— *Rejected:*
- full IDs in the module's files, as in the illustrations of `docs/concepts.md`: every reference would repeat the module's ID;
- IDs in standalone's styles — `logic.knights_liars`, `off_by_one`, `cal-12-d1-1` ([standalone@42b4408](https://github.com/mathtrail/mathtrail-standalone/tree/42b4408)): an ID becomes a file name, and one style is needed. Carrying over standalone's IDs — `.` and `_` into `-`, with a check for collisions — is the work of `modules`;
- a module as one file and tasks in groups by topic, as in standalone;
- translations in the module at once: what they are to cover is not decided, and to add them later is a minor version;
- the presentation style in the manifest: there is no list of styles either in the documents or in the components, and a field without a list would fix only a name (О-23);
- `dependencies` in a temporary form: the form of the ID of the taxonomy's dictionary was still to be decided, and an edit of the temporary form would be breaking;
- `const` for the format version — the argument above;
- SVG: it is code that the browser draws, and the ban on scripts in it is "For security purposes, some browsers place restrictions on SVG content when it's being used as an image. Specifically, the following limitations may apply: JavaScript is disabled" ([MDN, SVG as an image](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/SVG/Guides/SVG_as_an_image)): "some" and "may" are no promise;
- AVIF: "As support is not yet comprehensive (and has little historical depth) you should provide a fallback in WebP, JPEG or PNG format" (MDN, Image file type and format guide);
- Opus and Vorbis in Ogg: "Safari 18.4+ (on macOS 15.4+, iOS 18.4+, iPadOS 18.4+, and visionOS 2.4+) added support for Opus and Vorbis codecs in Ogg containers" ([MDN, Media container formats](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Media/Guides/Formats/Containers)) — devices older than that will not play them;
- `.jpeg` beside `.jpg`: two extensions of one format would give one file two names;
- SPDX expressions now: О-10 is open, and one license is enough for the official modules.

— *Consequence:* `docs/concepts.md` — the module ID, the local ID, the full ID, the module layout, the subject, the audience, the explanation language, the target language, the license notices, the age category codes and the field `module_format_version`; `docs/product.md` — О-23; `docs/architecture.md` — what is inside the module's folder; `docs/decisions.md`; `format/README.md`; the schemas `common.schema.json` and `manifest.schema.json`.

## AI providers and age

**R47. Google's generative AI is closed on the platform — the Gemini API, Vertex AI and, on the device, the Prompt API in Chrome: for all learners on both AI routes, for the other parts of the platform, and in a separate deployment for adults only too. It is returned to if a product for adults only appears.**
- **What the terms say.** Google Cloud's Service Specific Terms, section "20. Generative AI Services", item "d. Age Restrictions": "Customer will not, and will not allow End Users to, use a Generative AI Service as part of a website, Customer Application, or other online service that is directed towards or is likely to be accessed by individuals under the age of 18". Item "f. Suspected Violations": "Google may immediately suspend or terminate Customer's use of a Generative AI Service based on any suspected violation of … subsection (d) above" — a reference to another item of the same terms is left out ([Google Cloud Service Specific Terms](https://cloud.google.com/terms/service-terms), "Last modified November 18, 2026"; sources 2.1).
- **Vertex AI is generative AI of these terms.** Among the Generative AI Services is "Generative AI on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (formerly Generative AI on Vertex AI)", and also "Generative AI Services also includes any generative AI features or functionality of a Service" ([Google Cloud Platform Services Summary](https://cloud.google.com/terms/services), "Last modified October 30, 2026"; sources 2.1).
- **What follows from it** is our conclusion, not a legal one. The condition concerns the service as a whole, as for the Gemini API in the AI Studio variant, and NovaTrail is open to children: a learner is of any age. So Google's models are closed for all learners, adults too — both through platform AI and with an own key: with an own key the key's owner accepts the terms, but the service in which the call runs is still NovaTrail.
- **Not only learners.** The condition speaks of the service, not of who calls the model. So a part of the platform that serves not learners — for example, the authors' pipeline of stage 4 — takes no Google models either: it goes to AI providers through `tutor`.
- **On the device too.** The Prompt API in Chrome — Google's generative AI on the device, Gemini Nano — is closed by this decision; a model that reads the work on the device is `tutor`'s own code, admitted by its eval. On Chrome's pages about this API `tutor` found no age terms, and it did not read Google's general terms, to which their footer refers. For the same model on Android, the [ML Kit GenAI terms](https://developers.google.com/ml-kit/genai-terms) say: "You must be 18 years of age or older to use the APIs" (read by `tutor` 2026-10-25). Besides, `tutor` found that this API has no tablets and no Russian.
- **A deployment for adults only.** "Until a lawyer answers otherwise" is read as every legal question of a platform without a lawyer — decided on Claude's analysis of the primary sources —, and the answer is that Google's models stay closed in a separate deployment or service for adults only too. It would do only as a truly separate service, and Google may stop a service on a mere suspicion. Return if a product for adults only appears.
- The rule "The providers' rules about age are kept" does not change: this entry applies it. Without Google the platform keeps OpenAI and Anthropic: no other provider's terms on age have been checked yet.

— *Why:*
- Vertex AI and the Gemini API: item (d) binds Vertex AI too — it is in the Service Specific Terms, and with the same text it stood already in the revision of 2024-07-18: `tutor` checked it by the archive of the terms 2026-10-21. The study "A child's handwriting on the canvas and the AI tutor" («Рукопись ребёнка на канве и ИИ-наставник»), by its own reading, also not a legal one, comes to the same. And item (f) lets Google stop the service on a mere suspicion: a platform that kept learners on Google's models would risk this AI route as a whole. The item "Not only learners" is the executor's proposal, by the same reading of the condition.
- The Prompt API: this is Google's generative AI in a service open to children, and the terms of the same model require 18 years.
- A deployment for adults only (sources 2.5). Read 2026-11-09: [Gemini API Additional Terms](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/terms) — a redirect to the [Google AI Studio terms](https://aistudio.google.com/docs/terms), "Effective March 23, 2026" — the text on age is unchanged since 2026-10-18, and beyond it — "Use of Google AI Studio and Gemini API is for developers building with Google AI models for professional or business purposes, not for consumer use"; [Service Specific Terms](https://cloud.google.com/terms/service-terms), "Last modified October 30, 2026", in "20. Generative AI Services": "d. Age Restrictions" is the same, and "f. Suspected Violations" is "Google may immediately suspend or terminate Customer's use of a Generative AI Service based on any suspected violation of `Section 17(b)` or subsection (d) above"; [Google Cloud Platform Terms of Service](https://cloud.google.com/terms), "Last modified October 12, 2026": ""Customer Application" means a software program that Customer creates or hosts using the GCP Services", and para. 3.3(d)(iii) forbids "creating multiple Customer Applications, Accounts, or Projects to simulate or act as a single Customer Application, Account, or Project". Each text judges a separate site, application or service, and "likely to be accessed" is defined nowhere.

— *Rejected:*
- Google's models in a separate deployment for adults: by the study's reading the ban concerns a platform open to children as a whole;
- allowing Google's models in a deployment for adults on conditions — its own project, domain, accounts and build — and with a second admission table for it: a deployment with shared code, content and modules is easily held to be one service, and a suspension on suspicion would close it too;
- asking Google for an exception, and leaving the route open until the answer: the answer would come when learners' data had already gone;
- closing Google only to learners and leaving it to the other parts of the platform: the condition is about the service, and they are parts of the same NovaTrail;
- leaving the Prompt API open until Chrome's terms are checked: the terms of the same model on Android require 18 years, and the route would open to children at once.

— *Consequence:* `docs/privacy.md`; `docs/product.md`; `docs/architecture.md`; the admission table, `admission/`.

## Status badges

**R48. The README of every repository carries MathTrail's status badges — up to 14 in two rows, and a badge stands only when what it speaks of exists. Coverage goes to Codecov by OIDC, without a secret, and `codecov/patch` ≥ 90 % holds the merge; OpenSSF Best Practices comes first at `spec`, and its answers to the criteria are the file `.bestpractices.json` in the repository's root, in English: the site proposes them in its form, and the author saves them.**
- **The set** is as at mathtrail-standalone ([standalone@42b4408](https://github.com/mathtrail/mathtrail-standalone/tree/42b4408)) and canvas-api ([canvas-api@0901af0](https://github.com/mathtrail/canvas-api/tree/0901af0)). The first row is CI, Release, CodeQL, the release number, the language, coverage, OpenSSF Best Practices, OpenSSF Scorecard and the license; the second is the five measures of SonarCloud: code smells, reliability, security, maintainability and vulnerabilities. The addresses, the captions and when which badge appears are in `docs/repositories.md`.
- **A badge stands only when what it speaks of exists**: no "no releases", no "not found", no "unknown".
  - From day one, from the template: CI, CodeQL, Scorecard, the license and SonarCloud's measures. In all 13 repositories they work already now. A new repository gets their answers when it is set up to the end: with the shared checks, a SonarCloud project and the first run of Scorecard.
  - Release and the release number come with the first release, the language with the first code, coverage with the first upload to Codecov, Best Practices with the passing level.
  - These badges are put up by the repository's own session, as is what code adds to the CI files.
- **Coverage goes to Codecov by OIDC, without a secret:** "Any token supplied will be ignored, as Codecov will default to the OIDC token for verification. Note that the codecov action must have write permission for `id-token` for this to work" ([codecov/codecov-action, README](https://github.com/codecov/codecov-action/blob/v7.1.1/README.md), tag v7.1.1). Only the upload jobs get the permission `id-token: write`.
  - **A pull request from a fork** does not get this permission and does not ask for OIDC. Action v7.1.1 recognizes a fork by `head.repo.full_name` and sends the report without a token from the branch `owner:branch` (`action.yml`, the steps "Set fork" and "Override branch for forks"), and Codecov accepts it for a public repository: "Codecov should work smoothly on pull requests from forks out of the box", and "the repository is public **and** the upload is for a commit that is on an "unprotected" branch (like `forkname:main`)" ([Codecov Tokens](https://docs.codecov.com/docs/codecov-tokens)). The route was tried 2026-10-23, on the author's words «делай сам всё, что можешь»: for the draft pull request #44 from a fork the job "Coverage" sent the report without a token, and `codecov/patch` came from the Codecov app.
  - An upload for `main` without OIDC Codecov will not accept if the organization's settings turn on the token requirement: "For public repositories, a token is required if the upload is for a commit on a protected branch and the repository owner has not disabled token authentication for public repositories". The author turns it on: a new organization by default has "new organizations will start with tokens Not required" (ibid.).
  - **Dependabot.** GitHub writes both that its runs "are treated as if they were opened from a repository fork" and get a read-only token, and that "You can use the `permissions` key in your workflow to increase the access for the token" ([GitHub Docs, Troubleshooting Dependabot on GitHub Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/reference/supply-chain-security/troubleshoot-dependabot/dependabot-on-actions)). The changelog of 2021-10-06 says that such runs "will begin to respect the permissions specified in your workflows" ([GitHub Changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2021-10-06-github-actions-workflows-triggered-by-dependabot-prs-will-respect-permissions-key-in-workflows/)). And the page of the workflow syntax does not name this exception: "Workflow runs triggered by Dependabot pull requests run as if they are from a forked repository, and therefore use a read-only `GITHUB_TOKEN`" ([GitHub Docs, Workflow syntax](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax#permissions-for-workflow-runs-triggered-by-dependabot)). Of `id-token` nothing is said anywhere. So `codecov/patch` became required only once the first Dependabot pull requests got an OIDC token and it came on them. Should one not get it, the action's step that asks for the token fails, and the author chooses between a Dependabot secret at `spec` only and a check of its own of the changed lines in CI.
- **The CLI by its own sum,** as an archive that the Dockerfile downloads. The action would verify the CLI with a GPG key that it takes from Keybase during the run and whose fingerprint it does not check (`dist/codecov.sh` v7.1.1, lines 128–161). A substitution on both cli.codecov.io and the Keybase account at once such a check would not catch.
  - The job "Coverage" downloads CLI v11.3.1 itself and checks the sha256 pinned in `ci.yml`. The action gets the ready file through the input `binary` and downloads nothing.
  - The executor checked the sum once: the file of sums is signed by a key with the fingerprint `2703 4E7F DB85 0E0B BC2C 62FF 806B B28A ED77 9869` — the one the page [Codecov Uploader](https://docs.codecov.com/docs/codecov-uploader) names: "Key Fingerprint: `2703 4E7F DB85 0E0B BC2C 62FF 806B B28A ED77 9869`".
  - The version and the sum are raised by hand, together: Dependabot moves only the action's SHA.
  - **The CLI's plugins are off**, the input `plugins: noop`. By default the CLI runs `xcode`, `gcov` and `pycoverage` (`codecov_cli/commands/upload.py`, v11.3.1), and the upload job runs nothing but the upload.
- **Two uploads per commit, the status after both.** The job "Coverage" of `ci.yml` sends the lcov of `tools/`, and the job `coverage` of the shared `go.yml` of `.github`, "Go / coverage", sends the Go profile. `.github/codecov.yml` sets `codecov.notify.after_n_builds: 2`: "How many uploaded reports Codecov should wait to receive before sending statuses", by default 1 ([Codecov, codecov.yml reference](https://docs.codecov.com/docs/codecovyml-reference), read 2026-11-04). With one, `codecov/patch` would come by whichever upload came first — by half of the changed lines.
  - **The tests of `tools/` run in three parts**, a job each, "Tests (<k>/3)": `just coverage-part <k> 3` runs the test files that `node --test --test-shard=<k>/3` gives — every third, whole files ([`--test-shard`](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/v24.21.0/doc/api/cli.md#--test-shard) of Node.js 24.21.0) — and writes their lcov report, and the job "Coverage" sends the three reports in one upload, which Codecov merges, so `after_n_builds` stays 2 (`do_upload_logic` of [codecov-cli v11.3.2](https://github.com/codecov/codecov-cli/blob/2f5121284e3c7c3c2b691a09cb0ea135d226f112/codecov_cli/services/upload/__init__.py) sends one upload of every file it is given; Codecov's [Merging Reports](https://docs.codecov.com/docs/merging-reports)).
  - **A module that no test loads** does not get into Node's report, and `codecov/patch` does not see its lines. The guard asks of the three reports together, by `tools/coverage/untested.sh`, in the job "Documents and tools".
  - **The Go report** is the profile of `go test -coverprofile`, `coverage/go.out`, written by `ci-test` for all of `spec`'s Go modules as one profile with one line `mode: atomic`: the contract of `ci-test` of the wrappers of `.github`, the report in `coverage/`, for Go a profile. "Go / test" runs the Go tests, and "Go / coverage" sends their profile; the job of `tools/` runs none. A package without tests Go 1.27 puts into the profile itself, with zeros — checked with a trial module 2026-11-01 —, so Go needs no guard; `types/` has not a single statement: only types and constants.
  - **Paths.** The profile names a file by its import path, `github.com/altnovatrail/spec/tools/gomod/main.go`. Codecov turns it into the path in the repository itself, by the default rule `((.+/src/)?github\.com/[^\/\n]+/[^\/\n]+/)` — "Golang specific rule to strip out the github portion of a file path" ([Codecov, Fixing paths](https://docs.codecov.com/docs/fixing-paths), updated 2025-11-11, read 2026-11-01). There are no `fixes` of its own in `codecov.yml`.
  - **`just coverage`** runs every test of `tools/` at once, then the guard, then `ci-test`.
- **`codecov/patch` holds the merge:** the changed lines are covered at least 90 %, as at standalone ([standalone@42b4408](https://github.com/mathtrail/mathtrail-standalone/tree/42b4408)). It is a required check of the ruleset of every repository whose coverage goes to Codecov.
