  - **`codecov/project` does not come.** On the plan that Codecov gives a public repository there is no coverage status of the whole project: "The Team Plan shows Patch ONLY coverage" ([Codecov, Pricing](https://about.codecov.io/pricing/)), and the free plan `users-developer` in the plan data of Codecov's server is of the same tier, `team` ([codecov/umbrella](https://github.com/codecov/umbrella), `main` c6a2a28, `apps/codecov-api/core/management/commands/codecovPlans-Jan25.csv` and `codecovTiers-Jan25.csv`). standalone's `codecov.yml` sets it, but neither pull request #144 nor `main` c6cbeb2 has it (GitHub's API). `spec`'s `codecov.yml` still makes it informational only — in case Codecov sets it. The coverage of all the code is shown by the badge.
  - **Without changed lines** in the report, `codecov/patch` is success "Coverage not affected". So Codecov's server sets it (ibid., `apps/worker/services/notification/notifiers/mixins/status.py`), and so it came for standalone's pull request #144, where only `.md` files changed. A pull request of `spec` with documents alone passes.
  - **The cost:** no upload means no status, and the merge waits. A Codecov failure turns the job "Coverage" on the pull request red, and it is rerun. A run in which one of the two uploads did not come — a check before it failed — gets no `codecov/patch`; the merge is held by the red check anyway, and a Codecov failure held it with one upload too.
- **OpenSSF Best Practices.** The project on bestpractices.dev is set up by the author, signing in through GitHub. First `spec`, project 15977, then every repository with code and automated tests: without them the passing level cannot be had (run/DEBT.md, Д34).
  - The criterion `test` — "The project MUST use at least one automated test suite that is publicly released as FLOSS", of the category MUST and without "N/A" ([best-practices-badge](https://github.com/ossf/best-practices-badge), `criteria/criteria.yml` and `config/locales/en.yml`, `main` e4c99b5).
  - The badge is by the project's ID: "We recommend individual projects use the id-based interface listed above" (ibid., `docs/api.md`).
  - **The project is set up by entering the address.** The list "Select a GitHub repository (optional)" has no repositories of `altnovatrail`. The site takes 50 public repositories of the user by the token of its OAuth app (`projects_controller.rb`, `repo_data`), and for a new organization GitHub restricts such apps itself: "When you create a new organization, OAuth app access restrictions are enabled by default" ([GitHub Docs, About OAuth app access restrictions](https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/managing-oauth-access-to-your-organizations-data/about-oauth-app-access-restrictions)). What is public it reads anyway: "If the organization does not approve the application, then the application will only be able to access the organization's public resources" ([GitHub Docs, Authorizing OAuth apps](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/oauth-apps/using-oauth-apps/authorizing-oauth-apps)) — that is why the file was read. Both pages of GitHub Docs were read 2026-10-26. The addresses of the repository and of the home page the author enters into the fields by hand. The author does not approve the app in `altnovatrail`: it gives the badge nothing, and the site would get the permission `read:org` over the organization (`config/initializers/omniauth.rb`).
- **`.bestpractices.json`.** The site's code was read 2026-10-26 and 2026-10-27 in ossf/best-practices-badge on the branch `production`, 2ea9de2: the site runs from it.
  - **The site reads the file itself:** "If a project repository has either a `.bestpractices.json` file at its top level or a `.project.d/bestpractices.json` file, that information is used to fill in proposed answers" (`docs/bestpractices-json.md`). The keys are `<criterion>_status` ("Met", "Unmet" or "N/A") and `<criterion>_justification` (`app/lib/repo_json_detective.rb`). This is a proposal, not an answer: the confidence of an answer from the file is 3.5, and automation overrides a person's answer only from 4 — "Below CONFIDENCE_OVERRIDE, automation only fills blank/unknown fields" (`app/lib/chief.rb`). The author saves the answers.
  - **So it went at project 15977.** All 67 statuses of the file are saved. Justifications from the file — 63; for `floss_license`, `floss_license_osi`, `repo_track` and `repo_distributed` the site, as expected, wrote its own. That the answers came from the file, and not from the links with answers that the executor gave the author besides, is seen by `repo_public`, `discussion` and `contribution`: they keep the file's justifications. Without the file they would have kept the site's own texts: its GitHub detector proposes them with confidence 3 and 2 (`app/lib/github_basic_detective.rb`), and of two proposals the more confident wins — the file has 3.5 (`app/lib/chief.rb`, `merge_changeset`). A justification that already exists a link with answers does not change: "Justification fields: silently skip (many valid wordings)" (`app/controllers/projects_controller.rb`, `classify_non_status_pass`).
  - **Language and place.** Outside `docs/` everything is in English, and the site's form is English anyway. The answers are read also by a visitor of the project's page who does not read Russian.
  - **What is in the file** is the status and the justification of each of the 67 criteria of the passing level: 43 MUST, 10 SHOULD and 14 SUGGESTED (`criteria/criteria.yml`). A reader of the site does not know the R numbers, so a justification leads by a link to a file, and names the decision in words. The answers about cryptography name the SHA-256 that `format-check` computes of the package's digests through `node:crypto`, and the check of a release file's signature by the recipe `release-verify`, through sigstore-js, among the cryptography the project calls. The answers on how to obtain spec, contribute and run the checks — `interact`, `documentation_basics`, `documentation_interface` and `test` — name [docs/README.md](README.md), where contributing is told: the README is a description alone, with the badges at its head.
  - **The file is kept current.** An edit that changes an answer changes the file too, in the same pull request; the first fuzz test, for one, changes `dynamic_analysis`. The site does not take a changed answer from the file: automation changes a saved answer only with confidence from 4 (`chief.rb`, `update_value?`), and the file has 3.5; "Save (and continue)" shows the new status with the sign "≠" and does not apply it, and a new justification with the same status it does not show at all (`classify_non_status_pass`, ibid.). So the session builds from the file a link with answers — the changed fields and `overrides` for them: "To force proposals, add `overrides=` followed by a comma-separated sequence of globs to force" (`docs/automation-proposals.md`). If a status changed, `overrides` names it, and the justification goes with it: "When a status field is forced via `overrides`, its paired justification field is also forced automatically" (ibid.). If only a justification changed, `overrides` names the justification itself, and the site applies it (`projects_controller.rb`, `apply_url_proposals`). The author opens the link, checks the fields the site highlighted in orange, and saves. What is saved on the site is given by `https://www.bestpractices.dev/projects/<ID>.json`.
  - **The rule on tests** is in RULES.md: code comes with its tests, and where coverage goes to Codecov, the merge waits for `codecov/patch`. So `test_policy` gets the rule in words, and `tests_documented_added` through the CONTRIBUTING of `.github`, which leads to RULES.md. The rule was held before too by `codecov/patch` in the ruleset of `main`, but it was written in words nowhere.
  - **The site's terms.** Free: "Projects can voluntarily self-certify, at no cost" (`config/locales/en.yml`). Answers sent to the site come out under CDLA-Permissive-2.0: "By submitting this data about the project you agree to release it under at least the Community Data License Agreement – Permissive, Version 2.0", and "You retain copyright (if any), and the project license is unaffected" (ibid.). In the repository the file is under Apache-2.0, like everything.
  - **The other repositories** start their file from `spec`'s file and edit it for themselves, as the site itself advises: "Edit the result to record just what's true, and put it in your other project" (`docs/bestpractices-json.md`).
- **The services.**
  - shields.io draws the release number, the language and the license, and through it the Scorecard badge too. "Shields.io is non-tracking and privacy-respecting", "We do not store any logs of your visits, requests, or other activities on our site" ([Privacy Policy](https://shields.io/privacy)). It requires nothing of the repository's owner.
  - Codecov: "Codecov will always be free for open source projects" ([Codecov for open source](https://about.codecov.io/for/open-source/)), and "If you are a GitHub user you MUST install the Codecov GitHub app for your organization - Codecov can't function without it" ([Quick Start](https://docs.codecov.com/docs/quick-start)). An upload carries the report and the paths of all the repository's files: its CLI takes them from `git ls-files` (codecov-cli v11.3.1). There are no learners' data in the repositories, and all NovaTrail repositories are public.
  - The reader's browser takes the badge's picture not from the service but from GitHub's proxy: "Camo generates an anonymous URL proxy for each file which hides your browser details and related information from other users" ([GitHub Docs, About anonymized URLs](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/keeping-your-account-and-data-secure/about-anonymized-urls)).
- **Named as exceptions of the license rule** are the CI tools that ship nowhere:
  - `codecov/codecov-action` — MIT;
  - the CLI that the job "Coverage" downloads itself and checks by the pinned sha256, `codecov/codecov-cli` — Apache-2.0 (GitHub's API, the repositories' licenses);
  - Codecov itself — a service on terms that are free for open source.

  NovaTrail does not distribute them, and is built, run and deployed without them. The CLI's telemetry is turned off by the action's input `disable_telem`.

All was read 2026-10-23 unless said.

— *Why:*
- The set is that of the README of mathtrail-standalone. OIDC, the 90 % threshold and Best Practices at `spec` now are the plan's options. OIDC because the shared workflows of `.github` take no secrets, and OIDC has no token that would be stored and could leak. A badge of what does not exist yet would show an error.
- The CLI by its own sum: the pinned sha256 catches a substitution that the action's check by a key from Keybase misses.
- `.bestpractices.json`: the file is one English text that the site reads itself, so the author carries no answers into the form by hand, and no second text diverges from it.
- Three parts of the tests of `tools/`: for the speed of CI; three parts, the number of jobs, and the Go tests out of the job of `tools/` are the executor's choice. The step Tests took 425 s of the 556 s of its job, about 9 minutes of a processor (measurements 3.1). The checks that read the documents keep what they parsed in the process, by the sha256 of the text, and the tests of `format-check`, `admission-check` and `new-repo` take a fraction of the time (measurements 3.2); the parts then run on three runners side by side. Three parts, not two: a part is bounded by its longest file — the tests of `contracts-check`, which run `buf` and `go`, then those of `format-check` —, and on 2026-11-16 two parts put both in one, while three put them apart (measurements 3.2). The Go tests: their run in the job of `tools/` sent nothing to Codecov.

— *Rejected:*
- a row only of the services that exist already; a README without badges;
- the secret `CODECOV_TOKEN`, as at standalone and canvas-api: a shared workflow would take a secret, which shared workflows do not, and a copy of the token would live in the secrets of every repository and of Dependabot;
- an upload without a token for all: no permissions need changing, but anyone could send a report for `main`;
- `codecov/patch` for information only: standalone's threshold would then hold no merge;
- the action's own check of the CLI, by the GPG key from Keybase;
- both uploads of the Go profile — its own and "Go / coverage": `spec` would send the same profile twice, and `after_n_builds` would have to count three;
- `just coverage` without the Go tests: it would stop running all tests at once, as CLAUDE.md and the README call it, and a run of the Go tests with `-race` costs about ten seconds;
- the guard in each part — a module that one part alone loads would fail the others; one lcov file joined of the three — Codecov's documentation says it merges reports, uploaded at once or apart ([Merging Reports](https://docs.codecov.com/docs/merging-reports)), not how it reads one file that names a source file three times; an aggregator job in the toolchain image — a second load of the image on the way to the required check, for git, sed and comm;
- Best Practices at all 13 at once — at repositories without code the badge would not appear while there are no tests — or at none yet;
- English Markdown outside `docs/`, like standalone's `docs/openssf-best-practices.md`: the author would carry 67 answers into the form by hand at every edit;
- a Russian `docs/openssf-best-practices.md`, as at canvas-api: the English text of the form would live separately, and the two texts would diverge; both files at once are two copies;
- a check of `.bestpractices.json` in CI: the site shows a missing criterion with the sign "?", and the author checks every section when saving — the plan's proposal;
- SonarCloud from CI for the sake of coverage, as at standalone ([standalone@42b4408](https://github.com/mathtrail/mathtrail-standalone/tree/42b4408)): it needs `SONAR_TOKEN`, and the automatic analysis is enough for the five measures of the set.

— *Consequence:* `docs/repositories.md`; `docs/architecture.md`; `docs/decisions.md`; the README of `spec` and of the template; `docs/README.md`; `CLAUDE.md`; `RULES.md`; `.bestpractices.json`; `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, `.github/codecov.yml`, the justfile, `tools/coverage/untested.sh`; `.claude/rules/ci.md`; `run/DEBT.md`, Д34.

## Skill graph

**R49. The skill graph is the file `skill-graph.yaml`: the module's skills are a dictionary by local ID, with a title, a description, prerequisites and assessability. The tier is computed from the graph, and the author gives the tiers names. The mapping table is `retired_skills`, in a comparison of versions a withdrawn version counts as published, and the grade is the label `audience.grades` in the manifest.** Normatively it is written in English in the [format text](../format/README.md), in its parts on the manifest and the skill graph, and in the schemas `skill-graph.schema.json` and `manifest.schema.json`; here is what was decided, why, and what was rejected.
- **The skill graph** is `skill-graph.yaml` by the schema `skill-graph.schema.json`.
  - `skills` — the module's skills under their local IDs: `title`, an optional `description`, `prerequisites`, `assessability` and, for a skill that teaches an anchor skill of the shared taxonomy, `teaches`. A prerequisite is a skill of the module by its local ID or an anchor skill by its own ID, and all are needed: "to take on B, you need A".
  - A module has one graph or none, and a module without a graph is without skills.
  - Rules: `skill-graph.acyclic` — prerequisites make no cycle, and a skill that names itself as a prerequisite is a cycle too; `skill-graph.known-skills` — a local ID among the prerequisites and a skill in `replaced_by` are skills of the module, while an anchor skill that is not in the dictionary is rejected by the schema; `skill-graph.retired-ids` — the ID of a retired skill does not name a skill of the module; and `skill-graph.own-anchors`, of anchor skills. `module-kit` checks them, and `spec`'s CI checks the YAML and the schema of their vectors.
  - `tiers` and `skills` with all the skill's fields are open: by them the app draws the skill map. `retired_skills` is closed: it lies in the server part, like the whole canonical view, and the server transfers progress.
- **The tier** is computed from the graph and is not written in the module. A skill without prerequisites among the module's skills has tier 1, the others 1 above the highest tier of their prerequisites in the module; anchor skills do not count toward it. So the tier is the number of skills in the longest chain of prerequisites that ends in the skill, and a prerequisite always stands a tier lower. There is no limit on the number of tiers. `module-kit` computes the tiers when it builds the package and puts each skill's tier into the package's canonical view, `skill_tiers`; the tier vectors lie in `format/vectors/tiers/`. The tiers come with the open view of the skill graph, which `PackageService` gives by the digest of any package of `api`'s image, so a connected module has its tiers before the first attempt.
  - Names for the tiers are an optional list `tiers` in the explanation language: the first name is tier 1's. A tier without a name is shown by its number, and a name past the last tier names nothing.
- **A skill's assessability** is one of three: `verdict` — the skill's tasks are checked by a key or a predicate, and their verdicts are evidence for the learner model; `rubric` — on the skill the learner gets feedback by a rubric, without a verdict; `none` — the skill is trained but not assessed. The engine adapts to the learner only for a skill with `verdict`. Whether it matches how the items are checked is the format rule `task.assessability`: the primary skill of an item with a key or a predicate is `verdict`, of an item with a rubric `rubric`, and a skill `none` is only ever supporting.
- **The order of lessons** is set by the prerequisites too. Lesson A goes after lesson B when a skill of A needs, through the module's prerequisites, a skill of B that is not among the skills of A, and this order has no cycle (`lesson.order`). For skills with `rubric` and `none`, "the order is set by the author" means the order of the graph and of the lesson's segments, and where the graph gives no order, a rule of the engine chooses without the learner model.
- **Retired skills are a mapping table.** A published ID of a skill does not name another skill, and a skill whose meaning changed gets a new ID: a change of meaning cannot be seen from the module. `retired_skills` are the skills of earlier versions that the module no longer has, under their earlier IDs, and each has `replaced_by`, the skills of this version that replaced it:
  - a renamed one has one skill, a split one several, and merged ones each name the same one;
  - `[]` — nobody replaced it, and the progress in it passes to no skill;
  - if a skill from `replaced_by` is later retired itself, the record names its replacement instead;
  - the evidence of a retired skill goes to each skill that replaced it, and with what weight `learner-model` decides;
  - the record stays in all the following versions, so that progress of any age passes over. To retire a skill is a major change of the module.

  That each skill of the earlier version stayed in the module or was retired, and that no entry has gone, is seen only by comparing two versions: by `diff` of `module-kit`, by the format's rules of comparing versions. `diff` compares the new version with the package of each published version, across a format change too, and the `replaced_by` of a record of `retired_skills` is only unfolded between versions. A new meaning is a new ID for a task, a lesson and a technique too, not only for a skill.
- **A withdrawn version is a published one in a comparison**: withdrawal from the module index does not free its skill IDs. No version names another skill by its ID, a version above it by semver names each of its skills in `skills` or `retired_skills`, and a fix of a withdrawn version stands above it by semver. "An earlier version" in the [format text](../format/README.md) is a version lower by semver, withdrawn ones too, not one that came out earlier.
- **The grade** is the module's label `audience.grades`: school grades from 1 to 12, as the module's author counts them; the platform does not convert one country's grades into another's. A module with grades asks the learner's grade, and the answer may be outside the list. Unlike the age categories, the grade closes nothing: a skill opens by its prerequisites. The starting point by grade is the difficulty band to which the manifest assigns the grade: a learner of a grade begins in the band whose `grades` name it, like `Start(grade)` in standalone; where a learner outside the bands begins and how far apart the bands stand, `learner-model` decides. There is no grade 0 and no grades above 12 in version 0.1: to add them later is a minor version.

— *Why:* a dictionary of skills instead of a list with `id`, the rule `retired-ids`, a name past the last tier, an optional graph, `minItems` and `minProperties` are the plan's proposal after an independent agent checked the draft. All was read 2026-10-26.
- **The tier is computed** — as in standalone: "a topic's layer is the longest chain of bases below it — 0 the foundations, 1 the rules, 2 the hard problems — computed rather than drawn" ([SPEC.md](https://github.com/mathtrail/mathtrail-standalone/blob/c6cbeb2/SPEC.md), section 8.12.2, line 1706; commit c6cbeb2). standalone's decision log rejects tiers that the author types: "layers typed by hand, which drift from the links" ([docs/decisions.md](https://github.com/mathtrail/mathtrail-standalone/blob/c6cbeb2/docs/decisions.md)). A computed tier will not drift from the graph.
- **There is no depth limit.** standalone's map draws three layers, the catalog's test keeps chains within three, and for that one edge is not drawn: "a link from divisibility would make a fourth layer through calendar and divisibility, and the map draws three" (ibid.). And an edge is a teacher's judgement: "which topic is a good base for another is a teacher's judgement the data only supports" (ibid.). The format should not fit the graph to the map's drawing, and the map can fold the far tiers into a row, as the prototype does ([draft/README.md](../draft/README.md)).
- **The author gives the tiers names** — as in the prototype: the module Goroutines has its own steps — Basics, Waiting, Many goroutines and Review — and the caption is "Step N · name" or, without a name, "Step N" (`draft/NovaTrail Widget.html`). The olympiad module has standalone's names: Foundations, Rules, Hard problems.
- **Three values of assessability.** A key and a predicate both give a verdict, and the engine and the learner model behave the same with either. And for a skill that is trained by tasks both with a key and with a predicate, none of four values — key, predicate, rubric and none — would be right.
- **A dictionary of skills by local ID.** The uniqueness of IDs is held by the rule `yaml.unique-keys`, not by a rule of its own, and the order of skills carries no meaning, like the order of keys.
- **The table is in the graph, with skills without replacement too.** A skill retired without replacement is recorded in the same place as the others, and its ID is protected from reuse too. standalone has no mapping table.
- **The grade is a point on the ladder of tasks, not at the skills.** In standalone the grade decides one thing: "Start is where a child of this grade begins: the shift of the level the grade falls into. It is the one thing the grade decides" ([`internal/domain/rating/ladder.go`](https://github.com/mathtrail/mathtrail-standalone/blob/c6cbeb2/internal/domain/rating/ladder.go), commit c6cbeb2), and a task's level is "the band of grades it is written for" (SPEC 1.1 standalone). So the starting point is given by the scale of task difficulty, and the label is needed by itself: by it the app asks the grade.
- **The MIT notice** on the example of the olympiad graph is kept, since MathTrail's code under MIT carries over freely: MIT is compatible with Apache-2.0, and the MIT notice is kept. standalone's topics and their links are under MIT, "Copyright (c) 2026 MathTrail" ([LICENSE](https://github.com/mathtrail/mathtrail-standalone/blob/c6cbeb2/LICENSE), commit c6cbeb2). A file `NOTICE` beside the example `format-check` would not accept, so the notice stands in the example's opening comment.

— *Rejected:*
- the author sets the tier: it would drift from the graph, which is what standalone's decision log warns against;
- computing the tier, but no deeper than three, as standalone's map: the graph would be fitted to the drawing;
- tiers without names: the steps that the module names itself would be lost;
- four values of assessability — key, predicate, rubric and none;
- skills as a list with a field `id`, as in the physics illustration in `docs/concepts.md`: the uniqueness of IDs would be held by a rule of its own;
- `formerly` — a list of earlier IDs on the new skill: a skill retired without replacement is recorded nowhere, and its ID has nothing to protect it;
- the table as a separate file `skill-mapping.yaml`: a layout row of its own, and the references to skills a rule between two files;
- everything about the grade in the decision on the scale of task difficulty; grades on skills, like the `grade_levels` of standalone's topics: there the starting point was given by the level of tasks, not by the grades of topics;
- an example without standalone's topics, and their re-release by the author under Apache-2.0;
- the graph and the shared taxonomy as one task — larger than one review;
- comparing with the newest version not withdrawn — a fix of a withdrawn 2.0.0, compared with 1.x, could take the ID of its skill for another meaning, and the evidence waiting in `api`'s log would count toward another skill, or silently lose its skills;
- "earlier" by the order of publication — a backport 1.1.0 released after the withdrawn 2.0.0 would retire its skills, and retirement is a major change.

— *Consequence:* `docs/concepts.md`; `docs/architecture.md`; `docs/repositories.md`; `format/README.md`; `format/schemas/skill-graph.schema.json` and `manifest.schema.json`; `format/vectors/tiers/`; `docs/decisions.md`.

## Shared taxonomy

**R50. The shared taxonomy is a dictionary of anchor skills in the module format: the schema `format/schemas/shared-taxonomy.schema.json`, where each anchor skill is a branch of `oneOf` with the ID `core.<name>`, a title and a description. A module's skill rests on an anchor skill as a prerequisite and teaches it with the field `teaches`, a task may name one as a supporting skill, and the manifest names the anchor skills on which the module's skills rest in `dependencies`. The dictionary is part of the format version.** Normatively it is written in English in the [format text](../format/README.md), in its part on the shared taxonomy and in those on versions, the manifest and the skill graph, and in the schemas `shared-taxonomy.schema.json`, `skill-graph.schema.json` and `manifest.schema.json`; here is what was decided, why, and what was rejected.
- **The dictionary** is the format's schema `shared-taxonomy.schema.json`. Its instance is the ID of an anchor skill: at the root a string and the form of the ID, and each anchor skill is a branch of `oneOf`, where the ID is `const`, the title `title`, the description `description`. An ID that is not in the dictionary the schema itself rejects. It describes no part of a module and is never a module's file: it is referred to by the parts that name anchor skills. The platform curates the dictionary, in `spec`.
- **The ID** is `core.<name>`, where the name is in kebab-case starting with a letter: `core.multiplication-table`.
  - The dot separates the namespace: the ID of an anchor skill cannot be confused with a local ID or with a module ID, which have no dots.
  - The ID has no subject: a module of any subject may rest on an anchor skill.
  - The ID is the same in a module and outside it. An anchor skill has no full ID: it is not part of a module, and the learner model, the engine and progress know it by this ID.
- **The title and the description** are English text of the schema, not text of a module: an anchor skill has no explanation language. The description says what a learner who knows the skill can do, and it is normative: it is the meaning of the anchor skill.
- **Where a module names anchor skills:**
  - in a skill's prerequisites — what it needs. A prerequisite is a skill of the module by its local ID or an anchor skill by its own ID: in the schema this is an `anyOf` of the two;
  - in a skill's `teaches` — what it teaches: a learner who knows the skill can do what the description of each anchor skill says. One anchor skill may be taught by several skills of one module or of different ones;
  - in a task's supporting skills — the primary one is only a skill of the module. An anchor skill that a skill of the same module teaches the task does not name; it names that skill — the rule `task.own-anchors`, like `skill-graph.own-anchors` for prerequisites. A supporting anchor skill does not enter `dependencies`;
  - in the manifest's `dependencies` — what the module's skills rest on. A module whose skills need no anchor skills does not write the field. So one manifest shows what the module rests on.
- **Rules:**
  - `skill-graph.own-anchors` — a skill does not name as a prerequisite an anchor skill that a skill of the same module teaches, itself included. A skill that needs what its own module teaches names the module's skill: so the module's graph holds this link, and the tiers and the check of cycles see it;
  - `manifest.dependencies` — `dependencies` names exactly the anchor skills that the prerequisites of the module's skill graph name: each, and no other. The rule links two files, and its vectors are folders laid out as a module.

  `module-kit` checks them, and `spec`'s CI checks the YAML and the schemas of their vectors. Anchor skills do not count toward the tier: they are not skills of the module, and a skill all of whose prerequisites are anchor skills stands in tier 1.
- **Versions.** The dictionary is part of the format version:
  - a new anchor skill and the mark `"deprecated": true` are a minor version: a module may name a marked anchor skill until a major version removes it;
  - the removal of an anchor skill and a change of its meaning are a major one. The meaning under the same ID does not change: a skill with a new meaning comes under a new ID, and the earlier ID is removed;
  - other words of the same meaning in the description are an editorial change, without a new version;
  - the ID of an anchor skill is not reused;
  - v1 holds only the anchor skills that a module of the first slice names.
- **The learner model and the engine.** Whether a learner knows an anchor skill `learner-model` decides by the skills that teach it, in the learner's modules. An anchor skill that no module of the learner teaches does not hold back a skill that needs it: the engine counts it as unknown. The format checks each module separately, so it does not see a cycle of prerequisites between modules through anchor skills.
- **The first anchor skills** are `core.multiplication-table`, `core.division-with-remainder`, `core.fractions-of-a-whole` and `core.linear-equations`. In the format's examples the first three are taught by the school mathematics of grade 3, and the olympiad one rests on division with remainder and fractions of a whole. The fourth is taken by no module of the slice: it is for the third-party physics module of the illustration in `docs/concepts.md`, and it will not enter v1 unless a module of the slice takes it.
- **What is not decided here:**
  - how a third-party author proposes an anchor skill of their own — that is the publication rules (О-9);
  - the index of the modules that teach an anchor skill — that is the module index: each record of it has `teaches`, the anchor skills that the skills of its graph teach;
  - how `learner-model` derives knowledge of an anchor skill from the skills that teach it — and from skills with `rubric` or `none`, which have no verdict (О-17) — and what the engine does with a cycle between modules: that is their detailing;
  - which version part of a module an edit of `teaches` or `dependencies` raises — the rules of comparison of versions. To remove `teaches` is to take an anchor skill away from the modules that rest on it;
  - translations of the titles and descriptions of anchor skills: there are no translations in format v0.

— *Why:* the rules `skill-graph.own-anchors` and `manifest.dependencies`, the meaning of `teaches`, the tier without anchor skills and what an anchor skill means for the learner model and the engine are the plan's proposal. All was read 2026-10-26.
- **A schema, not a data file.** An unknown anchor skill the schema itself rejects, and no format rule of its own is needed for it. `const` "is functionally equivalent to an "enum" … with a single value" ([JSON Schema 2020-12 validation](https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/json-schema-validation), §6.1.3), and a branch of `oneOf` carries a title and a description besides: "A title will preferably be short, whereas a description will provide explanation about the purpose of the instance described by this schema" (ibid., §9.1). The mark `deprecated` in a branch concerns only its own anchor skill: it "applies to each instance location to which the schema object containing the keyword successfully applies", and it means that "applications SHOULD refrain from usage of the declared property. It MAY mean the property is going to be removed in the future" (ibid., §9.3). The dictionary goes into the releases as one more schema, together with the others.
- **The prerequisite and `teaches`** are as in schema.org. `teaches` — "The item being described is intended to help a person learn the competency or learning outcome defined by the referenced term", and `competencyRequired` — "Knowledge, skill, ability or personal attribute that must be demonstrated by a person or other entity in order to do something such as earn an Educational Occupational Credential or understand a LearningResource". Among the values of both is `DefinedTerm`, a term of a vocabulary ([schema.org, teaches](https://schema.org/teaches) and [competencyRequired](https://schema.org/competencyRequired), V30.1 of 2026-09-16). So both what a skill needs and what it teaches are linked to an anchor skill.
- **Modules only through the dictionary.** In the prototype a module rests on another module by the package name and a range of versions — `math-g3 ^1.5` ([draft/README.md](../draft/README.md)) —, and then renaming or retiring a skill in one module would break another. An anchor skill a module will neither rename nor retire.
- **`dependencies` is exactly the anchor skills of the graph's prerequisites.** A list that the author writes by hand beside the graph would drift from it, as tiers typed by hand would drift. The rule holds them together, and the manifest shows what the module rests on, without the graph.
- **The tier is without anchor skills.** The tier is difficulty within a module, and an anchor skill from another module would shift the tiers, though nothing changed in the module itself.
- **A new meaning is a new ID**, as for a module's skill. The learner model knows an anchor skill only by its ID, and from v1 the platform reads two major format versions at once: if the meaning changed under the same ID, the evidence of the earlier meaning would count toward the new one. This reading of the rule that a removal and a change of meaning are a major version and an ID is not reused was proposed by the review.

— *Rejected:*
- the ID `core.<subject>.<name>`, as in the physics illustration in `docs/concepts.md`: the subject would bind the anchor skill to itself forever;
- a data file `format/shared-taxonomy.yaml` with a schema of its own: it needs code of `format-check`, a rule for an unknown anchor skill and a second file in the release;
- the shared taxonomy as one task with the skill graph — larger than one review;
- dependencies without a field in the manifest, which `module-kit` computes into the package, like the tier. The field is in the manifest: the manifest shows what the module rests on, without the graph, and the rule `manifest.dependencies` — the plan's proposal — does not let the field drift from the graph.

— *Consequence:* `docs/concepts.md`; `docs/architecture.md`; `docs/repositories.md`; `format/README.md`; `format/schemas/shared-taxonomy.schema.json`, `skill-graph.schema.json` and `manifest.schema.json`; `docs/decisions.md`.

## Task

**R51. A task is a file `tasks/<id>.yaml`: the task statement, the canvas, the items with their answer slots, the skills, the band and the difficulty, and where needed the age categories it suits. An item's key is the check of each of its answer slots. A module's difficulty scale is the bands in the module manifest, and the digit height on a crop is there too, 24 px unless given, from format version 0.2. A task's lines in the workbook fit the page as the format's layout lays them out, `task.workbook-page`. A picture's background is opaque and light, a SHOULD. The rule `module.media` checks the media files, and `spec` builds the open view itself.** Normatively this is written in English in the [format text](../format/README.md), in its parts on open fields, test vectors, a module, the manifest and the task, and in the schemas `task.schema.json`, `manifest.schema.json` and `common.schema.json`; here is what is decided, why, and what is rejected.
- **A task** is `tasks/<id>.yaml` by the schema `task.schema.json`, and its `id` is the file's name without `.yaml`: the rule `module.file-ids`.
- **The task statement** is parts in order: a paragraph `text` or a picture.
  - A paragraph is plain text in the module's explanation language. There are no formulas and no sound in a statement in v0: each will come with a minor version.
  - A picture has `picture`, a path in `media/` to a PNG, JPEG or WebP file; `alt`, what is on it in words: a screen reader reads it, and it stands in the picture's place until the picture has arrived, and it is empty only for a decoration; `width` and `height`, the size in CSS px, each at most 2^53−1.
  - **A picture's background** is opaque and light: a SHOULD of the format, not a rule. `module-kit` warns about a picture that has at least one pixel not fully opaque, and a PNG with an alpha channel where all the pixels are opaque does not get the warning. The warning has neither an ID nor vectors, and it does not reject the module. It concerns every picture of a module — of the statement, the solution and the lesson; normatively, the [format text](../format/README.md), in its part on the task and, on a picture in a sheet area, in its part on lessons. The cost: an opaque picture in a sheet area covers the grid under it.
  - The statement is part of the author's template, which the learner neither erases nor changes. Whether it is above the canvas or on it, the canvas kind decides: the handwriting sheet shows it above the sheet.
  - The parts of a statement `statement_part`, the canvas `canvas` and the zone's rectangle, as `sheet_rectangle`, are in `common.schema.json`: a lesson takes them too, and a part's schema does not refer to another part's schema. A lesson refers to tasks by local ID.
- **The canvas belongs to the task,** one for all the items. `kind` is `handwriting_sheet` or `workbook`.
  - The handwriting sheet is 1000 × 1400 units from the top left corner, and the size is a constant of the kind. The task gives it a grid `grid` — `squares`, `lines` or `dots`, without the field squares — and its step `grid_step` from 20 to 500 units, without the field 50.
  - The workbook is a page of lines, a line per item. How the lines lie on the page the format decides, and `canvas` brings a change of it by a row «в реестр spec».
  - Every task has a pen and an eraser. There is no field of tools in v0: it will come with a minor version, with the first module that needs a ruler or a calculator. What it takes in is known: the names `pen` and `eraser`; a list without `pen` is an error, since the sheet writes with the pen; the sheet skips unknown tools; undo and clear are not tools.
  - Until its move to the types of `spec`, `canvas` keeps its temporary field `canvas.tools`; without the field the sheet gives a pen and an eraser, as the format has it.
- **The page of a workbook.** A task's lines in the workbook MUST fit on the page as the layout lays them out: the rule `task.workbook-page` of format 0.4. A task whose lines do not fit, `canvas` rejects: `TypeError` on `task.items[i]`.
  - The layout of `canvas` is a norm of the format whole, with the positions: its numbers and its table of widths are the file `format/page.yaml` with its own schema, and its cases, the 19 of `vectors/pages.json` of `canvas`, are the vectors `format/vectors/pages/`. The CI of `canvas` and of `module-kit` pass them.
  - `just types` writes the JSON of the page and of its vectors in `types/page/`, and `types-check` compares it file for file, like the code of the contracts. `canvas` takes them from the npm package `@altnovatrail/spec`, from line 0.10, and keeps no copy of its own.
  - **A change of the numbers** is a format version, by the rules on versions of the [format text](../format/README.md): a tighter layout, by which a valid task becomes invalid, is a major version, and in v0 the next 0.y; a roomier one is a minor one, like a higher limit, and while the format is v0, also the next 0.y. The measurement of the type size and the fonts on children's tablets by `canvas` brings its change so.
  - With the numbers of `page.yaml`, a page holds up to 10 rows, and a row is two short items or one long one. A short item is a line no wider than 384 units, on a page 1000 wide and with a box 100 wide: "347 ÷ 6 = [ ] r [ ]" is still short, and «47 : 6 = [ ] (ост. [ ])» is already long. A long item on one line is up to 864 units, about 55 characters with a box; a wider long item wraps and takes more than a row, and a short item before a long one stands alone in its row.
- **Items and answer slots.** An item is named by its place in the task, from 1, and an answer slot by its place among the item's slots.
  - On the sheet, an item has slots `answer_slots` and, where needed, `text`: what it asks, "a)".
  - In the workbook, an item is a line `line`: pieces of text and boxes in order, at least one box, and a box anywhere — "7 × [ ] = 56", "56 [ ] 65", "[ ] apples". The line's boxes are its answer slots. A two-storey fraction and column arithmetic will come later.
  - Every answer slot has a check `check`, closed whole, and the item's verdict is made up of the slots' verdicts.
- **The bindings of v0** are what the modules of the slice and a workbook of school maths need:
  - `anywhere` — anywhere on the sheet: AI finds the final answer;
  - `sheet` — the whole sheet, the work as a whole, like an essay;
  - `zone` — in a zone: a rectangle of the sheet, `left` and `top` from the left and top edges, `width` and `height`, in units of the sheet. The names are not `x` and `y`: a plain `y` breaks `yaml.plain-strings`;
  - `choice` — a tapped choice among the options `options`: two or more, without repeats, in order. A choice by hand is a check kind, with the options in the check itself;
  - `box` — a box of a workbook line.

  On the sheet, `anywhere`, `sheet`, `zone` and `choice`; in the workbook, `box`. A slot `anywhere` or `sheet` is the only one in its task: AI would not tell two final answers "anywhere" apart. Keyboard input, an edit in a text and a widget's state will come later, with a minor version, and v1 will take in only what a module of the slice took: nobody takes `zone` yet.
- **Skills** — `primary`: the module's skills by local ID that the task trains, and a wrong answer is evidence against them; `supporting`: the skills the answer needs and that a wrong answer does not lower — skills of the module or anchor skills. An item's own `skills` replace the task's skills for it.
- **What a task writes itself** beside the catalogs: the givens and the unknown, `givens` and `unknown`, are open; the techniques `techniques`, the traps from AI `traps`, the solution `solution`, the leak phrases `leak_phrases` and an item's simpler case `simpler_case` are closed. The schema requires the solution of a task that has an item with a verdict, and `task.known-pictures` covers the pictures of the solution too.
- **A task template** is a task with the field `template`, closed whole: the parameters, the derived numbers and the constraint. Every string of the task outside `template` may hold placeholders `{name}`, and in a key and a trap value `number` and `fraction` a placeholder stands in the place of an integer, a numerator or a denominator: `"{second}"`, `"{part}/{whole}"`.
- **The difficulty scale is bands and a difficulty inside a band, as in standalone.** The module manifest lists the bands `bands` in order, from the easiest: `id`, `title` and, for a module with grades, `grades`. A task names its band `band` and its difficulty `difficulty` from 1 to 5 inside it.
  - The band that holds a learner's grade is where the learner model's start is computed from, not the start itself: the estimate of a new learner starts a band's width below it, below the lowest band too. The [format text](../format/README.md), in its part on the manifest, still says "A learner of a grade starts in the band that holds the grade": its next version words it so (Д260).
  - Where a learner outside the bands starts and how far apart the bands are, `learner-model` decides.
- **The digit height on a crop** is `canvas.digit_height` in the module manifest: whole px from 1 to 256, 24 unless given, from format version 0.2; a module of format 0.1 without the field is read at 32 px. The setting is one per module. `app` gets it, and the explanation language, in the open view of the module manifest, which `api` gives by the digest of any package of its image — of an attempt, of a lesson run, of the current version of a connected module and of a module of the catalog —, through `PackageService`.
  - The modules of the slice, those for adults too, set no `canvas.digit_height` and are read at 24 px. A column fraction at 24 px is not measured: Д18 `tutor` holds it.
- **A task's age categories** are `age_categories`: fewer than the module's, and the platform gives the task only to learners of those categories. A lesson that has a task with age categories goes only to a learner whom that task suits. To a learner under 18 a module gives made-up and general topics, and a topic about the learner's life it marks with the task's `age_categories` as not for their category.
- **There is no provenance in a module:** everything in a module comes from the author, and a task has no field for it. A program computes a template's key — the template's expressions or its solver —, and the template itself shows it. "Entered by an adult" and "derived by AI" are the provenance of tasks from paper, which modules do not have.
- **standalone's pictures** are files in `media/`: in the port, `modules` draws them into files with a description. Kinds of pictures that `canvas` draws will come later, with a minor version.
- **Open and closed.** Open are `id`, the statement, the canvas, the givens and the unknown, and the items with all their fields but their skills, their simpler case and each slot's check: the app shows them. Closed are the skills, the band, the difficulty, the age categories, the techniques, the traps, the solution, the leak phrases and the template: the server reads them. Opening a field later is a major version.
- **Rules:**
  - of the module manifest — `manifest.bands`: if bands are written, their IDs differ; in a module with grades each band names its grades, and each grade of `audience.grades` is in exactly one; in a module without grades the bands name no grades;
  - of a task — `task.known-skills`, `task.skill-roles`, `task.own-anchors`, `task.known-band`, `task.workbook-page`, `task.known-pictures`, `task.age-categories` and `task.zones`; zones touching at their edges is not an overlap. `module-kit` checks them, and the CI of `spec` checks their vectors' YAML and schemas;
  - of the whole module — `module.file-ids` and `module.media`. These, like `module.manifest` and `module.layout`, `format-check` checks itself.
- **Media files** go by the signatures of [WHATWG MIME Sniffing](https://mimesniff.spec.whatwg.org/), "Last Updated 19 October 2026", read 2026-10-26: PNG — `89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A`, JPEG — `FF D8 FF`, WebP — "RIFF", four bytes and "WEBPVP" (§6.1); MP3 — "ID3" or a frame header of layer III (§6.2). The signature is what `module.media` reads: the rest of the file is the author's concern.
- **The open view** `spec` builds itself: the vectors `format/vectors/open-view/` and their check in `format-check`.
- **What is not decided here:** sound and formulas in the statement, the field of tools, styling for the learner's interests and kinds of pictures that `canvas` draws — they come with minor versions, with the module that needs them.

— *Why:*
- The rules, the forms of the schema, the names of the fields, the check of the media and of the open view are the plan's proposal after an independent agent checked the draft. All read 2026-10-26.
- **Bands and difficulty are as in standalone,** commit c6cbeb2: "a task has a level — the band of grades it is written for — and a difficulty inside that level" ([SPEC.md](https://github.com/mathtrail/mathtrail-standalone/blob/c6cbeb2/SPEC.md), section 1.1), and the starting point is the band of the grade: `Start(grade)` in `internal/domain/rating/ladder.go` returns the offset of the band the grade falls in. The bands are 2.5 apart and overlap: a task's hardness there is its band's offset plus the difficulty minus 3. One scale of rungs would not express the overlap, and the numbers are the model's business, not the format's.
- **The term is "difficulty band":** "level" already means the learner's level in the learner model, and a term means one thing.
- **The bindings follow the slice.** Anywhere on the sheet is as in canvas-api: «Поля ответа нет: ребёнок решает и пишет итоговый ответ где угодно на листе … а итог находит модель» ("There is no answer field: the child solves and writes the final answer anywhere on the sheet … and the model finds the final answer") ([docs/decisions.md](https://github.com/mathtrail/canvas-api/blob/0901af0/docs/decisions.md) of canvas-api). The box is for the workbook, the whole sheet for an essay, and the choice for the assignments with a key among the essays and for standalone's tasks: there an answer is always a choice among five options. What the slice does not take will not enter v1, and so it is not in v0 either.
- **The workbook line:** a box in a workbook example happens both at the start and in the middle, and text and boxes in order write any such example without a markup language.
- **The statement above the sheet** is how `canvas` shows it, and so do the others: canvas-api — «текст над листом, а не часть листа» ("the text above the sheet, not a part of the sheet") ([canvas-api@0901af0](https://github.com/mathtrail/canvas-api/tree/0901af0)) —, the review board of `tutor` and the prototype of `spec`. The picture's description and size: without a description a picture that has not arrived cannot be read, and without a size the sheet shifts under the pen when it arrives.
- **The skills are closed:** a skill's title — "gaps and posts" on a task about a staircase — hints at the way to solve it, and what gives the way away is closed. Opening it later is a major version, and then it will also be decided what to show before the solution.
- **There is no provenance:** standalone has none either — "Nobody else's wording, anywhere. The ideas come from open sources; the text is ours" (SPEC 1.5 standalone) —, and the tasks that AI helped to write the author checks before publication.
- **Pictures are files:** standalone's 13 kinds of pictures are drawn by its card — "an object of one of thirteen kinds, which the card draws as SVG" (SPEC 4.4 standalone). Taking them into the format would mean 13 schemas and 13 drawers in `canvas` for the sake of one module, while a file with a description any browser shows.
- **The open view goes by the annotations of 2020-12:** the definition "a mark counts only where the subschema passes" is exactly the collection of annotations by the 2020-12 core, §7.7.1.2, and the two implementations — `format-check` and `module-kit` — are compared by the vectors.
- **Two bugs of `ajv` 8.20.0.** `unevaluatedProperties` counts a place's fields as unevaluated when beside it stands `dependentSchemas` without its own key, or `$ref` together with `oneOf` or `anyOf` whose passing branch is not the first. By 2020-12 such a part is valid, while `format-check` would reject it. The format's schemas take neither, and a test of `format-check` pins the behaviour of `ajv`: if it changes, the test will say so.
- **The tools.** v0 has no field `tools` in the task's canvas, though `canvas` proposed one; what it proposed for the field is of use to that minor version.
- **The digit height of 24 px** is the middle between the advice of the rule that `tutor` wrote down before the run, 16 px, and the former height, 32 px; it is not the recommendation of `tutor`.
  - The measurement of `tutor`'s epic E4, recorded in `tutor`'s `docs/architecture.md`, compared the heights 16, 24 and 48 px with 32 px in pairs, by sheets, without the key, on Haiku 5.5 · `low` and Haiku 5.5 · `low` without thinking. On 68 test sheets, 16 and 24 px are no worse than 32 px on both; 48 px on Haiku · `low` is worse: 12 extra "unreadable" against 5, p 0.033, and there were no other errors at the heights. On 15 test workbook pages, 16, 24 and 48 px are also no worse than 32 px on both, and there are no new false "correct". A sheet's picture at 16 px is about 90 tokens against about 200 at 32 px; the crop of a workbook box at 16, 24 and 32 px is one and the same: 200 × 200, 64 tokens.
  - Why 24 and not 16: the handwriting of the measurement is synthetic data, even and large, while live handwriting is smaller and less even, and 24 px leave a margin. The gain in price at 16 px is small — the whole input about 1,300 tokens against 1,400. On sheets with lowercase letters the digits on a crop are, besides, larger than the height from the module manifest, by the crop rule.
  - Why a format version: a new default value changes the behaviour of a module without the field, and "A minor version only adds", while of default values the text puts among the patch changes only "a parameter whose default keeps the previous behaviour" ([format text](../format/README.md)).
  - The recheck, its outcome for each result decided beforehand: the modules of the slice came out without `canvas.digit_height`, and `novatrail` reads them at 24 px, while the reading was admitted at 32 px. `tutor` v0.1.48 read the author's 60 sheets with Haiku 5.5 · `medium` at 24 px and at 32 px, 645 calls, $0.2610: at 24 px one more "unreadable", p 0.5, no false alarm of 35 and no false "correct" of 25. 24 px is no worse, and so this decision stands, and the modules for adults set no `canvas.digit_height`.
- **The picture's background** is the recommendation of `canvas`: only the author knows on which background their drawing reads, and an underlay of the canvas would cover the grid on light paper too. A transparent picture with dark lines is not visible on the dark paper of `canvas` (`--novatrail-canvas-paper`) and in forced colors, and only its description `alt` remains of it.
  - Forced colors change the colors of properties, not the pixels of a picture: "When forced colors mode is active and forced-color-adjust is auto on an element, the color components of all properties on the element are force-adjusted to the user's preferred color palette", while a picture by its address is kept: "background-image computes to none unless the original value contains a url() function" ([CSS Color Adjustment Module Level 1](https://www.w3.org/TR/css-color-adjust-1/), W3C Candidate Recommendation Snapshot, 16 December 2025, read 2026-11-01). In practice `canvas` checked this: in Chromium in forced colors, a picture on the sheet has the colors of its file.
  - A warning, not a refusal: by the [format text](../format/README.md), a format rule is only a MUST with its own ID, and a new rule is a major change, in v0 the next 0.y; a SHOULD changes neither a verdict, nor the open view, nor the numbers, and gives no format version.
- **The page of a workbook** is by the recommendation of `canvas`, with the numbers, the table of widths and the line rules of `vectors/pages.json` of `canvas` (`main` 93decba: 19 cases, and in three the lines do not fit). The port of the layout in `tools/format-check/page.mjs` gives exactly the positions and the refusals of all 19 cases of `canvas` at commit 73807f2, read 2026-11-09.
  - The positions are normative: the boxes in the sample files are written by them, and `canvas` and `module-kit` do not differ in what the child sees.
  - The table is a data file, not text: hundreds of lines that code would otherwise copy by hand.
  - The JSON for `canvas`: the release builds the package without `tools/node_modules` and does not read YAML.

— *Rejected:*
- one scale of rungs with a starting rung for each grade; one number of difficulty for a task;
- a picture's size from its file; the statement on the template layer;
- a zone in cells of the grid — it would shift when the step changes;
- a canvas for each item;
- the bindings "keyboard input", "edit" and "widget state" in v0;
- the age mark later; styling for interests in v0;
- a field of provenance in a task;
- standalone's kinds of pictures in v0;
- the digit height in each task, as `canvas.digit` in the temporary type of `canvas`;
- only the module's skills among the supporting skills;
- the text of a workbook item, and the boxes after it;
- a field of tools of the pen and the eraser in v0, as `canvas` proposed;
- "difficulty level", `level`;
- the task's skills open;
- a digit height of 16 px — the advice by the rule, but checked only on synthetic data; keeping 32 px — 24 px is no worse on both parts of the measurement; 24 px in format 0.1, without a new version — the format's rules of versions do not allow it; format 0.2 in the same change as the decision on 24 px — the format version is in about 140 examples and vectors of `format/`, and the digests of the package and index vectors depend on it;
- leaving the recheck of 24 px with Д18 `tutor` until runs return, as `tutor` recommended — the answer was wanted at once; the modules for adults at 32 px until the run — a change of three modules before anything showed 24 px worse; an entry of `tutor`'s list naming the height it was measured at — code of `tutor` and a rule of `spec` for one case; measuring the column fraction at 24 px at once — calls to AI and money, for what Д18 `tutor` holds;
- a light underlay of `canvas` under each picture; leaving pictures as they are — on dark paper a transparent picture is not seen; a MUST rule instead of a SHOULD;
- the rule of a workbook page in format 0.2, in one merge with it — every repository's one move to line 0.6, with format 0.2, and the first release of `module-kit` with code would wait for the layout, a table of widths by Unicode ranges with vectors and their schema, though the first app, olympiad maths on the sheet, has no workbook; and the numbers would freeze in the format before `canvas` measured the type on children's tablets;
- no limit of a workbook's lines at all — the learner would see the error; a limit by a count of items and characters — it either lets through what `canvas` will reject or forbids ordinary tasks;
- only "fits or not" in the format — the implementations could differ in the drawing; the table of widths in the text; the archive `format-<version>.tar.gz` for `canvas` — it would need reading YAML and a comparison step of its own; a copy of its own in `canvas` — `canvas` rejects it itself.

— *Consequence:* `docs/concepts.md`; `docs/privacy.md`; `docs/architecture.md`; `docs/repositories.md`; `docs/decisions.md`; `format/README.md`; `format/schemas/` — `task.schema.json`, `manifest.schema.json`, `common.schema.json` and `page.schema.json`; `format/page.yaml`; `format/vectors/open-view/` and `format/vectors/pages/`; `tools/format-check/`; `types/page/`.

## The course of writing and AI

**R52. Nothing of the learner's writing history goes to AI — neither the order of writing, nor the action log, nor the frames before erasure, neither into reading nor into analysis: what goes to the check is an image or a crop, and the strokes with time and pressure stay on the device. So it stays until a measurement on live handwriting and free notation shows that the course of writing helps. Grown-up mode, at a grown-up's request behind the PIN, is the one place where the points of the strokes go, to the drawing alone, without time and pressure.**
- **What the measurement of `tutor` measured**, 2026-10-26, as `tutor`'s `docs/architecture.md` records it. The model assessed the finished sheet — `correct`, `error` or `unreadable` — and placed the box of the first error. This went in one call: the model saw the key and the reference solution, as on the review board. By the vocabulary of `spec` this is reading and analysis in one call, which the platform makes two calls, and there was no reading without the key in the measurement. The course of solution here is the course of writing: the order of writing, the pauses and the erasures, what is not on the final image. The forms are four:
  - (A) only the final image;
  - (B) the image and the action log: the lines in the order of writing, pauses from 6 s, erasures and returns to a line — without time, pressure, coordinates and what was erased;
  - (C) the image and up to two frames before erasure: on a frame is what was erased itself;
  - (D) both.

  There are 40 sheets, 30 of them test sheets, with 3 repeats per form. The judges are Opus 5.5 · `high`, Haiku 5.5 · `low` and Haiku 5.5 · `low` without thinking. The criterion was written down before the first run: form D against form A by sheets, the exact sign test, the threshold p < 0.05. Forms B and C against A the measurement counted without a threshold.
- **The answer by the criterion is "not shown" for all three judges.** On 30 test sheets, 90 answers per form, A → D:
  - Opus 5.5 · `high` — correct 90 and 90, false alarms 0 and 0;
  - Haiku 5.5 · `low` — correct 84 and 72, false alarms 3 and 9, p "harms" 0.10;
  - Haiku 5.5 · `low` without thinking — correct 65 and 77, false alarms 14 and 8, p "helps" 0.061.

  There is no false "correct" in any answer. Of the comparisons without a threshold, `tutor`'s record names one thing for forms B and C: the log without frames gave a false alarm less often for Haiku without thinking — 14 in A, 5 in B and 8 in D. But even in D this judge is right less often than Haiku · `low` by the image alone: 77 against 84.
- **The measurement's caveats.** 39 sheets of the 40 were drawn by code: the handwriting is even, without blots, and the erasures are exactly to plan. The solutions are written in lines from top to bottom, and there is no free notation — a number line, a drawing, a note at the side — on the sheets. Opus is right already by the image alone, and a help from the course of writing is not visible for it on these sheets by construction. The call "analysis of the course of solution and the hint" with a trap and a rung the measurement did not measure: the model only assessed the sheet and looked for the first error.
- **The measurement of free notation** of `tutor` answered "not shown" too. 40 sheets by code with free notation — a number line, a drawing, a note at the side —, 30 of them test sheets, with 3 repeats. The judges and the criterion are the same as above: form D against form A, p < 0.05.
  - By the criterion, for all three judges: Opus 5.5 · `high` is nearly faultless by the image alone too, correct in 87 answers of 90 in both forms; for Haiku 5.5 · `low` p is 0.094, for Haiku without thinking 0.123. There is no false "correct" in any answer.
  - Without a threshold the log of parts helps a weak judge to find the first error in a drawing. On the 6 sheets where it is in a drawing, Haiku · `low` is right in 10 answers of 18 by the image alone and in 15 with the log, and Haiku without thinking in 1 and in 13. In text and in a note at the side there is nothing of the kind. On the author's three sheets, live writing with a mouse, the measurement went without a threshold.
- **So** the rule applies that of the kinds that give the same benefit, the one poorest in data is taken. The benefit of the course of writing is not shown: form D, which has both the log and the frames, gave it to no judge, and the log and the frames separately were not measured by the criterion. So one image goes to AI — both into reading and into analysis. What stays on the device and what goes to the check do not change, and neither does `tutor`'s own decision on its measurement. The check request in the contract `app` ↔ `api` carries the work as an image or a crop, without fields of the course of writing. `tutor` reads the work by one final image, and nothing changes in its code.
- **Grown-up mode** is no check. Its drawing acts on the sheet as a grown-up asks, and gets the strokes the crop of the work shows: each its ID and its points in the crop's pixels, thinned, with no time, no pressure and nothing erased, but in the order of the sheet and each in the direction it was drawn — the part of the course of writing the points keep. A line that must end on a curve, or a region bounded by it, needs the points: the picture alone does not place them exactly. The Check and every other call still get the picture alone.
- **A measurement is not a check of a learner.** The measurement samples from adults carry a writing history, and a measurement of `tutor` sends the model the forms with the course of writing — that is how it measures. This decision is about a learner's work that the platform checks.
- **When to return** — with the measurement of `tutor` on the live handwriting of adult volunteers, where the answer "not shown" may become another. If a kind beyond the image shows a benefit, it will come with a new decision. It needs a change of what stays on the device and what goes to the check, and the lawyer's answer: how to count «процесс картинками» and a trace without time and pressure. If the course of writing returns into analysis, then analysis will go with it, and the hint without it. That is two calls instead of one call of analysis and hint, to be decided together with the calls of reading and analysis.

— *Why:* the argument of `tutor`: the recommendation of the question of what goes to AI beyond the image came true in its part on reading, while nobody has yet measured the benefit of the course of writing in analysis. A frame before erasure carries what was erased itself, and the log the order and the pauses of the learner's writing: without a shown benefit there is no reason for them to go to the provider.

What the measured call is named is the executor's proposal. `tutor` calls this call reading. But the model in it saw the key and the task's solution and looked for the first error, and in `spec`'s vocabulary that is the work of analysis, only in one call with reading. So the argument of `tutor` holds for the call of analysis and hint: its measurement did not measure that. And for the search for the first error with the key there are data, and they did not show a benefit of the course of writing.

The free notation, by the recommendation of `tutor`: the benefit is visible without a threshold, for a weak model and only on drawings, while Opus is right even without the course of writing.

— *Rejected:*
- the image in reading, and into analysis the log without what was erased, as the question's former recommendation had it. The log without frames against the image alone the measurement counted only without a threshold, and one thing is visible from it: fewer false alarms for the weakest judge. Opus, though, is right by the image alone, and no help is visible for it on these sheets by construction. To let the log go to the provider without a shown benefit is against the rule of the kind poorest in data, and it would need a change of what goes to the check and the lawyer's answer anyway;
- to wait with the answer for the measurement on live handwriting, an option of `tutor`: the contract would be planned with the question open, while the answer of this measurement is already there — "not shown";
- the course of writing into reading for Haiku without thinking: its gain is not significant (p = 0.061), and in form D it is still below Haiku · `low` by the image alone;
- the conclusion "the course of writing does not help": the measurement does not prove it — the handwriting is synthetic, there is no free notation, and Opus is faultless on these sheets even without the course of writing;
- the log of parts only for a weak judge and only on drawings — a rule for one model and one kind of notation by data without a threshold;
- to return the course of writing into analysis now: the benefit by the criterion is not shown.

— *Consequence:* `docs/decisions.md`; `docs/privacy.md`; `docs/architecture.md`; `contracts/README.md` — the check request of the contract `app` ↔ `api`, and the request of grown-up mode.

## The place on the canvas

**R53. A place on the canvas in the observation and in the contract `app` ↔ `api` is fractions 0–1000 of the crop that the device sent: `[ymin, xmin, ymax, xmax]`, integers. Into fractions the adapter of `tutor` converts from the units of its provider, into units of the sheet `canvas` does, and `sheet_box` does not leave the device. In the workbook what goes to the check is the crop of each filled box, without the item's text, and the place is the answer slot by place, `{ item, slot }`.**
- **The Anthropic adapter** takes pixels from the model and converts them into fractions itself. All read 2026-10-26:
  - the model names a place in pixels of the image it processed: "The coordinates Claude returns are pixel positions in the image Claude processes: your image after Claude resizes it to fit the model's native resolution". And in the same place: "Always ask for pixel coordinates and normalize in your own code if you need to" ([Coordinates and bounding boxes](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/vision-coordinates));
  - the adapter allows no resizing at the provider. It sends the image with `"oversized_image": "error"`, and, as `tutor`'s `docs/architecture.md` records, "No image that sets "error" reaches the model resized". An image larger than the model's limit it scales down itself and knows its size;
  - it divides by the size of the image it sent, not by the size with padding. The model pads every image to a multiple of 28 px on the right and at the bottom, and "Always normalize or rescale by the resized dimensions, not the padded dimensions" (ibid.). A box that went out onto the padding it first clamps to the image: "Clamp returned coordinates to the resized dimensions before rescaling" (ibid.).

  OpenAI has no box format, and Google's models, whose place is fractions 0–1000, are closed.
- **The data of the measurement of `tutor`**, as its `docs/architecture.md` records them. A sheet is the whole image 1000 × 600, without a crop, and the model does not scale it down. In the table of sizes, the row "1000x1000 px (1 megapixel)" has "Not resized" at both resolution levels ([Vision](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/vision), read 2026-10-26). For 1000 × 600 both the side and the number of visual tokens, 792, are below both limits. On sheets with an error, the box of the first error in pixels hit its line:
  - for Opus 5.5 · `high` — in 114 answers of 114;
  - for Haiku 5.5 · `low` — in 100;
  - for Haiku 5.5 · `low` without thinking — in 95.

  As a hit the measurement counted the line that has the most visible pixels in the box with a margin of 8 px: this is precision to the line, not finer.
- **In the same fractions** are:
  - the tutor's mark that is a box, `CropBox`, in whole thousandths of the crop; the box of the first error from analysis goes as a mark without conversion;
  - the group boxes, if Т-31 accepts them;
  - the zone of an answer slot, if it has to be shown to reading: `canvas` converts the zone, and the crop of the sheet stays one.

  A box's validity — integers 0–1000 and min < max — the adapter checks, and an invalid box has no place.
- **How the observation chooses a place:** for a slot `anywhere`, the box of the final answer on the crop in whole thousandths, if the reader named it and it is valid; for a zone and a workbook box, the slot itself; a group label only if the group boxes go with the work (Т-31). Normatively, the [contracts text](../contracts/README.md), in its part on the observation.
- **What `app` sends and where a mark stands** is written by the contract `app` ↔ `api`: from the sheet, one PNG crop without `sheet_box`; from the workbook, the crop of each filled box with its place. The tutor's mark is a slot by place or a box `CropBox`. The group label will come as an addition to the mark's place, if the group boxes go with the work (Т-31). A mark of an empty box circles the box itself.
- **A box's crop** in the workbook goes by `canvas`'s crop rule, by the box's strokes, at the digit height of the module manifest, ink only: without the box's frame and the line's text. Which stroke is in which box the box rule decides. The workbook's reading request, like the request of a sheet's reading, is a type of `tutor`, not the contract: it carries a list of "item, box, crop", and the contract gives it the place.
- **An empty box** gives no crop: its verdict is "unreadable" with the reason `blank`, and the empty boxes are named by the property `filled`.
- **The scratch work** — writing outside the boxes — does not leave the device.
- **The place** in the workbook is the answer slot by the place of the item and the box, from 1: in the observation and in a mark. There are no fractions of a crop, no stroke groups and no boxes of them in the workbook.
- **The item's text** does not go into the reading of a workbook slot, neither on the crop nor as a caption from `api`.
- **The size** is by the measurement of `canvas` on synthetic data: a box's crop at the digit heights of the eval is 200 × 200 px, 64 tokens, and a page of ten items with a box each is 640 tokens and about 11 KB of PNG. A crop of the whole sheet is no more than 1568 tokens.
- **The types** of the element `<novatrail-canvas>` — the marks with their place among them, `Marks`, `Mark` and `Anchor` — are `@altnovatrail/spec/canvas`, written by hand and reconciled with the message `Mark` of `novatrail.api.v1`.

— *Why:*
- Fractions: as `tutor` recommended, and as `canvas` had already decided for itself. The observation depends neither on the canvas kind nor on the provider. Only the adapter sees the image's resizing, and only it can recompute a place, while the server does not need the sheet's geometry. The measurement showed that Claude's pixels on an image not resized fall into the right line, and converting them into fractions is the adapter's arithmetic, as Anthropic advises.
- The crop of each box: the recommendation of `canvas`. The model need not look for what is in which box, and the eval protocol has already taken the crop rule. This is how `tutor` reads the slots, and the same image will be taken by the reading of digits on the device that `tutor` advises. The scratch work does not go: of the kinds that give the same benefit, this is the one poorest in data — so says the rule by which nothing of the learner's writing history goes to AI.
- No item's text: the recommendation of `tutor`, by its measurement, which its `docs/architecture.md` records. It compared a caption — the item's line with `[ ]` at each crop — with the crops alone, on 15 synthetic pages. The rule was written down before the run: a false "correct" that exists only with the caption means that the item's text does not go into reading. There are fewer errors with the caption for all three configurations: for Opus 5.5 · `high` 17 against 22, for Haiku 5.5 · `low` 56 against 64, for Haiku without thinking 55 against 96. But it is significant only for Haiku without thinking, p 0.0002. And it is the one that has, with the caption, one false "correct" that there is not without the caption: a quotient written "3" instead of 4, in the line «… = [ ] (ост. [ ])», read as 4. Without the caption nobody has a false "correct". The rule fired: the caption prompts the model with the answer, and a false "correct" is what the workbook cannot afford. And the caption is a contract of `api`, one for all models.

— *Rejected:*
- units of the sheet: the adapter would need `sheet_box` from the device, and the sheet's geometry would go to the server;
- fractions, with `api` converting into units of the sheet by `sheet_box` from `app`: the same, and `api` would know the canvas's geometry;
- fractions that the model itself gives: "Claude does not work well when you ask for normalized coordinates" (Coordinates and bounding boxes, ibid.);
- one crop of the strokes of all the boxes, with the boxes as boxes in its fractions: the model would look for what is in which box;
- a crop of the whole page: the scratch work would go to the AI provider;
- a caption for the models to which it gives no false "correct"; a caption always.

— *Consequence:* `docs/repositories.md`; `docs/architecture.md`; `docs/privacy.md`; `docs/concepts.md`; `contracts/README.md`; `types/canvas/index.d.ts`.

## The tutor's words

**R54. The tutor's words go to the device whole: `api` gives them when the whole text has passed its checks — the leak check, and for a hint the form check and for rubric feedback the feedback rule —, and otherwise the fallback text, or for feedback the phrase of `app` "no feedback this time". Nobody gives them out as a stream; a stream is only for the reading call, whose answer a program reads, and the verdict is by the observation whole, when the reading has ended.**
- **Why not a stream.** The leak check looks in the model's text for the key and the leak phrases that the author gave, and a text that did not pass it the fallback text replaces. It runs before any text of the tutor goes to the device. A hint that is shown in parts cannot be checked whole before it is shown: the beginning, already shown to the learner, cannot be replaced with the fallback text if the leak is further on.
- **How the leak check looks** for keys and leak phrases, the [format text](../format/README.md) says normatively, in its rule on the leak check. A key that already stands in the statement or in the text of its own item is not looked for: there the author's leak phrases guard the answer.
- **Beside the leak check** `api` checks a hint by the form check — one question, no more than two sentences, the letters of the explanation language and a word limit — and rubric feedback by the feedback rule.
