A hint that fails gets the fallback text, as at a leak, and feedback that fails, the phrase of `app` "no feedback this time". The words go after all the checks.
- **What we pay.** A stream would show the first words earlier. On `tutor`'s review board, where the answer goes as a stream, the first token of Opus 5.5 · `high` came after 1.6 s of 2.5 s. The learner will see the tutor's words when the model has finished writing them whole. A real-time channel is still not needed (Т-25).
- **Grown-up mode.** Its answer goes whole too — the words and the act on the sheet, which one undo takes back —, but past no leak check and no form check: the solution is what the grown-up asked for, behind the PIN.
- **Where the stream stays.** The reading call may stream: its answer a program reads — `module-kit` gives the verdict by the observation —, and the learner sees the verdict, not the model's text.
- **No early verdict by lines** in format v0: `module-kit` gives the verdict by the observation whole, when the reading has ended. Only a program check by lines can judge a line while the next ones arrive, and there is no check kind "steps" in format v0, so the stream stays for reading, but the verdict waits for the end of the observation. The early verdict waits for a check kind by steps in a new format version: return with it, if the stream shows that the lines arrive noticeably before the end of the answer.

— *Why:*
- The words whole: the leak check is a safeguard, not a proof, but there is no other between the model's text and the learner, and what is shown before it bypasses it.
- No early verdict: there is no check kind by which a program could judge a line before the answer has ended.

— *Rejected:*
- a stream after the check of the whole text: there is no gain — the first words come at the same time as the whole text;
- a leak check by sentences: the beginning, already shown to the learner, cannot be recalled if the continuation does not pass;
- a verdict by lines as they arrive — for now there is nothing to judge lines by.

— *Consequence:* `docs/architecture.md`.

## The term "solution"

**R55. "Solution" («решение») is the task's solution or the learner's solution, and where the context does not show whose, it is written in full. "Analysis of the course of solution" stays the name of an AI capability, and the order of writing, the pauses and the erasures are the course of writing, not the course of solution.**
- **The task's solution** is its course of solution, the field `solution`: it is shown when the attempt is closed — by a correct answer, or by the button that shows it, to a learner of the category `adult` from the start of the attempt and to a child from the fourth wrong answer, and for a task with a rubric by the learner's "Done" —, and before it does not enter the open view. In a module it is from the author; for a task from paper the model's Check derives it, hidden, and it never goes to the device. In code and schemas `solution` is only this.
- **The learner's solution** is how the learner solves the task on the canvas: lines, a drawing, a note at the side. It is part of their work, which goes to the check. Reading reads it, and the analysis of the course of solution looks for the first error in it.
- **Where to write it in full** — where both meanings occur side by side: "the model sees the key and the task's solution and looks for the first error in the learner's solution". Where it is clear whose solution is meant, just "solution": "showing the solution" is always the task's solution, and "the learner's free solution" is already named in full.
- **The course of solution** is the steps of a solution, the task's or the learner's, as they are seen in the notation: "analysis of the course of solution" analyses the steps of the learner's solution in the image.
- **The course of writing** is the order of writing, the pauses and the erasures: what the writing history carries beyond the final image. The decision log calls it the course of writing.

— *Why:* it needs the fewest changes both in `spec` and in the components, and "analysis of the course of solution" stays the capability's name. A term means one thing in every document, and each meaning now has its own full name. The names are the executor's proposal after review. «Решение автора» ("the author's solution"), as in the option of `tutor`, already means a decision of the project's author, while the solution of a task from paper is not always from the author. "Course of writing" is `tutor`'s word: it separates what the writing history carries from the steps of a solution, which "analysis of the course of solution" analyses.

— *Rejected:*
- "solution" only for the task's solution, and for the learner "work": work is wider — it is also a text, a typed answer and a widget's state —, and the capability "analysis of the course of solution" would have to be renamed in the documents of all the components;
- «решение автора» ("the author's solution") — it already means a decision of the project's author, and the solution of a task from paper may be from AI;
- leave it as it is: one term would have two meanings.

— *Consequence:* `docs/concepts.md`; `docs/architecture.md`; `docs/privacy.md`; `docs/decisions.md`.

## Slot check

**R56. The check belongs to each answer slot: the field `check` with the check kind and its parameters, closed whole, together with the kind. The kinds of format v0 are `number`, `fraction`, `choice`, `predicate`, `rubric` and, from format 0.4, `time`. How each reads the value and gives the slot's verdict, how the item's verdict is made up of the slots' verdicts, and how a reader gives a fraction written vertically and a mirrored digit, the [format text](../format/README.md) says, in its rule on checks. The verdict vectors are `format/vectors/verdicts/`, and `spec` computes them itself, but for what Starlark gives a predicate.**
- **The check is at the slot** — at a slot of the sheet and at a box of a workbook line. The kind and the key stand beside what they check, and the kinds in one line may differ. Which kinds suit which binding, the schema says: `sheet` only a rubric, `choice` a tapped choice, `anywhere`, `zone` and `box` a number, a fraction, a choice by hand and a predicate. An item's "own key" in the vocabulary reads as the keys of its slots.
- **The kinds of v0** are what the modules of the slice and a workbook of school maths need: numbers and fractions for the workbooks of school maths, numbers, choice and time for olympiad maths, rubric and choice for short essays. And the predicate: it will enter v1 only if a module of the slice takes it.
  - `number` — an integer, a decimal with a point or a simple fraction; the comparison is by value, in rational numbers, exact. `units` are the words after the number that the check discards.
  - `fraction` — a simple fraction. `form`: `any` — any fraction of the same value, `reduced` — only an irreducible one, and a reducible one of the same value is "not yet".
  - `choice` — by tap, from the options of a slot with the binding `choice`, or by hand, and then the options are in the check itself. So the signs <, > and = in a workbook box are checked: what is read not from the options is "unreadable", not "not yet". This holds for a handwritten choice without the mark: with `notation: word` the key is one word of letters, and a value that is one word not among the options is "not yet" and a rung.
  - `predicate` — a Starlark expression of the read integer `value`, no longer than 1000 characters, in the solver's dialect: it names nothing but `value`, the dialect's built-in names, `chr` and `ord` too, and the names the expression binds itself, as in a list comprehension (`task.predicate-expression`). `True` is "correct", `False` is "not yet"; an error, a result that is not a `bool`, a count of steps that reaches 1,000,000, or the clock of `module-kit` — "unchecked". The steps are counted by go.starlark.net `v0.0.0-20261021141710-4f4267fb140d`, and the evaluation stops when the count reaches the limit.
  - `rubric` — the criteria `criteria`, only on the whole sheet; the result is feedback, not a verdict.
  - `time` — a time `H:MM`, correct when its hours and minutes as numbers equal the key's.
- **The key is a string,** `key: "7"`: a plain `0.1` in YAML is a binary fraction, and an exact comparison with it would give a false "not yet".
- **Trap values.** The checks `number`, `fraction` and `choice` have `trap_values`: a trap value is compared like the key, with the same normalization, and at "not yet" it names the trap. The verdict vectors name it, and `format-check` computes it. In the leak check a key that already stands in the text of its own item is not searched for.
- **In a template** a placeholder stands in the key and the trap value of `number` and `fraction` in the place of the integer, the numerator or the denominator; outside a template a placeholder in them breaks `task.placeholders`. The key of a template is computed by an expression. Template expressions are a narrow subset of the same Starlark as the predicate's, but without a step limit of their own: they have no more steps than characters.
- **A Starlark program** in the format is only a template's solver, the field `template.solver`, and its limit is in the format too: 100,000,000 steps in the count of go.starlark.net for all instances of the template together. The check's predicate stays an expression.
- **Value and normalization.** The reader gives a slot's value as it is written, and the check kind normalizes it: NFKC, minus signs and dashes into `-`, the slashes of a fraction and of division into `/`, White_Space spaces one at a time.
  - For numbers, `=` at the start and `.!?` at the end are discarded, the units too, and a superscript or subscript digit, or a fraction like `½` that a number adjoins, is "not in notation".
  - For a choice, also a plain lowercase letter, and nothing is discarded.
  - A notation is up to 16 characters.
- **The value read.** Two cases are read one way by every reader, so that the verdict does not depend on the reader:
  - **A vertical fraction** is given in a line, "numerator/denominator": `3/4`. A two-storey fraction in an item line will come to the format later, but in a box of the workbook the learner writes a fraction vertically too. It is the same fraction, and the notation in a line is the only one the kind `fraction` takes.
  - **A mirrored digit** is "unreadable": the reader gives it as an ambiguous notation, and the learner rewrites it — so until the measurement on children's handwriting. The rule works only if the reader sees the mirroring. The target of the first slice — no more than 1 % false alarms — does not change, and a false alarm on a mirrored digit is in it. The workbook's eval set measures mirrored digits as a separate row: how many go to "unreadable" and how many to a false alarm. The rule does not concern letters: a mirrored b is a d.
  - **The module format version** does not change by these rules: they are about the reader, not the module, and with the same read value the verdict is the same.
- **A slot's verdict:** empty — "unreadable" with the reason `blank`; not in a notation — with the reason `notation`; matched — "correct"; otherwise "not yet". **An item's verdict:** all slots correct — "correct"; at least one "not yet" — "not yet"; otherwise "unreadable", and if there is no such either, "unchecked".
- **The observation.** Whether the writing is legible, whether it is unambiguous and how many final answers there are is the observation type, the contract `novatrail.observation.v1`, not the format. The format judges the read value, and the reasons for "unreadable" from the observation — `illegible`, `ambiguous`, `no_final_answer` and `several_final_answers`, and for an empty answer slot also `blank` — are given by the contract, in the [contracts text](../contracts/README.md).
- **Closed whole.** The app gets neither the key, nor the options of a choice by hand, nor the predicate, nor the rubric's criteria, nor the kind: the slot checks lie in the canonical view — the server part —, and the open view does not have them. What the learner is to know — which signs the box awaits, by which criteria the essay is judged — the author writes in the task statement.
- **Assessability is a rule,** `task.assessability`: the primary skill of an item with a key or a predicate is `verdict`, of an item with a rubric `rubric`, and a skill `none` is only supporting.
- **The task's rules** are `task.choice-key`, `task.choice-options`, `task.fraction-key`, `task.predicate-expression`, `task.trap-values` and `task.assessability`. `module-kit` checks them, and their vectors the CI of `spec` checks by the schema and the YAML rules, like the vectors of the other rules of a task; `task.trap-values` is among the rules of the answer slot that `spec` checks at a vector's item.
- **The verdict vectors** are `format/vectors/verdicts/<kind>/<case>.yaml` by the schema `verdict-vector.schema.json`: an item with its checks and its readings — the value of each slot with the verdict of the slot and of the item.
  - `format-check` computes the verdicts as a second implementation, as it builds the open view, and the CI of `module-kit` passes the same vectors.
  - The predicate is an exception: `spec` has no Starlark, and it computes only "blank" and "not in notation".
  - The rest of an observation the vectors do not hold: they hold only the value.
- **The predicate's step limit is in the format:** the same expression on the same value makes the same steps on any machine, and the verdict repeats by the stored value. The clock, its figure and concurrent runs are `module-kit`'s.
- **What v0 does not have:** text, edit, quantity, order and set, widget state and "steps" — a check of each line of the course of solution. Each will come as a new kind, with a minor version.

Normative: the [format text](../format/README.md), its rules on the task and on checks.

— *Why:*
- The check, its kinds and the vectors are the plan's proposal, and the predicate and its limits are decided together with them.
- **Normalization follows canvas-api** ([canvas-api@0901af0](https://github.com/mathtrail/canvas-api/tree/0901af0)): «Unicode NFKC; юникодные минусы и тире заменяются на `-`; пробелы по краям убираются», «Знак `=` в начале и знаки `.`, `!`, `?` в конце отбрасываются: «= 7» и «7.» — это 7», «Слово единицы в конце отбрасывается», and the whitelist of notations comes before parsing; the comparison is `big.Rat`, and «`3/6` и `0.5` равны». The differences:
  - a decimal and a common fraction are in one kind, `number`, like `number` of canvas-api, and an integer is in it too;
  - a superscript digit is "not in notation": NFKC makes `7²` the number 72 (Node 24.21, ICU 78.3, Unicode 17.0);
  - a fraction like `½` that a number adjoins is "not in notation": NFKC would make `1½` the notation `11⁄2`, eleven halves, and a mixed number would get "not yet" rather than "unreadable". A review found the error in the code of `format-check` on Node 24.21;
  - for a choice, `=` and a period are not dropped: they can be the answer.
- **In doubt, "unreadable", not "not yet"**: a false alarm is worse than no check, as in canvas-api ([canvas-api@0901af0](https://github.com/mathtrail/canvas-api/tree/0901af0)): «`INCORRECT` получает только разборчивый, однозначный ответ правильной формы». So a read value that is not among the options of a choice without `notation: word` is "unreadable" too: `7` in a box for a sign is a doubt in the reading, not the learner's error. But an answer slot read confidently and wrong is no longer a doubt, and the item with it is "not yet".
- **A reducible fraction where an irreducible one is needed is "not yet",** as `tutor` plans: «несокращённая дробь там, где нужна сокращённая, — «пока нет»» (RUN.md `tutor`, commit 49f4c6a).
- **The predicate is an expression,** not a program: a short check is visible in the task itself, and it needs neither a line of the layout nor a rule about files. standalone's solver programs — the files `content/examples/solvers/<id>.star` (SPEC 1.5 and 6 standalone, commit 99d8a65) — are needed by the keys of templates, and they come as the template's solver. The step limit is as in standalone, `thread.SetMaxExecutionSteps`, but smaller: an expression of one number does not need 25,000,000 steps.
- **The predicate's vectors are a part:** there is no mature Starlark in JavaScript. `starlark-webasm` 1.0.3 is Apache-2.0, about 5 MB of WASM, published 2022-04-11 (the npm registry, read 2026-10-27), and its go.starlark.net is older than the one `module-kit` will take.
- **Without "steps":** no module of the slice takes them, the measurement of AI reading did not return a verdict by lines, and canvas-api removed the exact equivalence of steps from the product ([canvas-api@0901af0](https://github.com/mathtrail/canvas-api/tree/0901af0)).
- **A vertical fraction:** without the rule one reader would write `3/4`, another "3 over 4", and the verdict would depend on the reader. The measurement of the workbook by `tutor`, «Итог замера тетради»: with such a rule of the prompt, Opus 5.5 · `high` gets 27 readings out of 33 correct for vertical fractions and 29 out of 33 for fractions in a line. Haiku 5.5 · `low` has three times more extra "unreadable" for vertical ones — 16 out of 99 against 5 out of 99.
- **A mirrored digit:** that the rule holds only if the reader sees the mirroring, and that the row of the eval set measures it, is the executor's proposal, and so is the rule about letters.
  - The first measurement of the workbook, on synthetic data without a caption, at 32 px: mirrored boxes were read correctly in 0 out of 15 by Opus, in 8 out of 45 by Haiku · `low` and in 5 out of 45 by Haiku without thinking. False alarms on them — 8 out of 15, 9 out of 45 and 14 out of 45: the models read a mirrored 5 as 2, and a 2 as 5, that is, they did not notice the mirroring. On boxes without peculiarities nobody has false alarms.
  - The large run of `tutor`, «Итог большого прогона»: the workbook of 300 pages of synthetic data without a caption at 32 px, with Opus 5.5 · `high`, Haiku 5.5 · `low`, Haiku 5.5 · `medium` and Sonnet without thinking. Nobody has a false "correct": 0 out of 600. The false alarms are almost all on two kinds of boxes: mirrored digits — from 279 out of 900 with Opus to 369 with Sonnet, 31–41 %; crossed out and written again — 93–104 out of 600, about 16 %, recorded only as data for the target; on boxes without peculiarities — correct ones and ones with a similar digit — 0–1 out of 900. On 900 boxes no model reaches the target, and a false alarm hits a correct solution, while "unreadable" does not punish the learner.
  - The first measurement of the rule, the row of mirrored digits of the workbook's eval set, `tutor`'s «Итог зеркальной цифры»: the rule works but does not hold the target, and synthetic data are data for the measurement on children's handwriting, not a reason to change the target or the rule. Version 2 of the workbook reading prompt, where the reader marks a mirrored digit and the box gets "unreadable", against version 1 on the same pages of the large run — 280 pages, 840 mirrored boxes: Opus 5.5 · `high` sent 653 mirrored boxes to "unreadable", 586 of them with the mark, false alarms 179, 21 %, and with version 1 254, 30 %; Haiku 5.5 · `medium` 612, 371 and 186, 22 %, and with version 1 324, 39 %; on the 1960 other filled boxes there are 0 and 2 marks "mirrored", and no more extra "unreadable" than with version 1: 68 against 73 and 110 against 136. The rest of the false alarms is the confusion of 2 and 5, where the mirroring is not visible, with no mark. Synthetic data give no admission, and the measurement on children's handwriting repeats the measure.
- **The observation:** the plan's recommendation.

— *Rejected:*
- the check on the item, with keys by the place of the answer slots: there would be one kind in a line, and the number of keys would need one more rule;
- a kind "text" with options and normalization for signs and words by hand — its defaults would freeze from v1, and for signs a choice by hand is enough; a separate kind "sign"; a workbook page without signs;
- open criteria of a rubric: then the kind by which the schema branches would be open too;
- assessability without a rule or only for items with a key;
- vectors only by the schema, without a second implementation; `starlark-webasm` in `tools/`;
- the predicate as a file `predicates/<id>.star` in the module layout;
- the key as a YAML number; a decimal comma and digit group separators in v0;
- "steps" in v0;
- a vertical fraction as "unreadable" until the format takes a two-storey fraction, or deciding it together with that: a correct fraction would wait for a format version;
- a mirrored digit given as the digit itself, counted in the 1 % target: no model holds the target, and a false alarm hits a correct solution;
- measuring mirrored digits as a separate row outside the target while the models do not read them: the target would stop counting an error that hits a correct solution; keeping mirrored digits as a separate target until the measurement on children's handwriting;
- not measuring mirrored digits; recording nothing of the first measurement of the rule.

— *Consequence:* `format/README.md`; `task.schema.json` — the field `check`; `verdict-vector.schema.json`; the examples of tasks with keys; the vectors of rules, of the open view and of verdicts; `format-check` — `verdicts.mjs`; `docs/concepts.md`; `docs/architecture.md`; `docs/repositories.md`; `docs/product.md`; `contracts/README.md`; the README and CLAUDE.md of `spec`; `docs/decisions.md`.

## Traps, techniques, solving steps and hints

**R57. The trap and technique catalogs and the solving steps are files at the root of the module: `traps.yaml`, `techniques.yaml` and `solving-steps.yaml`. The solving steps are data of the format, which the platform does not run. A trap by a wrong value is in the slot check, and the traps that AI may suppose are named by the task. The task carries the "givens and unknown", the techniques, the solution, the leak phrases, and its item the simpler case. The fallback texts of the ladder are the trap text, the trap advice and the module's rung template from the manifest. The leak check is strict and searches tasks, their instances and lessons; how it searches is said normatively by the [format text](../format/README.md), in its rule on the leak check, and its vectors are `format/vectors/leaks/`, and `spec` computes them itself.**
- **The catalogs are files at the root,** dictionaries by local ID, like the skills in the skill graph:
  - the trap catalog `traps.yaml` — the description, the skills and the advice `trap_advice` of each trap;
  - the technique catalog `techniques.yaml` — the name and the description of each technique;
  - the solving steps `solving-steps.yaml` — the steps in order.

  Each of them is optional. A published trap ID names no other trap.
- **A trap by a wrong value is in the slot check,** `trap_values`: the value, the trap and, optionally, the trap text — what the learner will read at this error.
  - The value is compared by the check like the key, with the same normalization, and names the trap only when the verdict is "not yet".
  - Such traps exist for `number`, `fraction` and `choice`: a predicate has no key, and a rubric has no verdict.
  - The rule `task.trap-values`: a trap value gets "not yet", for a choice it is an option as written, and no two values of one check are equal by its comparison.
  - The verdict vectors name the matched trap, and `format-check` computes it.
- **The traps that AI supposes** by the kind of error in the work are the task's field `traps`; their provenance is "derived by AI". Traps of both kinds come only from the catalog (`task.known-traps`).
- **The trap advice is `trap_advice`,** as the term of the glossary and the format's example: what to suggest to an adult or the learner at this error. Progress shows it, and it is also the fallback text when a trap value has no text of its own. The skills of a trap are the IDs of the module's skills (`traps.known-skills`).
- **The fields of a task**:
  - `givens` and `unknown` — the "givens and unknown", open;
  - `techniques` — techniques from the catalog (`task.known-techniques`), closed;
  - `solution` — texts and pictures, as in the task statement, closed. The schema requires it of a task that has an item with a verdict: a format rule is only what the schema does not express;
  - `leak_phrases` — leak phrases, closed;
  - `leading_question` — from format 0.4, a leading question, closed, which "Hint" gives with the technique before the first incorrect answer;
  - for an item, `simpler_case`, the simpler case, closed.
- **Open** is what the learner may see before the answer and what does not suggest the method: the solving steps with exit conditions, the "givens and unknown" and the technique catalog, like the skills in the skill map. **Closed** are the task's techniques — their name suggests the method of solution, like the names of a task's skills — and also the trap catalog, the traps and texts of the task, the simpler case, the leak phrases and the solution. `api` gives a task's technique at the learner's request, and records this.
- **Where they lie:** the trap catalog and the closed fields of a task lie in the canonical view, the server part. The open views of the technique catalog and the solving steps, the latter unused, `api` gives by the digest of any package of its image, through `PackageService`, like the open view of the manifest with its rung templates.
- **A solving step** is a name `title`, `gives` — what the step gives, `givens` or `techniques`, — and an exit condition `exit_condition`: `givens_ticked`, `answer_slots_filled` or `none`. A step with `givens_ticked` gives `givens`, and the widget's state will come with stage 4. No screen leads a learner by them: a task of a module is solved on the sheet of a task from paper, with no steps.
- **Fallback texts**:
  - at rungs 1–2 — the text of the trap value, without it the advice of its trap, and without that the rung template;
  - at the third rung — the item's simpler case, and without it the same as at the second.

  A rung, its words and the fallback text speak of the rung's answer slot — the first answer slot "not yet" in order in the submission that gave the rung: items by place, answer slots by order in the item; so the fallback text speaks of one answer slot when a submission has several wrong ones. The rung templates belong to the module: two different texts `rung_templates` in the manifest, in the explanation language. A module with an item with a verdict cannot do without them (`manifest.rung-templates`).
- **A request before the first wrong answer** gives the "givens and unknown" and the task's technique — without AI and without reading the work; a submission that had only "unreadable" or "unchecked" gives no rung. There is no sketch "how to start" in v0: it will come as a minor version when `canvas` learns to draw it. A request after a wrong answer gives the words of the current rung once more, without AI, and "explain differently" the same rung in other words.
- **The leak check** — normatively, the [format text](../format/README.md), in its rule on the leak check:
  - searched for are the keys `number`, `fraction` and `choice` of all items of the task and all its leak phrases;
  - a key that itself is found in the text of the task statement and in the `alt` of its pictures, in the text and line of its own item and in the options of its answer slots `choice` is not searched for: the leak phrases hold it. So the key of a tapped choice is never searched for;
  - the normal form is step 1 of the normalization of numbers and the normalization of a choice, as the format's rule on checks gives them; the letters of a word are the categories L, M and N;
  - a string is found whole, with a boundary where its edge is a letter of a word; a number by value and by absolute value;
  - numbers in words and notations that the check does not read as a number are caught only by leak phrases;
  - the rule `task.no-leaks` checks the author's texts that the learner sees before solving, the leading question among them.
- **The check stays strict.** The false leaks of the AI's hints — a hint that repeats the learner's own correct line, or carries a number of the key not as the answer — are handled by the prompt and the fallback text, not by exceptions in the check.
- **At a template** `task.no-leaks` goes over each instance: the instance's texts and the path of each of its pictures against its keys, and the text of the whole module against the keys of all instances. So the rung template, the trap advice and a technique hold no numbers that the key of an instance may be. The trap values, simpler cases, solution and leak phrases of a template carry placeholders and are checked on the instances.
- **In lessons** the rule `lesson.no-leaks` searches for the keys and leak phrases of each task of a lesson in all its texts — in the title, in the explanations, in the task statement and demo of worked examples, and after the task too: the open view of a lesson goes to the device whole, and the key does not go there before solving. `task.no-leaks` searches the module's texts outside lessons. No rule searches for a task in the texts of other lessons and in the texts of another task of the same lesson: a worked example SHOULD NOT solve a task of the module, and a lesson SHOULD NOT name two tasks where the texts of one give the answer of the other, as the [format text](../format/README.md) says in its rules on the leak check and on lessons. In a worked example on the workbook `lesson.no-leaks` finds a leak only when a line of the example with its values equals a line of a task of the lesson with its keys, and the search for numbers sees neither the separate numbers of its lines nor the numbers of `numbered_list`.
- **A number in the text of the whole module** — the rung template `rung_templates`, the trap advice `trap_advice`, the name and description of a technique — `module-kit` warns about but does not refuse. The warning is about each number of the text, as the leak check reads it (the [format text](../format/README.md), "What is read as a number"). It is not a rule, like the one about a picture with transparent points: it has neither an ID nor vectors, it does not reject a module, and it does not require a format version. It is `module-kit`'s.
- **Leak vectors** — `format/vectors/leaks/<case>.yaml` by the schema `leak-vector.schema.json`, the fourth schema without a part. `format-check` computes them with a second implementation, `leaks.mjs`, and CI of `module-kit` passes the same vectors.
- **Step 1 of normalization** also replaces a fraction like `½` that a number adjoins: otherwise NFKC makes `1½` the notation `11⁄2`, and the learner would get a false "not yet".
- **The format example** `format/examples/traps/valid/olympiad-math.yaml` holds no numbers in its trap advice: the advice of `wrong-parity` is "Check the rule on a few small sums first, then say it out loud.", the advice of `time-unit-mixup` is "Draw a clock face and count on in minutes, remembering how many minutes an hour has.", in the words the module already writes.
  - The `skills` and descriptions of two traps follow standalone's tasks at 42b4408, not its SPEC ([standalone@42b4408](https://github.com/mathtrail/mathtrail-standalone/tree/42b4408)). The `skills` of a trap decide against which skill the error counts, so the example takes them from the tasks: for `part-whole-swap` — `fractions-parts`, `percent-basic` and `ratio-sharing`, for `percent-wrong-base` — `percent-basic`. One task of `logic.sets` with each of `part_whole_swap` and `ratio_total_confusion` is a case, not the skill of the error, and does not go into `skills`. The description of `part-whole-swap` names the trap by its ID in the format, `percent-wrong-base`, and the description of `percent-wrong-base` names each wrong quantity of its tasks: the new instead of the old, the part instead of the whole and the other way round. The vectors name the IDs of these traps, and read neither `skills` nor descriptions.
  - The trap `twelve-hours-off`, which `modules` set up for the 12-hour slip at the kind `time`, is taken word for word: the description "Wrote an afternoon or evening time as a clock face shows it, counting the hours again from noon.", the skill `time-clocks` and the advice "After noon the hours of the day go on counting, so add the hours from midnight to noon to the hour on the clock face.", without numbers. The trap's name is in the vector `format/vectors/verdicts/time/hours-and-minutes.yaml`, and its values in five tasks `clk-*` of `modules` with a key after 12:59. The kind `time` does not know a 12-hour clock face: the trap holds the slip, and a parameter of 12 or 24 hours waits for a request from content.
  - These are editorial changes of the example, without a new format version, and the file's header names the texts that are not from standalone.

Normative: the [format text](../format/README.md), its rules on the module, the manifest, the task, checks, the three catalogs, hints, the leak check and lessons.

— *Why:* the plan's proposal.
- **Traps follow standalone:** "The catalog stays closed for the same reason the topic catalog does: `trap_hit` is what makes a wrong answer a diagnosis, and free-form trap names cannot be counted" and "Each trap carries its advice" (SPEC 1.3 standalone, commit 99d8a65, read 2026-10-27). The differences: a task's trap is found by the value, not by the letter of an option, and a trap has skills, as the vocabulary defines a trap.
- **A trap by value and the fallback texts follow canvas-api** ([canvas-api@0901af0](https://github.com/mathtrail/canvas-api/tree/0901af0)): the task has `traps: {"6": "…"}`, and «Ответ совпадает с ловушкой по тем же правилам»; «на ступенях 1–2 — текст ловушки, который автор задачи написал для этого неверного ответа, а если такого нет — шаблон ступени; на ступени 3 — случай попроще от автора задачи». The difference is that the rung template belongs to the module, not the service: a module has one explanation language, and the platform does not need to translate templates into the language of each module.
- **A key from the text of its own item is not searched for** — this is a departure from canvas-api ([canvas-api@0901af0](https://github.com/mathtrail/canvas-api/tree/0901af0)), where «Ключ запрещён всегда — даже если это слово есть в самом условии». Because of this rule canvas-api removed a task in which the leak check «пришлось бы запрещать «no», «never», «cannot»», and `tutor` asked how not to take for a leak «законную цифру ключа — «2 ноги»» (RUN.md `tutor`, commit 8451728). standalone did not count as giving away what is said in the task statement either ([standalone@42b4408](https://github.com/mathtrail/mathtrail-standalone/tree/42b4408)).
- **Numbers in words are leak phrases,** not tables of the platform. canvas-api translated "seven" into 7, but such a table is needed for each language, and modules are written in any. In the measurement bank of `tutor` the leak phrases are «сверх самого ключа» (`tutor`'s `docs/architecture.md`, commit 8451728).
- **What is open follows the prototype:** "Understand: tap what we know and what we need to find", "Plan: a technique card" ([draft/README.md](../draft/README.md)). standalone's hint "arrives with the task and is revealed locally, and the fact that it was opened travels with the answer" ([standalone@42b4408](https://github.com/mathtrail/mathtrail-standalone/tree/42b4408)). A technique, though, is closed, like a task's skills, and `api` gives it.
- **The solution is by the schema:** a format rule is what the schema does not express, and "has an item with a verdict" the schema expresses by open fields.
- **`gives` of a step:** physics has no step "plan", so the step itself says what it gives.
- **The check stays strict:** the check is a safeguard: if it did not search for the key and phrases that the reading found in the learner's notation, it would depend on the AI's reading. What the measurement of hints of `tutor` found, «Итог замера подсказок»: on 34 synthetic sheets with an error, three configurations gave 612 hints, and the leak check caught 49:
  - 30 repeat the learner's own correct line — "3x = 12", "x − 3 = 5": the leak phrases of the measurement banks are solving steps, and those are what the learner writes. All are Haiku's;
  - 13 carry a number of the key not as the answer, most often in the similar case of rung 3: "□ + 2 = 5" with the key 2. Here belong all 6 caught at Opus 5.5 · `high`;
  - 4 name or confirm the answer — all Haiku's;
  - 2 are a phrase of the bank in the reasoning of rung 3, where the bank expected it.

  The rule "a key that already stands in the text of its own item is not searched for" does not cover the first two kinds. With Opus, 6 hints out of 204, about 3 %, got the fallback text because of a leak: its prompt tells it to name the learner's notation in words and not to copy its numbers.
- **The warning about a number:** the [format text](../format/README.md) says SHOULD of such a number in its rule on the leak check, and the rule `task.no-leaks` finds it only when it is already the key of a task that shows the text: so epic E3 of `modules` found numbers in the advice of `wrong-parity` and `time-unit-mixup` of the format example, by a task for each, over three tasks of the epic. The warning finds a number before a task or a template instance with such a key comes.
- **The skills of the example's traps:** standalone's SPEC names for `percent_wrong_base` the topics `percent.basic` and `ratio.sharing`, and for `part_whole_swap` `fractions.parts` and `percent.basic`, but the tasks at 42b4408 give `part_whole_swap` in five tasks of `ratio.sharing` too, and `percent_wrong_base` only in `percent.basic`, and not only "from the new price instead of the old one" (`content/examples/` and `SPEC.md` of [standalone@42b4408](https://github.com/mathtrail/mathtrail-standalone/tree/42b4408)).
- **`twelve-hours-off`:** the example takes the trap that `modules` set up, an editorial change like the edit of the advice of `wrong-parity` and `time-unit-mixup`.

— *Rejected:*
- catalogs as folders, a file per trap, and one file of all catalogs;
- a trap beside the slot check and a trap in the task by the places of the item and the answer slot;
- a key that is always searched for, as in canvas-api, and a length threshold below which a key is not searched for;
- open techniques of a task and closed "givens and unknown";
- the rung template at the platform, and a template at the module or the platform;
- the sketch "how to start" in v0, and also nothing before the first submission;
- rules of the leak check only as data, and leak vectors at `module-kit`;
- the solution as a format rule, not by the schema;
- `advice` instead of `trap_advice`; the exit condition `givens_marked`: «пометка — mark» is already taken;
- not searching for the key and phrases that the reading observation found in the learner's notation;
- the similar case of rung 3 only from the module, `simpler_case`, not from AI. Return to this if modules give simpler cases;
- a rule with an ID for a number in the text of the whole module — SHOULD is not a rule, and a number in advice is harmless while no task that shows it holds it as its key; only an edit of the example — the next number would again be found only by the key of a new task; leaving the example — a module that takes the catalogs word for word would depart from it;
- widening `time-unit-mixup` to the 12-hour slip — one advice would mix minutes and hours; a parameter of the kind `time` — a new format version.

— *Consequence:* `format/README.md`; the schemas `traps`, `techniques`, `solving-steps` and `leak-vector`, and those of the task, the manifest and the verdict vectors; the examples of the three catalogs, `format/examples/traps/valid/olympiad-math.yaml` among them, solutions and rung templates in the examples of tasks and manifests; the vectors of rules, of the open view, of verdicts and `format/vectors/leaks/`; `format-check` — `leaks.mjs`; `docs/concepts.md`; `docs/architecture.md`; `docs/repositories.md`; `docs/decisions.md`.

## Lessons

**R58. A lesson is a file `lessons/<id>.yaml`: the module's skills it teaches, and segments in the author's order — explanations, worked examples and the module's tasks by ID. The demo is parts of a worked example on its canvas, a handwriting sheet or, from format 0.4, a workbook. The order of lessons is set by the skill graph: there is no separate field of order.**
- **The lesson's skills** are `skills`, the module's skills by local ID (`lesson.known-skills`). They are closed, like a task's skills: the app needs only the lesson's title, and the engine reads the skills. Each task of the lesson trains at least one of them as primary — its item's skill or, without one, the task's skill (`lesson.task-skills`).
- **The lesson's segments** are `segments`, in order and without repeats. A segment is an object with exactly one field:
  - `explanation` — an explanation: paragraphs and pictures, like the parts of a task statement, and the numbered list `numbered_list` — texts in order, whose numbers the app draws and the search for numbers does not see;
  - `worked_example` — a worked example;
  - `task` — a task of the module by its ID (`lesson.known-tasks`), or a template. The next segment comes when the task has ended. In a lesson the learner goes through one instance of a template — by the seed of their attempt.

  There is no special check segment at the end: the check is the last tasks of the lesson, and the format does not mark them.
- **A worked example** is not a task: no answer slots, no key, and it does not serve as evidence.
  - It has a task statement, a canvas — a handwriting sheet or, from format 0.4, the canvas `workbook`, the example's lines with boxes — and `demo` — the demo: parts of the example's solution, which the learner opens one at a time and can hide all at once. A part is a paragraph, a picture beside the sheet or a picture on a sheet area; on a workbook, the demo fills the boxes step by step, and the lines fit the page by the workbook's page, `page.yaml`.
  - The area `area` is a rectangle of the sheet in its units, like a zone, and it lies on the sheet (`lesson.areas`). A picture on an area stands on the layer of the demo, at the size of the area.
  - The learner does not write on the example's canvas: there is no work of the learner there.
  - The example is open: what the open view keeps from the learner is the key and the solution of a task, and an example is not a task. So its parts are `demo`, not `solution`: a task's solution is never opened.
- **The order of lessons follows the skill graph.**
  - Lesson A comes after lesson B when a skill of A needs, through the module's prerequisites, a skill of B that is not among the skills of A. Anchor skills give no order.
  - A graph without cycles does not guarantee an order without a cycle: a lesson [a, c] and a lesson [b], where b requires a and c requires b, each come after the other. Hence the rule `lesson.order`.
  - Where the graph gives no order — two lessons of one skill, skills without a link — the engine's rule chooses.
  - **The graph is a chain** when the module has no fewer than two skills and each stands in its own tier: then one chain of prerequisites passes through all the module's skills, and the module is sequential. An extra link — a skill needs both `a` and `b`, and `b` needs `a` — does not change the order of lessons and does not break the chain, and an anchor skill gives no tier. The app infers the mark "sequential" from `skill_tiers`.
- **Adaptation.** The segments go in the author's order, and the engine does not reorder them.
  - In a lesson whose skills are not all with a verdict, the engine adds nothing and skips nothing: the lesson goes in the author's order, without adaptation.
  - Whether the engine adds consolidation to a lesson whose skills are all with a verdict, and whether it ends it early, is decided by the detailing of `engine`.
- **Age** is the lesson's `age_categories`, as for a task, closed. A lesson is given only to a learner whom both the lesson and each of its tasks suit. Otherwise a task only for adults would reach a child in a lesson where nothing is skipped. The rule `lesson.age-categories`: the lesson's categories are from the manifest, and at least one category suits both the lesson and each of its tasks: a lesson that no learner will get is an error.
- **Open** are `id`, `title` and the segments with all their fields: the app runs the lesson. **Closed** are the skills and the age categories: they lie in the canonical view, and the open view of a lesson `api` gives whole and only to a learner whom the lesson and each of its tasks suit. So there are no open views of lessons in the device part, one for all learners.
- **The leak check in a lesson** is the rule `lesson.no-leaks`: neither the lesson's title, nor its explanations, nor the task statement and demo of its examples contain the keys and leak phrases of its tasks, searched as the leak check searches; for a template, the key of each instance. All texts are searched, after the task too: the open view of a lesson goes to the device whole, and the key does not go there before solving. In an example on a workbook it finds a leak only when a line of the example with its values equals a line of a task of the lesson with its keys, and does not see the separate numbers of its lines. `format-check` computes the rule itself, like `task.no-leaks`.
- **The lesson's pictures** are files of the module (`lesson.known-pictures`).
- **Common definitions.** The parts of a task statement, the canvas and the rectangle of a sheet are in `common.schema.json`, so that the lesson does not refer to the task's schema.

Normative: the [format text](../format/README.md), its rule on lessons, and its rules on open fields, test vectors, the module, the skill graph, the task and the leak check.

— *Why:* the plan's recommendations, and a finding of the review: the leak check searches all the texts of a lesson, not only those before the task's segment. The rest here is the plan's proposal.
- **The order through the graph:** "A sequential module's graph is a chain, and the engine goes along it as along any graph", and "the next lesson is still chosen by the engine".
  - In the prototype the mark *Sequential* cannot move the package: "Next in a sequential module" is only a line (`draft/NovaTrail Widget.html`, commit 4846d00, read 2026-10-27).
  - In standalone the author does not set the order either: "those never handed out come first, in catalog order", and "Nor does the rule read the links between topics" (SPEC 3.1 and 3.2 standalone, commit 4dece74, read 2026-10-27).
  - The difference is that here the rule reads the graph: the engine orders lessons by the skill graph.
- **The chain by tiers** is the recommendation of `app`.
- **A worked example on the sheet** follows the demo layer of the canvas in the vocabulary and in `canvas`: it has the layer `show`, «HTML и SVG; в первом коде пуст», and HTML on the sheet is «блок 1000 × 1400 единиц с матрицей» (`canvas`'s `docs/architecture.md`, commit f162153, read 2026-10-27). A picture on a sheet area is what this layer will draw without a new format of strokes.
  - Closest to a lesson in MathTrail is the topic page of standalone's site: "how such tasks are solved: the steps of the move, then examples worked through to their answers" ([standalone@42b4408](https://github.com/mathtrail/mathtrail-standalone/tree/42b4408)). Its examples are `examples[]` with `question`, `steps` and `answer` in `site/content/en/topics/gaps-and-boundaries.yaml`.
- **The lesson's skills are closed** — by the same argument as a task's skills: the name of a skill suggests the method of solving the lesson's tasks.
- **A segment is one field with `minProperties` and `maxProperties`,** not `oneOf`. In ajv 8.20.0 a `oneOf` of three `required` gives four errors for one breakage, and an invalid example names one. `$ref` beside `oneOf` is settled by the format's conventions for writing a schema.
- **Names.** «Шаг» (step) is already taken by the solving step, «решение» (solution) is closed, «разбор» is the short name of the review of the course of solution, and «место» and «область» are the place of a schema, a place on the canvas and the area of an item. Hence «звено урока | segment», «показ автора | demo» and «участок листа | area».

— *Rejected:*
- a mark "sequential" in the manifest with a list of lessons; a lesson that names the lesson before it as the default path;
- a strict path, where a skill has no more than one prerequisite in the module and no more than one skill after it — a graph with an extra link, as in the vector `format/vectors/tiers/longest-chain.yaml`, orders the lessons the same way but would not get the mark; not defining the chain — `app` and the skill map could mark the module differently;
- a lesson without a rule about the skills of its tasks; the lesson's skills inferred from its tasks — then there is no lesson without tasks, like a lesson of reading sample essays;
- a worked example outside the canvas, with the demo layer as a minor version; the demo over a lesson's task too;
- a check segment at the end, without hints and with the solution after the whole check;
- a lesson in which the engine never adds or skips anything, and consolidation with an early end, allowed by the format itself;
- the leak check in a lesson's text only as SHOULD advice, and only before the task's segment: the text after the task is already on the device;
- a segment through `oneOf`; a reference of the lesson's schema to the task's schema; a field `solution` of an example; the names `place`, `working` and `steps`.

— *Consequence:* `format/README.md`; the schema `lesson`; the parts of a task statement, the canvas and the rectangle of a sheet in `common`; the examples of lessons of the three modules of the slice, invalid examples and the module `with-lessons`; the vectors of the rules of a lesson and of its open view; `format-check` — `lesson.no-leaks` in `leaks.mjs` and `cases.mjs`; `docs/concepts.md`; `docs/architecture.md`; `docs/repositories.md`; `docs/product.md`; `docs/decisions.md`.

## The generator of randomness

**R59. The platform's generator is PCG, as in Go's `math/rand/v2`, and the stream of a place of randomness is derived as in standalone's simulator: FNV-1a 64 of the seed and the place's names, and the seed itself. Over the stream five Go functions are normative. The text is the [format text](../format/README.md), in its rule on randomness, and the vectors are `format/vectors/random/`, and `spec` computes them itself.**
- **The generator** is PCG with 128 bits of state, exactly the `PCG` of Go's package `math/rand/v2`:
  - the state is two words, the high and the low, taken from the words of the seed as they are;
  - the step is `state · M + C mod 2^128`, with Go's constants;
  - the output is DXSM after the step.

  This is not numpy's PCG64DXSM and not a cryptographically secure generator. The algorithm is set by the format itself, not by a library.
- **A place of randomness** is a seed, an unsigned 64-bit integer, and a non-empty list of names. A name is a non-empty string without "|", and names are compared as written.
  - The stream of a place is a generator with the words: FNV-1a 64 (RFC 9923) of the UTF-8 text "the seed in decimal digits, and then '|' and the name, for each name" and the seed itself.
  - A new place is new names, and it does not shift the numbers of the earlier places. `seeded` of standalone's simulator is a place of the main seed with the names "experiment, unit, assignment".
  - For reference: the places of one seed share the low word of the state, and FNV-1a is not resistant to collisions. For the places of a module and of a run this does not matter.
- **The functions**, as Go's methods, and how many integers each takes: an integer (`Uint64`), a number below a bound (`Uint64N`: a power of two by a mask, otherwise Lemire's method with rejection), a number in a range (`a + Int64N(c − a + 1)`), a fraction of 53 bits (`Float64`) and the Fisher–Yates permutation (`Perm` and `Shuffle`). The format has no normal and no exponential distributions.
- **The platform's seeds:**
  - `api` takes the seed of an attempt from a cryptographically secure source and keeps it with the attempt. Neither it nor the state of its places goes to the device: the state of a place shows its seed;
  - the places of a module are places of the seed of its attempt, and the first name says whose place it is. A task template has one place, the seed of the attempt with the names `template`, the task's ID and `instance`, and it gives one call `below(count)`: the number of the instance. A template has no other places in format v0, and a new one is a minor version;
  - a widget has its own seed, and how it gets it is decided by the widget protocol (Т-24);
  - `engine`, if it needs randomness, and `sim` have their own seeds, of the choice and of the run, and their own names.
- **The vectors** are `format/vectors/random/<case>.yaml` by the schema `random-vector.schema.json`: the start of the stream — the words and, if the stream is a place, its seed and names — and the calls of the functions in order, each with its value. `format-check` derives each state and computes each value with a second implementation, `random.mjs`. And `random.mjs` repeats the golden outputs of Go and RFC 9923 in its tests.
- **Versions** are the format's: the generator has no version of its own.

Normative: the [format text](../format/README.md), its rule on randomness, and edits of its opening, its versions, its files and its test vectors.

— *Why:*
- **Not waiting for `module-kit` and `engine`:** neither had started its first task, nor the tasks before it (`module-kit`, commit 1a54028; `engine`, commit 08bc48a; read 2026-10-27). The generator is a question of the register of `spec`, and the format's tasks after it would wait with it.
- **PCG from Go** is the generator that standalone's simulator and `tutor` already take. Go promises the streams not by the package's documentation but thus:
  - the blog post "Evolving the Go Standard Library with math/rand/v2" (go.dev/blog/randv2, 2024-05-01): "Go 1 compatibility included the specific random outputs for a given seed", and "The concrete rand.Rand API is now locked in to that value stream";
  - and `regress_test.go`: "Do NOT make changes to the golden outputs" (Go, commit b98d22c1, read 2026-10-27).

  So the format sets the algorithm itself, and the vectors will catch a divergence. A port on BigInt repeated Go's golden outputs exactly.
- **The derivation as in the simulator** — the platform's one generator takes the simulator's scheme as it is, and with it `sim` will repeat its streams. The simulator keeps the same promise: "a generator added leaves every child of the others as they were" (docs/learners.md standalone, commit 4dece74). FNV-1a 64 is RFC 9923, February 2026 (read 2026-10-27). There is nowhere to take a synchronous SHA-256 in the browser from: `crypto.subtle.digest` returns a Promise (W3C Web Cryptography Level 2, draft 2025-04-22, read 2026-10-27).
- **Go's functions, without the normal and the exponential distributions:** otherwise two consumers would make a range differently. And `Math.exp` and `Math.log` in JS give implementation-approximated values (ECMA-262, draft 2026-10-23, read 2026-10-27), and Go on arm64 fuses a multiplication with an addition: "On arm64 the last digits may differ, since Go fuses a multiplication and an addition there" (docs/learners.md standalone, commit 4dece74, read 2026-10-27).
- **The seed of an attempt does not go to the device:** the state of a place contains the seed itself, and the generator is not cryptographically secure. The seed carries nothing about the learner, so this does not change privacy.

— *Rejected:*
- waiting for the recommendations of `module-kit` and `engine`;
- SplitMix64 — it does not repeat the simulator's numbers — and ChaCha8, complex in JS;
- a derivation where the second word is SplitMix64 of the first;
- only a stream of integers, without functions over it;
- a document and a version of its own for the generator; vectors that only `module-kit` computes;
- Go in the container of `spec` for the sake of the vectors: Go's golden outputs in the tests of `random.mjs` and CI of `module-kit` check the same without it;
- the vector fields `n`, `pcg` and `uint64`: `n` is rejected by the rule `yaml.plain-strings`, and the others are not words.

— *Consequence:* `format/README.md`; `format/schemas/random-vector.schema.json` and the vectors `format/vectors/random/`; `tools/format-check/random.mjs`; `docs/concepts.md`; `docs/architecture.md`; `docs/repositories.md`; `docs/decisions.md`.

## Task templates

**R60. A module's tasks are a published pool and templates with parameters; there is no generation on the fly. A template is a task with the field `template`: parameters with domains, derived numbers, a constraint and, optionally, a solver, and the expressions are a narrow subset of Starlark. The key of each instance is known already at the module's check: `module-kit` enumerates all combinations, no more than 10,000, and checks each instance by all the rules of a task, and an attempt gets an instance by its seed. The text is the [format text](../format/README.md), in its rule on templates, and the vectors are `format/vectors/templates/`, and `spec` computes them itself.**
- **Tasks with the help of AI** only in the preparation of a module, and the author checks them; there is no generation on the fly.
- **A template** is a task in `tasks/<id>.yaml` with the field `template`, closed whole:
  - `parameters` — a name and a domain, integers from `from` to `to`, each within ±(2^53−1);
  - `derived` — derived numbers, each an expression of the parameters;
  - `constraint` — a constraint, a boolean expression of the parameters and derived numbers;
  - `solver` — optionally, a Starlark program and the names of its results.

  A name is lowercase letters, digits and `_`, starting with a letter, no longer than 14 characters, and not a keyword or a reserved word of Starlark. A lesson names a template as a task, and the learner model and the engine see one task.
- **Expressions** are a narrow subset of Starlark: integers and names, `+`, `-`, `*`, `//`, `%`, comparisons without chains, `and`, `or` and `not`. Types are checked: arithmetic and comparisons are of integers, logic of `bool`. The meaning is Starlark's: integers without a bound, division rounding down, an error at division by zero, and `and` and `or` evaluate the right operand only when the left does not decide. An expression is up to 1000 characters; from format 0.4 it begins with a token and is nested no deeper than 64 levels — a bracket, a unary `-` or `not` —, and `format-check` checks both. Expressions run in the dialect of all of the format's Starlark, go.starlark.net at the version the format pins. An expression calls no functions and holds no loops, so it has no step limit.
- **Instances:** combinations in counter order — names by code units, the first changes slowest of all —, and on each first the derived numbers, then the constraint. The product of the domains is no more than 10,000, the derived numbers are within ±(2^53−1), and there is at least one instance.
- **An attempt's instance** is the number `below(count)` of the place of its seed with the names `template`, the task's ID and `instance`. The same package and the same seed give the same instance.
- **Placeholders** are `{name}` in each string of the task outside `template`; `{{` and `}}` are a curly brace of the text; substitution goes in one pass. In the key and the trap value of `number` and `fraction` a placeholder stands in the place of the integer, the numerator or the denominator: `"{second}"`, `"{part}/{whole}"`; a decimal fraction has no placeholders. The results of a solver are more names of placeholders, but only in the key and the trap value of `number` and `fraction`, in the solution and in the leak phrases; `task.template-names` and `task.placeholders` know them too.
- **The key in advance:** a template's key is computed by an expression or by the solver, and the rules of a task and `lesson.no-leaks` are applied to each instance at the module's check. `spec` checks the instances without the solver's results and takes them only from the template vectors. At an attempt Starlark is not run: the package carries the template itself in `tasks` and the numbers of each of its instances, in order, in `instances`, and the server takes number `below(count)` and substitutes the numbers without executing expressions.
- **To the device** goes the open view of the instance — without `template`, without the seed and without numbers that are not in its open fields.
- **Five rules:** `task.template-names`, `task.template-expressions`, `task.placeholders`, `task.template-instances` and `task.instances`. `format-check` checks them itself, with the earlier rules of a task on the instances.
- **The vectors** are `format/vectors/templates/<case>.yaml` by the schema `template-vector.schema.json`: the template, the number of its instances and attempts — the seed, the numbers of the instance and the instance itself. `format-check` computes them with a second implementation, `expressions.mjs` and `templates.mjs`, and its tests compare the expressions with the examples of the Starlark specification. The vectors of `task.template-expressions` hold the beginning and the depth of an expression.

Normative: the [format text](../format/README.md), its rule on templates, and edits of its opening, its versions, files, open fields and test vectors, and of its rules on the task, checks, the leak check, lessons and randomness.

— *Why:*
- **A pool and templates, without generation on the fly:** a module is data, and a program gives the verdict. A text that a model writes at an attempt passes no rule of the format. In standalone such a task was checked by a solver written by the same model: "the program is written by the same model that wrote the task, so if the model misread its own wording, the program will confirm the misreading" (SPEC 6.1 standalone, commit 4dece74, read 2026-10-27). standalone has no parametric templates. Closest to them is GSM-Symbolic, which the simulator's review retells: "Templates name variables, their domains and conditions that keep answers whole" (`research/literature/generation-verification.md` standalone, the same commit).
- **The key in advance:** the В1 of `module-kit` — where to compute a template's key — waited for the cost of running a solver (RUN.md of `module-kit`, commit 1a54028, read 2026-10-27). All 2^64 seeds cannot be enumerated, but a seed only chooses the number of an instance, and there are no more than 10,000 instances. Then each instance passes all the rules of a task, the leak too, before the first attempt, and an attempt has neither the solver's clock nor its refusal.
- **A subset of Starlark:** the language is the same as the check's predicate, and `module-kit` computes the expressions with the same go.starlark.net. And a narrow subset `spec` computes itself too, so its template vectors are checked not by the schema alone. The Starlark specification (bazelbuild/starlark, commit c0af0ea03d, read 2026-10-27): "The `//` and `%` operations on integers compute floored division and remainder of floored division", and "Comparison operators, `in`, and `not in` are non-associative, so the parser will not accept `0 <= i < n`". `x or y` there "yields the value of `x` if its truth value is `True`", so `and` and `or` in the subset take only `bool`. The parser of go.starlark.net puts unary minus above `*`, `//` and `%`: "Unary MINUS, unary PLUS, and TILDE have higher precedence so are handled in parsePrimary" (`syntax/parse.go`, google/starlark-go, commit 4f4267fb14, read 2026-10-27).
- **The depth of 64** is with a margin below what the format's go.starlark.net parses, about 75 brackets, so every expression of the subset is parsed by the dialect.
- **The fields `derived` and `constraint`:** "values" would be confused with the value of an answer slot and with `trap_values`, and "condition" in Russian is «условие», which is both the check kind `predicate` and the task statement.
- **A derived number is only of the parameters:** the order of keys carries no meaning ([format text](../format/README.md)), and a chain of derived numbers would have to set an order of evaluation.
- **One call of `below`:** the choice is uniform over the instances, takes one integer — or slightly more at Lemire's rejection —, and `spec` computes it itself. Parameters one at a time with rejection by the constraint take an unknown number of integers, and a limit of tries would make some seeds a refusal that nobody will check.

— *Rejected:*
- only a pool in v0; AI generation on the fly, with a solver or without;
- the key at each attempt, with parameters one at a time and rejection; waiting for `module-kit` to decide where the key is computed;
- everything, the numbers of the task statement too, by a solver: then `spec` would check the template vectors only by the schema;
- the format's own language of expressions beside Starlark;
- `abs`, `min`, `max`, a conditional expression and derived numbers of derived numbers in v0: no example asks for them, and each will come as a minor version;
- parameters as a list, not a dictionary: names without repeats are given by `yaml.unique-keys` anyway;
- a template as a part of its own, `templates/<id>.yaml`: a lesson names a task, and the learner model sees one.

— *Consequence:* `format/README.md`; `task.schema.json` — the field `template` and placeholders in the key; `leak-vector.schema.json`; `template-vector.schema.json`; the examples of a task with a template and of the module `with-templates`; the vectors `format/vectors/templates/`, of the open view and of the template rules; `format-check` — `expressions.mjs` and `templates.mjs`; `docs/concepts.md`; `docs/architecture.md`; `docs/product.md`; `docs/repositories.md`; `docs/decisions.md`.

**R61. A template may carry a solver — the field `solver` with a program in Starlark and the names of its results. `solve` gets the numbers of an instance's open fields and returns a dictionary of results, and the results stand only in the key and in the trap value of `number` and `fraction`, in the solution and in leak phrases. The dialect is the one of all of the format's Starlark, with the options of standalone's solvers; the budget is 100,000,000 steps for all the template's instances together. Only `module-kit` runs the solver; in template vectors and in the package its results are data. Text — [the format text](../format/README.md), in its rule on solvers.**
- **The field** `template.solver`, closed, like all of `template`:
  - `program` — the program, no longer than 8192 characters, most conveniently as a block scalar;
  - `results` — the names of the results, at least one and without repeats. A name is like a parameter's, and a parameter, a derived number and a result never share a name (`task.template-names`).
- **The input of `solve`** is a frozen dictionary of the numbers that the template's open fields show: each parameter and each derived number whose placeholder stands in the statement, the data, the unknown, an item's text, a piece of a line or an option of a slot with the binding `choice`. The names are inserted in the order of code units. The numbers of only closed fields — the key, the trap value, the solution — do not go into the dictionary.
- **The output** is a dictionary with exactly the names of `results`, and each value is an `int` in ±(2^53−1). A result is a number of the instance, like a derived one, and its placeholders are replaced by it.
- **Where the results stand** — only in the key and in the trap value of `number` and `fraction`, in the solution and in leak phrases. Everything the learner sees before solving, `spec` builds without the solver, and a placeholder of a result anywhere else breaks `task.placeholders`.
- **The dialect** is the one of all of the format's Starlark: go.starlark.net `v0.0.0-20261021141710-4f4267fb140d` with the `syntax.FileOptions` options of standalone's solvers: `Set`, `While`, `TopLevelControl` and `GlobalReassign` on, `Recursion` off, `load` forbidden. The built-in names are the list of the 33 names of its `starlark.Universe`, Starlark's own: none of the modules `math`, `json`, `time`, nor the 13 helpers of standalone's sandbox. `print` writes nothing, and the dialect has no randomness and no clock.
- **The run:** the program is executed once, on one thread, and `solve` is called on each instance in the order of instances, on the same thread. The top level and all the calls together take no more than 100,000,000 steps in this version's count of go.starlark.net, and the run stops when the count reaches the budget. The budget is the template's, not the instance's, and it is in the format, like a predicate's step limit; the clock and concurrent runs are `module-kit`'s.
- **The rule** `task.template-solver`: the solver gives its results on each instance — the program parses and executes in the dialect, `solve` is a function of one parameter, and on each instance, within the budget, without an error, it returns exactly its results as integers within the bounds. Only `module-kit` checks it. The rule's vectors are checked by `spec`'s CI as it checks the vectors of `task.predicate-expression`: by the schema, the YAML rules and by their not breaking the rules it checks itself. The vector `past-the-budget-of-the-template` is a loop of 2,000,000 iterations, so that the call of `solve` is a fraction of the budget.
- **What `spec` does:** on an instance without results it checks the task's rules on whatever has no results, and skips the key, the trap value and the leak phrase with a result. A template vector with a solver names `inputs` — the names that `solve` gets — and the results at each attempt: `spec` compares `inputs` with the template's open view and checks the task's rules on the instance with these results, and `module-kit`'s CI runs the solver and compares.
- **The package** carries the solver's results among the numbers of each instance, in `instances`, and the server does not compute them. In package vectors they are the vector's data, as in template vectors.
- **Provenance:** a key that the solver computes is "checked by a solver", like a key from a template expression.

Normative — [the format text](../format/README.md), its rule on solvers, and the edits to its opening, its versions and test vectors, and to its rules on the task, checks, the leak check and templates.

— *Why:*
- **Only the numbers of open fields:** the solver solves the task that the learner sees. If it got all the numbers, it could return a closed parameter, and "checked by a solver" would check nothing. standalone's solver, too, gets only what the learner sees — the texts of the options: "`options: {"A": "4", "B": "5", "C": "6", "D": "8", "E": "12"} — the task's own option texts`" (SPEC 6.2 standalone, commit 4dece74, read 2026-10-28). The order of the names is fixed, because a Starlark dictionary is iterated in insertion order, and the result must not depend on it.
- **Results only in closed fields:** `spec` does not run Starlark, and it must build an instance's open view itself: its vectors of the open view and of templates are then checked by more than the schema.
- **standalone's dialect:** its solvers already run in it — "`Set: true, While: true, TopLevelControl: true, GlobalReassign: true, Recursion: false, LoadBindsGlobally: false`" (`internal/infra/starlark/dialect.go`, lines 29–36 of standalone, the same commit). On recursion, SPEC 6.4 standalone: "A recursive Starlark function recurses on the **Go** stack, and a stack overflow in Go cannot be recovered". standalone rejects `load` at compilation: `if program.NumLoads() > 0` (`internal/infra/starlark/starlark.go`, line 214). No helpers — because each would become a normative contract that `module-kit` implements and holds with test vectors. The format example needs only `range`, `len` and `fail`, and a helper will come in a minor version when a module asks for it.
- **A budget per template:** 100,000,000 is the plan's recommendation. In standalone it is 25,000,000 steps per run: "`thread.SetMaxExecutionSteps`; the interpreter tests the counter on every instruction", and the heaviest of the 705 solvers takes 2,413,617 steps (SPEC 6.6 standalone); on the dialect's version it takes 2,725,355, by `module-kit`'s measurement. A budget per instance at 10,000 instances would give up to 250 billion steps for one template when a module is checked. One budget for all the instances bounds the cost of checking a module, and a template with a search for each instance searches only what is open, like standalone's solver templates: "A solver template searches only what the question leaves open, and every program runs under the one step budget" ([standalone@42b4408](https://github.com/mathtrail/mathtrail-standalone/tree/42b4408)).
- **The program in the task:** the template stays one file, closed as a whole, like a check's predicate, which has no file `predicates/<id>.star` either. The limit of 8192 characters is like standalone's "`MaxSource = 8 * 1024`" (`internal/infra/starlark/starlark.go`, line 36), only in characters: the schema measures a string's length in characters.
- **One thread and the order of instances:** a thread's steps accumulate, and the template's budget is simply the thread's limit. Starlark's global variables are frozen after the top level, so the calls do not affect one another.

— *Rejected:*
- `solve` gets all the numbers of the instance; the numbers as capitalized constants without an argument, like standalone's solver templates ([standalone@42b4408](https://github.com/mathtrail/mathtrail-standalone/tree/42b4408));
- 25,000,000 steps for each instance, without a shared budget; the helpers of standalone's sandbox in format v0;
- results also in trap texts, simpler cases and hints; a result only in the key;
- the program as a file `solvers/<id>.star` in the module layout.

— *Consequence:* `format/README.md`; `task.schema.json` — the field `solver`; `template-vector.schema.json` — `inputs` and the results in the numbers of an attempt; the example `number-thought-of-template` with standalone's solver and the MIT notice, and the incorrect examples of a solver; the template vector `number-thought-of`; the vectors of `task.template-solver`, `task.placeholders` and `task.template-names`; `format-check` — `templates.mjs`, `cases.mjs` and `verdicts.mjs`; `docs/concepts.md`; `docs/architecture.md`; `docs/repositories.md`; `docs/decisions.md`.

## Module package

**R62. A module package is two parts and an inventory. The server part is the canonical view: the module as one JSON object, with the tier of each skill and the numbers of each instance of a template. The device part is `LICENSE`, `NOTICE` and the media files. The package inventory names the module and both parts by digests; the canonical text is RFC 8785, the digest is SHA-256, and the package digest is the digest of the inventory. The open views are built by `module-kit` on the server, and they reach the app from `api` by the digest of any package that its image gives. `LICENSE` is a mandatory file of a module's folder, and the eval set does not go into the package. Text — [the format text](../format/README.md), in its rule on packages.**
- **The canonical view** is an object of `canonical-view.schema.json`:
  - each part is under its own member: a part that a module has one of is under its term in snake_case, `manifest`, `skill_graph`, `traps`, `techniques`, `solving_steps`, and parts that there are many of are under the name of their folder, `tasks` and `lessons`, as an object by local ID. The value of a part is the JSON value of its file as it is: a template as written, with no default values;
  - `skill_tiers` — the tier of each skill of the graph;
  - `instances` — by template ID, the numbers of each of its instances in the order of instances: parameters, derived numbers and the solver's results.

  A member whose part the module lacks is absent from the view too. The canonical view has no open fields: the app gets a part's open view, not it.
- **Not in the package:** `eval/`, files starting with `.`, comments of the module's files and everything that is not in the module's files — the version of `module-kit`, the time, paths. So the canonical view and the digest depend only on the module's files and the format version of its manifest.
- **The canonical text** is the RFC 8785 serialization: keys by UTF-16 code units, without whitespace, strings escaped as ECMAScript's `JSON.stringify` escapes them, UTF-8 without a BOM and without a newline at the end. A number of the format is an integer in ±(2^53−1), and it is written in decimal digits: `5e1` is `50`. The format text sets the serialization itself, as it set the generator, so that an implementation does not depend on a library, and it names no library and no version of one; `module-kit` writes it with its own code.
- **The digest** is `sha256:` and the SHA-256 in 64 lowercase hexadecimal digits, and the size is a number of bytes. The server part is named by the canonical text of the canonical view, and the device part by the canonical text of the list of its files: `license`, `notice` and `media` by path from `media/`. How the files travel — in an archive or one by one, compressed or not — does not change the digest.
- **The package inventory** is the glossary's term for the part that names the digests of both parts. The schema is `inventory.schema.json`: `module_format_version` at the root, in one place in all versions, `id`, `version`, and `server_part` and `device_part` — with a digest and a size. The package digest is the digest of its canonical text, and the attempt stores it.
- **The package as files** — `inventory.json`, `server.json`, `device.json` and `device/` with the files of the device part. In which archive the packages lie in a release of `modules` is for `modules` to decide.
- **The module index** names a package by the digest of its inventory, and `module_format_version` stands at its root and in each record in a fixed place. The index is signed, and whoever checked it trusts the packages by the chain of digests: index → inventory → parts → files.
- **Who reads what:**
  - `api` and the eval runner of `tutor` — through `module-kit`, and `canvas`'s CI — through its CLI;
  - `sim` — `server.json` by the types of the canonical view from `spec`'s releases, without `module-kit`;
  - `app` does not read the package. The open views of the manifest, the skill graph, the technique catalog and the solving steps are given by `api` by the digest of any package that its image gives — of an attempt, of a lesson run, of the current version of a connected module and of a module of the catalog —, and `app` caches them by it; the manifest goes to the canvas as the property `manifest`. The tiers `skill_tiers` come with the graph's open view, so a connected module has its tiers before the first attempt, and its name and explanation language come from the manifest.
