A lesson's open view comes whole when the lesson suits the learner, the open view of a task or an instance with each attempt, and the files of the device part are served by `api`. The messages are `PackageService`, the bytes of the format's JSON with the format version beside them ([the contracts text](../contracts/README.md)).
- **A template at an attempt:** the server takes instance number `below(count)` from `instances`, where count is their number, and substitutes its numbers. It executes neither expressions nor the solver at an attempt.
- **`LICENSE`** is a mandatory file of a module's folder: the text of the license that the manifest names — the rule `module.license`. `LICENSE` and `NOTICE` are UTF-8 without a BOM, and lines end with one LF — the rule `module.plain-text`, since the device part carries them byte for byte. License notices are only in `NOTICE`: comments do not go into the package.
- **Integers written with an exponent:** `1e20` passes `type: integer` and the rule `yaml.json-scalars`, and the canonical view writes only integers up to 2^53−1. So the `from` and `to` of a template's range and the width and height of a picture of a statement and of a demo have the bounds ±(2^53−1).
- **Vectors** — of tiers, `format/vectors/tiers/` with the schema `tier-vector.schema.json`, and of packages, `format/vectors/packages/` with the schema `package-vector.schema.json`. `spec` computes them itself, and the solver's results are the vector's data, as in template vectors.

— *Why:*
- **`spec` decides itself.** The recommendation of `module-kit` on the package was an input, but its detailing had not started (RUN.md of `module-kit`, `main` 1a54028, read 2026-10-28); `module-kit` checks its build against this decision.
- **A compiled view, not the YAML as it is.** A reader without `module-kit`, `sim`, needs neither parsing YAML with the format's restrictions, nor enumerating instances, nor computing tiers: all of this is already in the package.
- **One JSON, not a file per part:** the module of olympiad maths has 603 tasks ([standalone@42b4408](https://github.com/mathtrail/mathtrail-standalone/tree/42b4408)), and a reader would assemble the module from hundreds of files, and a part's digest would become one more list. An edit to one task is shown by a pull request of `modules` anyway.
- **RFC 8785:** "JSON object properties MUST be sorted recursively", the comparison is "code units are treated as unsigned integers", and "Whitespace between JSON tokens MUST NOT be emitted" ([RFC 8785](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8785), sections 3.2.3 and 3.2.1, Informational; read 2026-10-28). On the format's data — ASCII keys, integers, no surrogates (`yaml.characters`) — it comes down to sorting the keys and `JSON.stringify`. Only the object must be written by hand: JavaScript puts an integer key like `"1"` first in an object, and the sorting example of [RFC 8785](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8785), section 3.2.3, does not pass through `JSON.stringify` (checked in Node 2026-10-28). Go's libraries:
  - `Value.Canonicalize` of the package `encoding/json/jsontext` "canonicalizes the raw JSON value according to the JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS) as defined by RFC 8785". The package's files in go1.27.3 begin with `//go:build goexperiment.jsonv2` (`src/encoding/json/jsontext/value.go` and `doc.go`, tag go1.27.3, read 2026-10-28), but since go1.27 this experiment is on by default: in the `baseline` set of the file `src/internal/buildcfg/exp.go` there is `JSONv2: true` (tag go1.27.3; in go1.26.0 the field is absent). The release says: "Two new packages are now available", and the new implementation can be turned off, "setting GOEXPERIMENT=nojsonv2 at build time", and "This opt-out is expected to be removed in a future release" ([Go 1.27 Release Notes](https://go.dev/doc/go1.27), read 2026-11-02);
  - `encoding/json` escapes a string otherwise: "the string is encoded using HTMLEscape, which replaces "<", ">", "&", U+2028, and U+2029", and U+2028 and U+2029 "unconditionally" (`src/encoding/json/encode.go`, the same tag).

  So the format text sets the serialization itself, and the package vector `strings` holds these characters. It names no library: a fact about the version of one library ages with its releases, and a library that escapes more is caught by the requirement and the package vectors.
- **SHA-256 and the notation `sha256:`** — as in an OCI descriptor: "digest ::= algorithm ":" encoded", and "Implementations MUST implement SHA-256 digest verification for use in descriptors" ([OCI Image Spec, descriptor.md](https://github.com/opencontainers/image-spec/blob/main/descriptor.md), read 2026-10-28). The same algorithm is held by the Dockerfile's sums and the releases' `SHA256SUMS`.
- **The device part — by the list of files**, like the h1 hash of Go modules: "the go command computes the hash from the names and contents of files within the archive in a deterministic order. The hash is not affected by file order, compression, alignment, and other metadata" ([Go Modules Reference](https://go.dev/ref/mod), "Authenticating modules", read 2026-10-28). Hash1 is the SHA-256 of a list of lines "the file's hash, two spaces, the name" (`golang.org/x/mod/sumdb/dirhash`, `hash.go`, read 2026-10-28). So neither an archive's timestamps nor compression change the digest.
- **The open views — from `api`, not in the device part:** a lesson is given only to a learner whom the lesson and each of its tasks suit, and the device part is one for all the learners of a module, and a lesson only for adults would land on a child's device. A withdrawn version the device would then hold in its cache with all its texts. And `api` already gives a task's open view and serves the media.
- **The numbers of instances, not expanded instances:** a template has up to 10,000 instances, and an expanded package would hold up to 10,000 copies of a task. The numbers are the same as the "numbers of an attempt" of template vectors, and substitution is a replacement of strings, not Starlark.
- **`LICENSE` in the module's folder:** Apache-2.0 requires giving the recipient a copy — "You must give any other recipients of the Work or Derivative Works a copy of this License" ([Apache License 2.0](https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0), section 4(a), read 2026-10-28) — and the package travels to the learner's device too. A text from the module's folder keeps the package dependent only on that folder, suits any license of a third-party module and does not require of the format a list of licenses, which is still open (О-10). Go, for a module in a subfolder, takes `LICENSE` from the root — "the go command will copy the file named LICENSE from the repository root directory" — and itself writes that "this cannot be extended without breaking cryptographic sums of existing modules" ([Go Modules Reference](https://go.dev/ref/mod), "Special case for LICENSE files", read 2026-10-28).
- **The eval set outside the package:** the samples are needed neither by `api` nor by the device, and a new sample changes neither a verdict nor the digest. The eval runner takes the samples from the module's folder in `modules`'s CI. So the server part is not all the content, as first recommended, but the content that the platform executes.

— *Rejected:*
- waiting for the recommendation of `module-kit`; deciding the package and the index together;
- the author's YAML as it is; the canonical view as a file for each part;
- the module's open view in the device part — with lessons or without them. Return to it with storage and a CDN (Т-17);
- expanded instances of a template in the package;
- `LICENSE` from the repository's root, as in Go; license texts in the format itself — this would touch О-10; only `NOTICE` in the package;
- the eval set in the server part.

— *Consequence:* `format/README.md`; the schemas `canonical-view.schema.json`, `inventory.schema.json`, `tier-vector.schema.json`, `package-vector.schema.json` and `template-vector.schema.json`, and the bounds of integers in `task.schema.json`, `common.schema.json` and `lesson.schema.json`; `format/examples/` — `LICENSE` of each whole module, the inventory, the integers —, `format/vectors/tiers/`, `format/vectors/packages/` and the vectors of `module.license` and `module.plain-text`; `.gitattributes`; `tools/format-check/` — `canonical.mjs`, `package.mjs`, `module.mjs`, `cases.mjs` and `main.mjs`; `docs/concepts.md`; `docs/architecture.md`; `docs/repositories.md`; `contracts/README.md`; `.bestpractices.json`; `docs/decisions.md`.

## Module index

**R63. The module index is the file `module-index.json` in each release of `modules`: the canonical text of an object by the schema `module-index.schema.json`. The index is cumulative: it names each published version of each module by the digest of its package, with the tag of the release of `modules` in whose files the package lies, with the anchor skills that the version teaches, and with the withdrawal mark and its reason. A release builds the index from the index of the previous release, checked by `release-verify` before the build, and its own packages, and the index's rules reject the build. The name of a package's file in a release is derived from its record. A withdrawn version remains only for repeating a verdict, and the device learns of a withdrawal from `api`. Text — [the format text](../format/README.md), in its rule on the module index.**
- **What the index names.** At the root — `module_format_version`, the version by which the index is built, and `modules`: by module ID and by its version — a record. In the record:
  - `module_format_version` — the format version of the package, from its inventory;
  - `package_digest` — the package digest, that is, the digest of the inventory;
  - `release` — the tag of the release of `modules` in whose files the package lies: `vX.Y.Z`, as any NovaTrail repository numbers its releases. How the files lie in the release is for `modules` to decide. The place requires no trust: the package is checked by its digest;
  - `teaches` — the anchor skills that the skills of the version's graph teach, each once, in the order of code units. Its element is a string in the form of an anchor skill's ID, not a reference to the vocabulary: the record stays valid even when the next format version removes the anchor skill;
  - `withdrawn` — for a withdrawn version: the withdrawal reason, `wrong_key`, `answer_leak` or `unsuitable_content`.
- **One index for all the modules, cumulative.** A release's index names each version that any release of `modules` published, not only the versions of its own release. It is built by the CLI of `module-kit` in `modules`'s CI at a release, inside the shared release: after the number, since a new record names the tag of its release, and before publication. At the input — the index of the previous release, the release's packages, its tag and the withdrawals:
  - the first release has no previous index, and the build is told so explicitly. If the previous index cannot be read, it is a refusal, not a new index;
  - a record of the previous index stands in the new one as it was;
  - a package whose version is already in the index does not change the record, nor the tag: the same module gives the same package. So a release may build all the modules or only the changed ones — this is for `modules` to decide;
  - the other packages get new records;
  - withdrawals are marked last. A repeated withdrawal with the same reason changes nothing, so the list of withdrawals in `modules` can grow from release to release. A version that comes out in this same release can be withdrawn too.
- **The previous index** is got and checked by a step of the shared `release.yml` of `.github` on the runner, and the recipe `release-files` of `modules` gets an already checked file:
  - the caller names, as an input of the shared `release.yml`, the name of the previous release's file, for `modules` — `module-index.json`;
  - before the build, the shared release downloads this file with its bundle from the release with the previous tag — the step of the number knows the tag — and checks it with the recipe `release-verify` on the runner, from the caller's `spec` submodule, as the path of the repetition checks the npm archive;
  - the shared release gives the recipe `release-files` the checked file together with the number, and tells the first release explicitly that there is no previous one ([the format text](../format/README.md); the vector `first-release`);
  - if the file cannot be downloaded or fails the check, it is a refusal before the build: an index that failed the check is the same as an index that cannot be read;
  - the recipe itself does not go to the network and does not need `spec/`. Its interface changes only for a caller that set this input, and how the file reaches the recipe — a path as the second argument to a read-only file, or a file in the tree before the build — is for `.github` to decide;
  - a caller with this input needs `spec` v0.6.0 or newer: from it, it has `release-verify`, as the input `npm-package` has had since v0.1.13.
- **The index's rules** reject the build of the index, not a module: `module-index.entries-kept` — a record of the previous index stands in the new one as it was, `module-index.one-package` — a version of a module has one package, `module-index.known-withdrawals` — a withdrawal names a version that is in the index, `module-index.version-above` — a version of a module that is not in the previous index is above each version of this module in it: it catches a release where CI did not run the version comparison, `diff`. Their vectors are refusals among the index vectors, not folders of `vectors/rules/`.
- **The signature.** The index is a file of a release of `modules`, and it is signed by the shared release workflow of `.github` together with the other files. The signature is checked by `release-verify`: by the release of `modules`, before it builds the next index, and by the CI of the pull request of `api` that pins it. Whoever checked the index trusts the packages by the chain of digests: the index names the inventory, the inventory the parts, and the list of the device part the files.
- **A package's file in a release** is found by its record — its `release` and a file name derived from the record —, without going through the release's files and without the REST API. So it is taken by the build of the image of `api` and the recipe of the first app, `canvas`'s CI and a repetition of a verdict outside `api`. Which name is for `modules` to decide: [the format text](../format/README.md), in its rule on packages, gives it the layout of packages in the release. The recommendation is an archive per package, named by the hexadecimal part of `package_digest`: the digest is in every record, and two names will not collide.
- **Withdrawal.** Releases are immutable, so a version is withdrawn by the next release of `modules`: its index marks the version's record. A withdrawal is not undone: the fix is a new version of the module. What a withdrawn version means for the platform:
  - it remains only for repeating a verdict. New attempts do not take it, and the device does not load its device part and does not hold its open views. From stage 4 its widget bundles are not loaded either, and a reason for a dangerous bundle will come in a minor version with epic E5;
  - an attempt started on it is closed "unchecked", `unchecked`, with a neutral phrase: this is not the learner's mistake;
  - finished attempts remain in the history. With the reason `wrong_key` their evidence no longer goes into the learner model, and it is recomputed from the evidence log;
  - `api`: a pull request pins in the configuration the release of `modules` and its index, and this is the anchor of trust. `api` gives a new attempt only on a version that this index does not mark withdrawn, and the marks are not carried over by hand. A withdrawal takes effect with the pull request that moves `api` to the release with the mark, and with the build of the image. The form of the configuration is for `api` to decide;
  - the device learns of a withdrawal from `api`, by the request "which of these digests does the image no longer give", `CheckPackages`: `app` names the digests whose open views it holds, from the account and without a profile ID, and `api` does not store the digests ([the contracts text](../contracts/README.md));
  - `canvas`'s CI, before building the samples page, reads `withdrawn` in the index of the newest release of `modules` — only it knows of all the withdrawals — and does not build the page from a withdrawn version. A child sample session is run with the build of the latest release of `canvas`, and the page tells the adult this in the steps of the session (Д45);
  - from stage 4 the index is written by the registry service, and it puts the mark: only whoever signs the index can remove or forge it.

  How each component does this is for it to decide.
- **The fix of a withdrawn one.** A withdrawn newest major version is fixed by a version above it by semver — an edit to the key of a published task is itself major. When the fix is ready, it comes out in the same release that withdraws the version. The withdrawal does not wait for the fix.
- **Who teaches an anchor skill.** The modules that teach an anchor skill are those whose record names it in `teaches`. For each module what counts is the newest by semver non-withdrawn version whose format version the reader reads. A module is offered to the learner by `api` — only from those it holds itself and that suit the learner by the audience, the profile's age category. The explanation language does not select: a profile has no learner's languages. The module's card names the explanation language if it is not the language of the screen, and the adult chooses.
- **Versions.** The index stores the records of all format versions, so its members keep their place and meaning in all versions, and while the format is v0 too, like `module_format_version` in the manifest: `module_format_version` and `modules` at the root and `module_format_version`, `package_digest`, `release`, `teaches` and `withdrawn` in a record. A new version may add only an optional member and a withdrawal reason, and both are minor. A reader reads these members of an index of any version by their places, not by the schema of its own version, which would reject what the next one added. A record whose format version it does not read, it skips, rather than rejecting the index, and a version with any `withdrawn` it considers withdrawn, even if it does not know its reason. How a record is derived from a package is part of the format version.
- **Vectors** — `format/vectors/indexes/<case>/`: the release's modules in `modules/` and `index.yaml` by the schema `index-vector.schema.json` — the previous index, the tag, the withdrawals and either the index or a refusal by a rule. `spec` computes them itself, `tools/format-check/index.mjs`, and the vectors' digests are checked by an independent computation in Python. The modules of the index vectors are without a solver: `spec` does not run Starlark.

— *Why:*
- **The mark in the index already in v0.** The recommendation was to withdraw a version before stage 4 by a pull request to the configuration of `api`, and to put a signed mark in the index from stage 4. The mark is taken at once. `canvas`'s CI does not know the configuration of `api` and otherwise would not learn of a withdrawal, while so a withdrawal has one path at all stages — the signed index, and from stage 4 only whoever writes it changes. The pull request to `api` stays the anchor of trust: the mark reaches `api` together with it.
- **The reason in the mark.** With a wrong key the evidence of finished attempts is wrong, and with a leak or unsuitable content it is right, and without the reason `learner-model` cannot tell them apart. The values of the format's lists are terms of the glossary, and `key` there is the correct value. So the reasons are named "wrong key", "answer leak", "unsuitable content". And `reason` in the glossary is already the verdict reason, and the value of `withdrawn` is the withdrawal reason itself, without a field of its own.
- **A cumulative index.** A withdrawn old version can be marked only in an index that names it, and releases are immutable. And a repetition of a verdict by the digest of an attempt finds the package's release by the index, not by going through releases.
- **A tag, not a URL.** The records stay forever, and a URL would sew GitHub's address scheme into them, while the tag and the file name give the address anyway. The place requires no trust, so there is no need to sign it separately. The tag has the form `vX.Y.Z` of NovaTrail's releases, and `release` holds it: a tag outside the form or with the sign `-` in front the schema will not pass.
- **The previous index on the runner.** Otherwise the index would be taken by the recipe `release-files`. And that recipe runs in the container `toolchain`, which holds the commit's tree from `git archive`, without submodules and without `spec/` with `release-verify`, and where there is not a single token. The recipe could not check the index where it is got.
- **A file name from the record.** Going through the files was rejected by "A tag, not a URL", and the REST API without a token gives 60 requests an hour: "The primary rate limit for unauthenticated requests is 60 requests per hour" ([GitHub Docs, Rate limits for the REST API](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/rate-limits-for-the-rest-api), read 2026-11-01). The `/` of a module ID and the `:` of a digest do not suit a name: "GitHub renames asset filenames that have special characters, non-alphanumeric characters, and leading or trailing periods" (GitHub Docs, REST API endpoints for release assets, "Upload a release asset", read 2026-11-02).
- **The fix in the same release.** Otherwise the previous major would become current, and the withdrawn one's evidence about its skills would have no way to be transferred: `retired_skills` maps only old IDs to new ones.
- **`teaches` in the record, not a map at the root.** It is a fact of one package, and it has no way to diverge from the packages. A map at the root would force the index to decide whose version counts — the newest, non-withdrawn, at which format version — and that is decided by the reader by its window.
- **The index's template for all versions.** In v0 only the current format version is read, and without this rule each change of 0.y would break the chain of indexes: `module-kit` of the new version would not read the previous index. In the same way, the place of `module_format_version` in the manifest and in the inventory is one in all versions.
- **Refusals with vectors.** A broken build loses the history of the index or names one version with two packages, and a repetition of a verdict by the digest then finds no package. The refusal vectors bind this for both implementations, `module-kit` and `spec`.

— *Rejected:*
- an index without the mark before stage 4; a mark without a reason;
- only adding to the open question of withdrawal, and leaving attempts and evidence to the detailing of `api` and `learner-model`;
- an index of its own release only;
- URLs of the package's files; one digest without a place — a reader would look for the package by going through releases;
- a map `anchor_skills` at the root of the index;
- vectors of the build only, without refusals, and no vectors at all — only the schema and examples;
- `teaches` as a reference to the taxonomy's vocabulary: the record would fail when the next version removes the anchor skill;
- the previous index taken by the recipe `release-files` — for the reason above; a copy of the release's file in the tree; an index that the shared release will not see;
- a file name by module ID and version with `/` replaced — every reader would repeat the replacement rule; one archive for all the packages of a release — the build takes only the packages in the window; `spec` sets the name — the format text gave the layout to `modules`;
- a fix only by the same major — an edit to the key is major;
- selection of a module by interface language — with a Russian interface the English first batch is not visible; a field "languages" in the profile — the profile has the interface language instead.

— *Consequence:* `format/README.md`; the schemas `module-index.schema.json` and `index-vector.schema.json`; `format/examples/module-index/`; `format/vectors/indexes/`; `tools/format-check/` — `index.mjs`, `cases.mjs`, `main.mjs` and the tests; `contracts/README.md`; `docs/concepts.md`; `docs/architecture.md`; `docs/repositories.md`; `docs/decisions.md`.

## Files of the `spec` release

**R64. Code takes `spec`'s files from its releases. From line 0.3 a release carries each normative part with a version of its own as a file `<part>-<version>.tar.gz` — the module format from line 0.3, the AI admission table from 0.8, the deployment configuration from 0.11, the legal texts from 0.13, the table of the age of digital consent and the export format from 0.14 —, from line 0.4 the npm package of the types `@altnovatrail/spec` and from 0.7 that of the contracts' code `@altnovatrail/contracts`, each with a keyless cosign signature and under the attestation of an immutable release. Code in Go takes the same tag as the version of the Go module `github.com/altnovatrail/spec`, whose package `spec` embeds each part as an `fs.FS` of its own and which carries the format's types too, and the contracts' Go code as the nested module `github.com/altnovatrail/spec/contracts`, tagged `contracts/<tag>`. Format version 0.1 came out with v0.3.0, and `release-version` refuses a commit that gives the format a new version without a new line.**
- **The release file.** Each normative part with a version of its own comes out as a file `<part>-<version>.tar.gz` for each version that the platform reads. While the format is v0, the format is one file, `format-<version>.tar.gz`. The files are built by the recipe `just release-files <commit> <folder> <tag>`:
  - what a release carries is decided by `tools/release/files.mjs` by the commit's line: from `FIRST_FILES_LINE`, 0.3, the format's file, and before it nothing; from `FIRST_ADMISSION_LINE`, 0.8, `admission-<version>.tar.gz`; from line 0.11 `deployment-<version>.tar.gz`; from line 0.13 `legal-<version>.tar.gz`; from line 0.14 `consent-age-<version>.tar.gz` and `export-<version>.tar.gz`; from `FIRST_NPM_LINE`, 0.4, the npm package of the TypeScript types, `altnovatrail-spec-<X.Y.Z>.tgz`; from `FIRST_CONTRACTS_LINE`, 0.7, the npm package of the contracts' code, `altnovatrail-contracts-<X.Y.Z>.tgz`;
  - the file of a part is a `git archive` of the commit itself, not of the working tree: in it is the folder `<part>-<version>/`, and in that `LICENSE` and the part's folder, as in the commit. The recipe checks the archive against `git ls-tree`;
  - the recipe reads the commit's `admission/VERSION` after `format/VERSION`, and rejects a commit of line 0.8 or newer without it;
  - the third argument is the release's tag: "Build the files" of `release.yml` passes it the release's version, and "Release files" of CI the version that "Release version" prints;
  - the archive's bytes depend on gzip in git, so reproducibility is not promised: the check is the signature.
- **The npm packages.** The same file that the release carries goes to npm: the first version was published by hand, and then a step of `release.yml` publishes it. The types of the `canvas` element are not a normative part with a version of its own, but declarations of the npm package of the types: `./canvas`, from line 0.5, without a file `<part>-<version>.tar.gz` of their own.
- **The signature** is double:
  - keyless cosign puts `<file>.sigstore.json` beside each file. The shared release of `.github` signs files this way too, and cosign of the same version, 3.1.4, is pinned by its sum. The certificate names `https://github.com/altnovatrail/spec/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main`, and it is issued by `https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com`;
  - the attestation of the immutable release names both the files and their signatures.

  A consumer checks a file with the recipe `release-verify`, the one recipe of `spec` that checks the signature of every NovaTrail release file. For a file of `spec` it compares:
  - the SAN, the Build Signer URI and the Build Config URI — `release.yml` of `spec` on `refs/heads/main`;
  - the issuer, the address and the numeric IDs of `spec`, the branch `refs/heads/main` and the environment `github-hosted`;
  - the tag — by the file's content: for `format-<version>.tar.gz` the commit in the archive's header, for the npm package its `version`.

  The commands `gh release verify-asset <tag> <file> -R altnovatrail/spec` and `cosign verify-blob` with the bundle, this identity and this issuer check less: the attestation links the file with the release, not with the commit, and cosign's flags do not compare the Build Config URI and the IDs.
- **The Go module.**
  - `go.mod` lies at the root of `spec`: the module `github.com/altnovatrail/spec`, `go 1.27.0`, without `require`. From v2 the path ends in `/v2`, as Go requires.
  - The package `spec` is `spec.go`. `spec.Format`, `spec.Admission`, `spec.Deployment`, `spec.Legal`, `spec.ConsentAge` and `spec.Export` in it are each an `fs.FS` rooted at its part's folder — `format/`, `admission/`, `deployment/`, `legal/`, `consent-age/` and `export/`. The directive `//go:embed all:<folder>` takes the files starting with `.` and `_` too: a package vector holds `.editor-notes` on purpose.
  - Each part has its own `embed.FS`, and its name is a pointer to a value of the package with the part's variable and its folder, which runs `fs.Sub` at each call, without initialization code: a binary carries only the parts it reads, and the paths and errors are those of `fs.Sub`. The build test `spec_test.go` holds that a program that reads one part carries no bytes of the others: static initialization is the compiler's work, not a rule of the language.
  - The module carries the format's types too, the packages `types/formatv0` and `types/formatv0/open`.
  - The module's version is the release's tag, and it has no other tag. The Go proxy builds the module's zip from the tag, and the checksum database sum.golang.org records its hash forever. After that a version can only be retracted with the directive `retract`, not removed.
  - Code in Go takes the format so: `go get github.com/altnovatrail/spec@<tag>`, and then `spec.Format`.
  - The module's zip carries the whole repository except nested modules, the documents too; code imports only the package `spec` and the types. The zip is checked by the nested module `tools/gomod`: with the same code as the proxy, `golang.org/x/mod/zip`, it builds the commit's zip, reads it back and checks that it holds `LICENSE` and each file of each embedded part and of the format's types, byte for byte. `tools/gomod` itself is not in `spec`'s zip, and the module `spec` has no `golang.org/x/mod` among its dependencies.
- **The contracts' Go module.** The Go code of the API contracts is the nested module `github.com/altnovatrail/spec/contracts` in `contracts/`, with tags `contracts/vX.Y.Z`. It is not in the root's zip. Its observation test vectors are `contracts.Vectors`, an `fs.FS` rooted at `contracts/vectors/`: the root module does not embed the nested one's files, and the vectors lie beside the contract they hold. They have no release file of their own: the contracts have no version beyond the package.
- **The steps of `release.yml`:**
  - the number — the recipe `release-version` also checks the format version (below);
  - "Build the files" — the recipe `release-files` in a new copy of the checkout: the copy of the number's step has already had the container. On the runner the step checks that `dist/` holds only regular files with names by the pattern;
  - "Sign the files" — cosign on the runner, without the container: the OIDC token does not go into the container. The job gets `id-token: write`;
  - publication — `gh release create` with the files. A draft of this version left by an interrupted run is deleted before creation and after a refusal. The refusal path is `release-refusal`;
  - "Verify the release" — the files are downloaded from the release, compared with the list of those built, and checked by `gh release verify` and `gh release verify-asset`, in one loop of retries. A repeated run of a released commit checks the same way;
  - "Verify the Go module" — `go mod download -json` of the release's Go modules, `github.com/altnovatrail/spec` by the tag and `github.com/altnovatrail/spec/contracts` by the tag `contracts/<tag>`, in the stage `toolchain`, only through the proxy, `GOPROXY=https://proxy.golang.org`. It asks in rounds once a minute, 36 rounds for all the modules together, and in a round only about those that the proxy has not given yet. A broken zip fails the run already after the release is out, and a repeated run asks again;
  - the job's `timeout-minutes` is 85.
- **The link of the line with the format** — `tools/release/format-line.mjs`, only in `spec`: through it the recipe `release-version` passes what `version.mjs` prints. The check runs only if the commit gets a release, and the previous release is of line 0.3 or newer, that is, it already carried the format as files. Then `format/VERSION` of the commit and of the previous release hold the rules of the format's versions:
  - a different format version — only above the previous one and only in a raised line, so that a line holds one format version;
  - a new major format version — only with a new major version of `spec`;
  - while the format is v0, `spec` stays 0.x.

  The refusal is caught already by the CI step "Release version" on the pull request.
- **CI:**
  - the steps "Go module" — the recipe `go-check`, which checks what only it knows: that the module requires nothing, and the zip of `HEAD` — and "Release files". Vet and the tests of the root module and of the modules of `tools/` are the recipes `ci-lint` and `ci-test`, which the shared `go.yml` of `.github` calls;
  - Go — in the stage `toolchain` of the Dockerfile, in `/usr/local/go`, where the shared CodeQL looks for it, by its sum, like every archive the Dockerfile downloads, and with `GOTOOLCHAIN=local`. CodeQL reads Go too, and Dependabot watches `gomod` in `tools/gomod`;
  - the Go version is 1.27.4, `GO_VERSION` in `.devcontainer/Dockerfile`, with the sums that go.dev/dl names for `go1.27.4.linux-amd64.tar.gz` and `go1.27.4.linux-arm64.tar.gz` ([go.dev/dl](https://go.dev/dl/?mode=json&include=all), read 2026-11-11). The Go version is one for all the repositories: it comes from this stage into the copy of each, since `just new-repo` copies this Dockerfile, and the Go repositories take it by their move to a tag and drop any difference of their own. The `go` directives in the `go.mod` of `spec`'s modules name the least version, not the one in the container; the one that names the stage's Go is the lock file of gopls of the template's kind `go`, `repo-template/kinds/go/gopls/go.mod`, and the test of `tools/new-repo` holds this.
- **Go consumers** move the module's version in `go.mod` and the submodule `spec/` together, in one move to a tag, as `RULES.md` has a repository move to a newer tag of `spec`. They exclude the modules `spec` and `spec/contracts` from Dependabot's `gomod`, and the npm packages `@altnovatrail/spec` and `@altnovatrail/contracts` from Dependabot's `npm`: a release comes out on each edit to a document, and otherwise Dependabot would propose a new tag every week.
- **The tools stay in the submodule.** The list of licenses and the check of the lock file the other repositories take with `spec`'s recipes from the submodule, not from a release file: these are tools, not code.
- **What next by this path:** the vectors and conformance tests of the other normative parts — the eval protocol, the widget protocol, and the vectors of `canvas`, which the eval protocol puts in epic E3 — come by it too: as a file of their own if the part has a version of its own, and as an `fs.FS` of their own in the same module, without a new delivery; for the contracts, the same module is the contracts' module.
- **What this entry does not decide:** how a release and the Go module carry the previous major format version. From v1 the window is the current major version and the previous one, and `format/` holds one version. Two major versions in the window occur only from v2, and the path is decided by the pull request that opens it.

Normative — [the format text](../format/README.md), in its rules on versions and on files; `.github/workflows/release.yml`, `justfile`, `go.mod`, `spec.go`, `contracts/`, `tools/release/`, `tools/gomod/`.

— *Why:* all read 2026-10-28, unless a date is given.
- **The path apart from the types.** The path, the generator of types with open views and the types of the `canvas` element are three different circles, each for one review, by the plan's rule on the size of a task. The path is one for all the files, and the types only add files to the same release and the same module.
- **The Go module at the root.** The release tags `vX.Y.Z` are already versions of the module. A module in a subfolder would need tags of its own: "If a module is defined in a subdirectory within the repository … then each tag name must be prefixed with the module subdirectory, followed by a slash" ([Go Modules Reference](https://go.dev/ref/mod), Mapping versions to commits). That is a second kind of tags and a ruleset of its own, and `format/` would have to be copied inside: "Patterns must not match files outside the package's module" (the documentation of the package `embed`, Go 1.27.3). Only a release file for Go would mean gh with a token in the CI of each consumer, and the types of `sim` would have to be copied to it.
- **The contracts in a nested module.** For the contracts the cost of a second kind of tags is accepted, because the generated code requires the protobuf runtime, while the root module still requires nothing; there is nothing to copy — the `.proto` files lie in the module itself.
- **`all:` in `//go:embed`.** "If a pattern names a directory, all files in the subtree rooted at that directory are embedded (recursively), except that files with names beginning with ‘.’ or ‘_’ are excluded", and "If a pattern begins with the prefix ‘all:’, then the rule for walking directories is changed to include those files" (the same place).
- **An `embed.FS` per part.** One variable for all the parts, with `fs.Sub` at the package's start, made each part reachable from any import: `api`, which through `tutor/admission` needs only the admission table, also carried `format/` with its vectors — 1.4 MB more. A variable of its own per part does not change this by itself: `fs.Sub` at start holds them all. The measurement on `v0.12.0`, Go 1.27.3, `-s -w`, `CGO_ENABLED=0`, a program with only `spec.Admission`: 3,104,928 bytes with one variable, as many with a variable per part and `fs.Sub` at start, and 1,687,712 this way, against 1,659,040 without `spec`. The growth is less than the 5.9 MB of `format/`, because the linker stores identical files once. The consumers' import and code do not change, and the version of the module `spec` is chosen by the main module. The path — a pointer per part, `fs.Sub` at each call — is the plan's proposal, by this measurement.
- **Checking the zip before the tag.** "Module zip files do not include the contents of vendor directories or any nested modules (subdirectories that contain go.mod files)" (Go Modules Reference, Module zip files). Such a file in `format/` would vanish for consumers silently, and `go test` in `spec`, which reads the working tree, would not see it. `golang.org/x/mod/zip` is the code with which `go` and the proxy build a zip.
- **The cosign signature.** Without files there was nothing to sign but the tag, and so no cosign — now there is something. Scorecard's Signed-Releases looks for signatures among the files: "This check looks for the following filenames in the project's last five release assets: … *.sig, *.sign, *.sigstore, *.sigstore.json …", and "It ignores the source code-only releases that are created automatically by GitHub" ([ossf/scorecard, docs/checks.md](https://github.com/ossf/scorecard/blob/6b98ea0a6a1c017fd399e5777301263dc20badee/docs/checks.md), commit 6b98ea0). It does not read the release attestation, so it would score a file without a bundle at 0, and there would be an alert in the Security tab, which RUN.md's rule on the findings of analyzers closes before a new task.
- **The attestation.** "creating an immutable release automatically generates a release attestation, which is a cryptographically verifiable record of a release containing the release tag, commit SHA, and release assets" ([GitHub Docs, Immutable releases](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/concepts/supply-chain-security/immutable-releases)), and after publication "you cannot add, replace, or delete assets" ([GitHub Docs, Managing releases in a repository](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/releasing-projects-on-github/managing-releases-in-a-repository)). So the files are signed and checked before publication.
- **Drafts.** "When you attach assets, gh release create creates a draft release, uploads each asset, and then publishes the release. These steps use separate API requests and do not form a single atomic operation" ([gh manual, gh release create](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_release_create)). An interrupted run may leave a draft, and the next one deletes it.
- **The Go proxy in the release check.** "The new version should be available within one minute. Note that if someone requested the version before the tag was pushed, it may take up to 30 minutes for the mirror's cache to expire" ([proxy.golang.org](https://proxy.golang.org/), FAQ, read 2026-11-03). Hence the retries and the ban on asking for the version before the tag. With the default `GOPROXY`, `go` on a 404 answer would go to GitHub directly and would hide that the proxy does not give the version. The proxy remembers its own failure too, not only a request before the tag, of which the FAQ speaks. The release v0.7.9 (commit 3409b44, run 41694199762) came out, but the step, then 10 attempts 30 s apart for each module, failed in both attempts. At the first request for the contracts' module, at 18:32:47 UTC, the proxy itself did not reach GitHub — "git ls-remote … fatal: unable to access 'https://github.com/altnovatrail/spec/': Could not resolve host: github.com" — and then gave this 404 from its cache: at 18:52 the answer carried `cache-control: public, max-age=627` and `expires: Tue, 03 Nov 2026 19:02:42 GMT`, exactly 30 minutes from the first request. The root module `v0.7.9` it had given 6 seconds before that. The step's five minutes and a retry two minutes later fell into the same memory. 36 rounds — 35 minutes of pauses — outlive it, and the job's timeout has room for them. A rerun of the run after 19:02 got the module. The step was tested in a harness in the scratchpad: one module, both, given at the 32nd and at the 36th round, not given, the path `/v2`.
- **The Go version.** go1.27.3 has the vulnerability GO-2026-6859 of the standard library, "HTTP/1 server crash due to MaxBytesReader header race in net/http", published 2026-11-11 and fixed in 1.27.4: "fixed" `1.27.4` for line 1.27 ([vuln.go.dev](https://vuln.go.dev/ID/GO-2026-6859.json), read 2026-11-11). "Go / vuln" of `tutor` failed on it without an edit to the code, and `api` and `tutor` had raised Go themselves, as a difference from `spec`'s container. `spec`'s code makes no vulnerable call, and its `just ci-vuln` is green on 1.27.3, but a move to a tag of `spec` with 1.27.3 would bring the vulnerability back.
- **Dependabot and the contracts' packages.** Dependabot matches a dependency by name — "you should define a value that will match the dependency name specified in the lock or manifest file" ([GitHub Docs, Dependabot options reference](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/reference/supply-chain-security/dependabot-options-reference), read 2026-11-02).

— *Rejected:*
- the path, the types and the types of `canvas` as one piece of work; two — the path and all the types together;
- only a release file for Go; a Go module in the subfolder `go/` with tags `go/vX.Y.Z`;
- npm before the types, when the package would carry only schemas; no npm — rejected for UI packages too, which are published to npm;
- a trial release in a separate repository; only a build in CI, without a local run of the publication steps;
- the shared `go.yml` before the Go types, when the Go code was one package that embeds a folder, without dependencies, and a CI tool in a nested module: four shared Go checks with their tools and the ruleset's required checks gave little;
- only the attestation, with the open alert Signed-Releases and its reason on the list of analyzer findings that stay open;
- `SHA256SUMS` in `spec`'s release: the attestation already names the digest of each file, and the npm package is the same file as the release's;
- for the proxy: waiting by the clock, `SECONDS` — the harness checks the rounds without real waiting; checking the module in a separate job — it would need its own image of `toolchain`, and the rerun "Re-run failed jobs" asks again anyway;
- for the parts: a package per part, `github.com/altnovatrail/spec/admission` — `embed` takes no files outside the package's folder, and a Go file would land in the part's folder, in its layout and its release file, and a consumer would have to change the import; leaving one variable — each new part would grow each binary; doing it within the task that adds a part — two edits in one task;
- for Go: each repository raises Go itself, and the template with the next epic of `spec` — the differences multiply, and a move to a tag would bring back 1.27.3.

— *Consequence:* `format/README.md`; `docs/repositories.md`; `docs/architecture.md`; `CLAUDE.md`; `README.md`; `repo-template/`; `repo-template/kinds/go/gopls/go.mod`; `.bestpractices.json`; `.github/workflows/release.yml`; `.github/workflows/ci.yml`; `.devcontainer/Dockerfile`; `justfile`; `go.mod`; `spec.go`; `spec_test.go`; `contracts/`; `tools/release/files.mjs`; `tools/release/format-line.mjs`; `tools/gomod/`; `tools/new-repo/`; `docs/decisions.md`.

## AI providers beyond OpenAI and Anthropic

**R65. The terms of an AI provider beyond OpenAI and Anthropic are checked in full when the platform needs it — the way `docs/privacy.md` checked those of OpenAI and Anthropic. Until then the route to it is closed. First Cerebras, then Groq.**
- **`tutor`'s screening** — in `tutor`'s `docs/architecture.md`, from the terms `tutor` read on 2026-10-25. Six providers of fast inference and Mathpix went through four questions in order: a model with images, training on the customer's data, minors, retention. The outcome is in `docs/privacy.md`:
  - Groq, Together AI, Cerebras, SambaNova and Mathpix passed. But all of them except Groq are silent on learners, and where the terms are silent, it is "18+ only": for under 18, `docs/privacy.md` requires terms that expressly permit them;
  - SiliconFlow and Fireworks are stopped: their terms forbid passing on the personal data of children under 14 and under 13.
- **The order of checking.** First Cerebras: by its help pages and documentation, it stores no data, and it calls its model with images ready for production. Its DPA is needed, and a written confirmation that the line of its help pages "our products are not intended for minors" does not concern learners. Then Groq, when its model with images leaves Preview and its DPA covers it. The check is as for OpenAI and Anthropic: verbatim quotes with the date read, and whether a text permits minors is decided by the author on Claude's analysis of the primary sources, since the platform has no lawyer.
- **eval.** Together, Cerebras and Fireworks forbid benchmarking in their terms, and SambaNova forbids publishing its results without its consent. The check reads this too: an eval run of `tutor` at a provider and its published report go by that provider's terms.

— *Why:* those that passed the screening suit now only adult learners, and Groq's and SambaNova's models with images are for trial only. Terms change, and a check ahead of time would be outdated by the day the provider is needed: the terms are checked again before each decision on an AI route.

— *Rejected:*
- checking all who passed now;
- not checking: the route to a fast provider would be left without a rule.

— *Consequence:* `docs/privacy.md`; `docs/architecture.md`.

## Reading on the device

**R66. A model that would read the work on the device is code of `tutor`: its release carries it with the digest of its weights, its eval admits it, and the verdict on what was read is given by `module-kit` on the server, as for a typed answer. In the first slice there is no reading on the device.** The boundary "not in the first slice" is the executor's proposal: this entry says whose this reading is, and does not introduce it.
- **What it is for.** The answer slots of a workbook, a canvas kind of the format that no module of the first slice takes, are digits. A small network of its own on the device would read them without an AI call, and the strokes would stay on the device. By the assessment of `tutor`, only such a network passes the platform's rule of licenses for a model: code, weights and training data under ASF's category A. TexTeller does not pass it because of its training data, and for Pix2Text-MFR this cannot be decided: it discloses neither its data nor its initial weights.
- **Whose.** "Everything that calls a model is in `tutor`", by `docs/architecture.md`, and a model on the device is a model too. Its weights and their digest, the eval set and the admission are with `tutor`, and it is admitted, like any model of an AI capability, by eval. What runs it on the device — `app` or `canvas` — is decided when reading on the device comes.
- **The verdict** stays with `module-kit` on the server: the core is deterministic, perception is probabilistic. The server gets the read value the same way as a typed answer.
- **When it reads** — only on the learner's action, like the AI on the server: on "Check", never at a solving step, which the platform does not lead. If the device is not sure, the work goes to the ordinary reading call.
- **The Prompt API in Chrome** — Google's generative AI on the device — is closed, like Google's models, which are closed on the platform.
- **In the first slice** every answer is read by an AI call. `tutor` has no digit network of its own: its eval and its cost will be shown by its task.

— *Why:* so the rule that everything that calls a model is in `tutor` holds, and the server gets the value as a typed answer, and the platform needs no second path to the verdict.

— *Rejected:*
- the model as a part of `canvas`: the model, its eval and its admission would end up outside `tutor`, against the rule that everything that calls a model is in `tutor`;
- no reading on the device: it would close the path on which the strokes of a workbook do not leave the device.

— *Consequence:* `docs/architecture.md`; `docs/decisions.md`.

## Reading and analysis

**R67. Reading and analysis are two calls: reading without the key, analysis with the key and the task's solution. One call of a model is admitted only by a new decision, with a change to what `docs/privacy.md` says goes to the provider, once it has passed `tutor`'s threshold for reading with the key on the handwriting of adult volunteers. A task from the learner's paper, which has no key, is checked by one call, of one model at a time.**
- **The threshold.** With the correct key, there are no more false "correct" and false alarms than without the key — a paired test by sheets, a worsening at p < 0.05 is a failure. Not one incorrect line is read as the correct key, and not one correct line as a false one.
- **The measurement of `tutor`'s epic E4**, as `tutor`'s `docs/architecture.md` records it, applied the threshold to the observation on the test part of the synthetic data: 68 sheets — free writing, the lines of E2 and the near-key, where the key differs from the sheet by one similar digit. Opus 5.5 · `high`, Haiku 5.5 · `low` and Haiku 5.5 · `low` without thinking gave not one false "correct", not one false alarm and not one reading as the key, in any condition. By the threshold, one call is admissible for all three.
- **But the test has no power.** On no sheet did the reading with the key differ from the reading without it, so there was nothing to fail the paired test with:
  - the handwriting is synthetic data, and Opus without the key read 66 sheets of 68 correctly;
  - the near-key was measured at the weakest shift of a digit, 0.1. At a larger shift, Opus read fewer and fewer sheets correctly even without the key: at 0.2 — 9 of 12, at 0.3 — 7 of 12, at 0.4 — 5 of 12;
  - the key does shift the reading of Haiku, though — toward "unreadable". On the near-key sheets with an error, Haiku · `low` gave the correct verdict in 4 calls of 15 with the key against 12 without it.
- **The extended measurement of `tutor`**, as `tutor`'s `docs/architecture.md` records it, found the first data where the key shifts the reading toward a false "correct": on the near-key at a digit shift of 0.3 and 0.4.
  - **Even sheets.** On the 68 sheets of E4 and on the 300 sheets of lines of the synthetic data of `tutor`'s large run, on no sheet did the reading with the key differ from the reading without it. The threshold holds for all, but the test, as in E4, has no power.
  - **The near-key by shifts** — 40 sheets per shift, the same ones at each shift, for Opus 5.5 · `high`, Haiku 5.5 · `low`, Haiku 5.5 · `medium` and Sonnet without thinking:
    - up to the shift 0.2, nobody has false verdicts;
    - at 0.3, Haiku · `low` with the correct key has one false "correct" that it does not have without the key, and at 0.4 so does Haiku · `medium`. These are the first divergences of the reading with the key and without it in the whole measurement, and the item of the threshold with zero tolerance — not one incorrect line is read as the correct key — does not hold at these shifts;
    - at 0.4, one false "correct" each occurs without the key too — for Haiku · `low` and for Sonnet —, so the key gives only part of the errors at this shift;
    - Opus gave no false verdict at any shift, but at 0.4 without the key it did not read 22 sheets of 40.
  - Synthetic data is data, not admission: the threshold is repeated on the handwriting of adult volunteers.
- **The data at the provider.** With two calls, the key and the task's solution go to the model only for the analysis, after "not yet", while the tutor's panel is open or when the learner opens it: with the panel closed, the key and the task's solution do not go to the model.
- **A task from paper** has no key that a program holds: its Check is one call, in which the model reads the work and judges it by its own solution, and gives the place of a mistake and the hints with the verdict. The risk the threshold guards — a reading drawn toward the answer expected, here the model's own — is the Check's too, and the eval set of verdicts measures it, false "Correct" and false "Not yet" apart.

— *Why:*
- «Два вызова» ("Two calls"). The threshold is passed, but on even synthetic data and without a single divergence: it did not show that the model does not "read in" the key. The main risk of one call is a false "correct", as in MathTrail Canvas ([canvas-api@0901af0](https://github.com/mathtrail/canvas-api/tree/0901af0)), and the argument about 61 exams, where a reference answer in the prompt multiplied false "correct", stays in force.
- The extended measurement: these are the first data where the key shifts the reading, and they are on the side of two calls, and of one call only after the threshold on the volunteers' handwriting. That a false "correct" at 0.4 occurs without the key too is the executor's refinement.

— *Rejected:*
- one call for these three configurations already now, with a change to what `docs/privacy.md` says goes to the provider;
- one call only for Opus: it reads almost without errors even without the key;
- recording nothing of the extended measurement: until then the threshold had shown no power, and these data have it;
- on a task from paper, the work read by one call and judged by another: the reading of a grid of sums gave its answers to the rows alone and left the columns unread, and a call for the hints would read the work a third time.

— *Consequence:* `docs/repositories.md`; `docs/architecture.md`; `docs/privacy.md`; `run/EPICS.md`.

**R68. Reading has two modes, and the operator of a deployment chooses one. In `single`, the default, Haiku 5.5 · `medium` reads alone, for every learner at every rung. In `pair`, two readers of one provider read by two calls without the key, and an answer slot whose check gives a verdict and that they read differently is "unreadable"; `module-kit` joins the two readings. The pair that `tutor`'s first measurement took is Opus 5.5 · `high` and Haiku 5.5 · `low`; the pair that `tutor`'s list admits is Opus 5.5 · `high` and Haiku 5.5 · `medium`. A sheet under a rubric is read by one reader in both modes. On `novatrail` the mode is `single`. A task from the learner's paper is read in neither mode: its Check is one call, of one model at a time, by the cascade of its calls.**
- **The rule of `pair`.** An observation of an answer slot is issued only if both readers read the same value after normalization. Otherwise the answer slot gets "unreadable", as an ambiguous writing. The measurement computed this rule by sheets: a sheet is issued if both read it the same.
- **Who joins.** The rule of two readers is executed by `module-kit`, not by `tutor`: `tutor` gives the observations of both readers or the AI call outcome, and never gives one. "The same value after normalization" means values that the slot check compares as equal, like a value with a trap, and to which it gives one verdict; the joined value is that of the first reader of the pair, and different findings are "ambiguous". If the call of one reader failed, there is no observation, and the answer slots that the AI reads are "unchecked".
- **Two readers are for answer slots whose check gives a verdict.** A sheet under a rubric is read by one reader: a rubric has no verdict, and a false alarm from a wrong reading is counted along the whole path by the main measure of assessment by a rubric, the share of false alarms.
  - **Why the rule is not for an essay.** The second reader insures the verdict: an answer slot read differently goes to "unreadable", not to a false verdict. An essay has one answer slot — the whole sheet, and by this rule the learner would rewrite the whole essay because of one word.
  - **What was measured**, as `tutor`'s `docs/architecture.md` records it. In the first call of `tutor`'s large run, on 300 synthetic essays, Opus 5.5 · `high` read the text the same as Haiku 5.5 · `low` in 287 essays, as Haiku 5.5 · `medium` in 284, as Sonnet without thinking in 295. The texts were compared after collapsing spaces and line breaks, and without it the matches are 279, 278 and 280. Not one essay diverged only in case or punctuation. The pair would send 5–16 synthetic essays of 300 to be rewritten, and on live handwriting there will be more.
  - **The path of assessment by a rubric:** the reading of an essay by one reader, then the assessment of the text read. The essay's reader is Haiku 5.5 · `medium`, not Opus 5.5 · `high` as `tutor` chose.
- **The modes.** `pair` is the rule above, with the admitted pair. In `single` no answer slot gets "unreadable" because two readings differ: the one reader's observation is the reading's result, `module-kit` validates it and gives the verdict by it, with nothing to join; in [the contracts text](../contracts/README.md) this is an addition to `v1`, and no message gets another result. `single` is no admission by eval: `tutor`'s list admits the pair, and no eval admitted Haiku · `medium` alone as the reader of a verdict. The test vectors of the observation hold no case of `single` (Д264).
- **What was measured for the pair**, by `tutor`'s epic E4, as `tutor`'s `docs/architecture.md` records it. The measurement did not measure a pair of different providers: `tutor` has no OpenAI key. The pair of one provider — on the test part without the key, 68 sheets:
  - Opus with Haiku · `low` issued 61 sheets, Opus with Haiku without thinking — 51, and among those issued there are no errors;
  - but there are no errors for each reader separately either — neither false "correct" nor false alarms. So on these sheets the rule only took away coverage: down to 90% and down to 75%.
- **The extended measurement** of `tutor`, as its `docs/architecture.md` records it, measured four more configurations of Claude on the test part of E4, and the chosen ones on sets of hundreds of sheets. The most sheets are issued by the pair Opus 5.5 · `high` with Haiku 5.5 · `medium`, and no pair has errors among those issued. The pair of Opus with a fast reader, without the key:
  - on the 68 sheets of E4 — 67 sheets with Haiku · `medium` and 64 with Haiku · `low`;
  - on the 300 sheets of lines of the synthetic data of `tutor`'s large run — 290 with Haiku · `medium`, 259 with Haiku · `low` and 297 with Sonnet without thinking, but a call of Sonnet costs $0.0041, and Haiku · `medium` $0.0003 and Haiku · `low` $0.0002;
  - on the author's ten sheets, written with a mouse deliberately illegibly, Haiku · `medium` read all of them, and Haiku · `low` found three unreadable.
  - The synthetic data is even, and the ten sheets are data, not a criterion: the measurement gives no admission, and the thresholds are repeated on the volunteers' handwriting.
- **The first errors of a single reader**, against which the second reader insures and which E4 did not show:
  - on a sheet: on the near-key at a digit shift of 0.4, Haiku · `low` and Sonnet without thinking, without the key, gave one false "correct" each of 40 sheets — the first errors of a single reader without the key in the whole measurement. The pair with Opus would not have issued them: Opus gave no false verdict at any shift, so its reading would not have matched the false one, and the answer slot would have got "unreadable";
  - in a workbook without a caption: single readers gave no false "correct" in E4 nor in the later runs of `tutor`, and in its large run each of the four configurations had 0 of 600. In a run with the workbook reading prompt of version 2, Haiku 5.5 · `medium` had 1 of 560: on the near-key 3/7, 3/1 is written, the one leaning toward a seven, and Haiku read 3/7 without doubt. Opus 5.5 · `high` read this box as "unreadable": the readings would have diverged, and the answer slot would have got "unreadable". The mirroring mark has nothing to do with it.
- **The cost of `pair`.** Two reading calls for each check instead of one: the platform AI quota is spent faster (О-14), and both readers need admission. The work goes to one provider twice, and there is no new processor of data.
- **The pair.** The first measurement took the one that issued more sheets. Which models are in the pair in the product is decided by admission by eval, and `tutor`'s list admits Opus 5.5 · `high` with Haiku 5.5 · `medium`, Haiku · `medium` being the first candidate that the extended measurement named for the check on the handwriting of adult volunteers. A pair of different providers stays unmeasured: return to it when `tutor` has an OpenAI key — with its terms for children, which `docs/privacy.md` records among the providers' terms on age.
- **What brought `single`.** On `novatrail`, the first "Check" with platform AI on a task of `novatrail/check-board` — a legible solution, which the author reads with confidence — gave «Читается двояко»: the pair disagreed. The check cost 8676 millionths of a dollar, Opus 8276 and Haiku 400, by the lines `ai_usage` of `api` v0.1.55. In `tutor`, the author was satisfied with the reading by Haiku · `medium` alone.
- **What `single` accepts.** The error of a single reader that the measurements above recorded — a false "correct" by Haiku · `low` on the near-key at a digit shift of 0.4, and 1 of 560 boxes of a workbook by Haiku · `medium` itself — falls on the work of every learner, the author's, another adult's and a child's: a false verdict where the pair would give "unreadable", for the price, Haiku's 400 millionths of the check's 8676, and for fewer «Читается двояко». No eval measured Haiku · `medium` alone as the reader of a verdict, and none measured it on a child's handwriting: the models are checked on one person's handwriting. A child takes the verdict on their work for the truth about it, and the false verdict goes into the learner model as evidence. The DPIA assesses it as its risk 20, from its version 26.
- **Admission in `single`.** `api` accepts `single` at every rung. In `single` it asks admission as `tutor` asks it — by the pair's entry of `tutor`'s list, its reader Haiku 5.5 · `medium`, at the entry's rung —, and an entry that the rung does not admit refuses the reading as an admission refuses it, `model_not_admitted`, not the deployment's configuration at its start. In `single` the reading asks admission for its one reader, as the pair asks it for each of its two ([the admission table](../admission/README.md), its admission function).
  - Until 2027-01-17, while only the author learns, the pair's entry of `CallWorkbook` stands at the rung "author" by the author's word, not by an eval, as the author's word admits a model at that rung without a run of eval: so the admission by the pair's entry holds for a workbook with an entry no run measured, and in `single` its Haiku 5.5 · `medium` reads a workbook alone by the author's two words — the one that admits the entry and the one that chose `single` —, not by an eval of the pair. The error of a single reader on the work of another adult and of a child does not reach these entries: the author's word ends before the first of them.
- **What the texts say.** No text that a learner or an adult sees promises two readers: the terms of use, version 1 — "AI reads the work … and it can be wrong: when it cannot read the work, the tutor asks the learner to write it again" —, the privacy policy, versions 3 to 5 — "AI reads the work", and in versions 4 and 5, from 2026-11-28, "before a model reads a learner's work, we measure how well it reads handwriting. For now the models of the platform's AI have been checked on the handwriting of one person alone", which holds of Haiku · `medium`: its own readings were measured, on one person's handwriting, though no eval admitted it as the reader of a verdict alone; the two solutions of version 5 derive the key of a task from paper, not its reading —, the texts for the family and the child, the kinds of data of `docs/privacy.md` and the screens of `app` that spec's documents describe, whose «Читается двояко» is a reason to rewrite, not a promise (`grep -rn -i` of "two readers", "pair", «двух» and «два читател» over `legal/`, `docs/privacy.md` and `docs/dpia.md`, 2026-11-17). No version of `legal/` changes.
- **Where it lives.** `tutor` and `api` read in either mode, and `novatrail` reads in the mode `single`:
  - `tutor` — the mode in the library: in `single`, one reading call by Haiku 5.5 · `medium`, the second reader of the admitted pair, and one observation or the call's outcome; it asks the pair's entry with the reader Haiku in `single`, at the entry's rung;
  - `api` — the variable `API_READING_MODE`, `single` or `pair`, `single` when unset, read at the start and checked by `api check`; in `single` the one observation goes to `module-kit` without the join, and `api` keeps it as it keeps the joined one;
  - `infra` — `API_READING_MODE=single` at the service and the job `check` of `novatrail`;
  - `module-kit` — `observation.Verdicts` gives the verdict by one valid observation, without `Join` (`main` of `module-kit`, read 2026-11-17).

— *Why:*
- Two readers of one provider: «Два читателя одного поставщика» ("Two readers of one provider"). The second reader is insurance against an error that the synthetic data did not show, and its cost is about 10% of the sheets in "unreadable", which does not punish the learner: no verdict is better than a false alarm. A model's verbal confidence cannot be trusted, and a divergence of two readings is seen by the program itself.
- The pair stays as `tutor` measured it until an eval: the choice of models is admission by eval's, and synthetic data gives no admission. The argument about the first error of a single reader is the executor's proposal, by the numbers of the same run. The workbook's first false "correct" of a single reader is an argument for the second reader in a workbook too, as on the near-key of a sheet.
- One reader for an essay: the second reader insures the verdict, and an item with a rubric has no verdict.
- The join at `module-kit`: normalization and the key are there, by the slot check, and an equality of texts would send equal values to "unreadable".
- `single`, for everyone: «давай пока поставим только чтобы одна модель Haiku medium работала. Это меня абсолютно устраивало. Пускай будут разные режимы. Режим как сейчас и режим когда работает только Haiku medium — выстави сейчас этот режим» ("for now let's set it so that only one model, Haiku medium, works. That suited me completely. Let there be different modes: the mode as now, and the mode where only Haiku medium works — set this mode now"), and «оставить single для абсолютно всех» ("keep single for absolutely everyone"). The price — Haiku's 400 millionths of the check's 8676 — and fewer «Читается двояко» are weighed against the insurance of the second reader for every learner, and the reading by Haiku · `medium` was found good in `tutor`; the pair stays as a mode a deployment may choose.

— *Rejected:*
- one reader, until a pair of different providers is measured — the recommendation of `tutor`: on the synthetic data the rule did not catch a single error;
- waiting for a pair of different providers: it cannot be measured while `tutor` has no OpenAI key;
- the pair with Haiku without thinking: coverage 75%;
- writing in the pair Opus 5.5 · `high` with Haiku 5.5 · `medium` as the pair that `tutor` measured, on the extended measurement: synthetic data gives no admission;
- waiting for the volunteers' handwriting, writing nothing of the extended measurement down;
- recording nothing of the workbook's first false "correct";
- two readers for an essay too, with a divergence being "unreadable" for the whole sheet: 5–16 synthetic essays of 300 would go to be rewritten;
- two readers for an essay, with the words that they read differently marked for the assessment: a new mechanism that nobody has measured;
- the join at `tutor`, as `tutor`'s `docs/architecture.md` proposed: normalization and the key are at `module-kit`;
- equality of texts after normalization: "0.5" and "1/2", "3 / 4" and "3/4" would go to "unreadable";
- removing the pair: it stays, as the mode `pair`, chosen on purpose;
- `pair` as the default: a run with no variable, a local one too, read otherwise than `novatrail`, and a work one reader reads cleanly went to "unreadable" when the two disagreed — the author's word: the default is never `pair`;
- Opus 5.5 · `high` alone: dearer — 8276 millionths of the check's 8676 —, and Haiku was found good;
- the pair on `novatrail` until the eval on the volunteers' handwriting, with a task of `tutor` that analyses the disagreement: the reading by Haiku is wanted now;
- the pair for children, as a condition before the first child in the DPIA: `single` is for everyone;
- `single` for the author alone, the pair for other adults: `single` is for everyone;
- the refusal of `single` at the rung "full" at `api`'s start: the rung is a matter of admission, and `tutor` asks it for the reader of the mode by the pair's entry;
- `pair` kept as the default, with `single` set on `novatrail` alone: every other run, the stand of an epic too, would read by two models nobody chose.

— *Consequence:* `docs/repositories.md`; `docs/concepts.md`; `docs/architecture.md`; `docs/privacy.md`; `docs/dpia.md`; `contracts/README.md`; `admission/README.md`; `COORDINATION.md`; `run/EPICS.md`; `run/DEBT.md`; `docs/decisions.md`; `tutor`'s `docs/decisions.md`.

## Reading unfinished work

**R69. The work is read only on the learner's action, on "Check", never at a solving step: the platform leads no solving steps. On a pause, the app only blinks a button, without an AI call, and the pause does not go to the AI. A request for a hint does not send work not submitted for reading either. Once more for the tutor's words, the work goes to AI only while the tutor's panel is open, or once when the learner opens it.**
- **What the measurement of `tutor`'s epic E4 measured**, as `tutor`'s `docs/architecture.md` records it. Haiku 5.5 · `low` without the key read a sheet where the device itself would read it: after a line, on a pause from 0.4 s, and before erasing.
  - "Correct" or "not yet" before the answer is written: after a line — in 94 calls of 196, on a pause — in 46 of 131, before erasing — in 11 of 22. A result that the work does not yet give — in 113, 57 and 12: the last number on the sheet is read as the answer. This is the very "read 1" feared of reading on a pause.
  - The pauses were chosen, not all taken: the longest one in the answer line and in one other line. So the share on a pause is not the share over all pauses.
  - Readings per sheet beyond submission on the synthetic data: after each line — 2.9, on pauses from 0.4 s — 15.6, from 2 s — 2.9, from 6 s — 0.4. On the author's three sheets, live writing with a mouse — 15.0, 54.0, 7.7 and 1.7. A policy of pauses from 0.4 s would cost Opus about $0.15 per sheet of the synthetic data and about $0.69 per sheet of the author's.
- **A pause** is neither a reason to read nor a mark for the AI, nor a mark in the course of solution for review: nothing of the writing history goes to the AI.
- **No reading at a step.** The module format keeps its solving steps as data, which the platform does not run, and it has no check kind that would judge the work before the end of the solution: the verdict is by the observation as a whole. A model on the device, too, would read the work on "Check".
- **A request for a hint** never sends work not submitted for reading: the option "the request sends the work for reading without a verdict" is rejected. Before the first incorrect answer — not only before the first submission — the request gives "givens and unknown" and the task's technique, and from format 0.4 also the task's leading question, without AI and without reading the work. After an incorrect answer "Hint" gives once more the words of the current rung that the attempt keeps, without AI — without them, the rung's fallback text —, and "explain differently" gives the same rung in other words, one AI call per rung, within the quota and without the work.
- **The tutor's words.** The work goes to AI once more for the tutor's words only while the tutor's panel is open, or once when the learner opens it, for the last submission of the task: with the panel closed, "Check" reads the work for the verdict alone.

— *Why:*
- Reading on a pause gives a verdict on unfinished work in almost half of the cases and costs up to 15.6 readings per sheet of the synthetic data and 54 on live writing, and each reading gives the provider work not submitted. The request would read unfinished work in the same way. The data of E4 are only about reading unfinished work, and the hint after an incorrect answer rests on the hint ladder, not on them.
- The tutor's words: opening the panel and "Check" are both the learner's action, and the work is one already submitted for reading, so the rule of this entry holds; with the panel closed, less of the work goes to the provider.

— *Rejected:*
- reading on pauses — by any policy of the measurement;
- deciding later: the data that the question of a learner gone quiet waited for are there;
- deciding the hint after an incorrect answer by the data of E4, as `tutor` advised: E4 did not measure it;
- reading at a solving step, with a verdict or with the AI's words alone: a verdict before the learner's own check of the answer, each step a call and money, a capability of `tutor` of its own with an eval, and reading without a verdict was rejected for a request for a hint too.

— *Consequence:* `docs/product.md`; `docs/concepts.md`; `docs/architecture.md`; `docs/privacy.md`; `api`'s `docs/architecture.md`; `app`'s `docs/architecture.md`.

## Checks of the tutor's words

**R70. The model's words that the learner will see are checked by a program not only for a leak. A hint — by the form check: exactly one question, no more than two sentences, the letters of the explanation language and a word limit by language — 30 in Russian, 35 in English. Feedback by a rubric — by the feedback rule: no more than three sentences and 80 words in English, and a stretch in quotation marks of four words or more is only the learner's words. The tutor's words do not give away the learner's gender.**
- **The form of a hint.** The glossary's rule of a hint, in `docs/concepts.md`, prescribes: one question, no more than two short sentences. Only the prompt held this rule, and `api` checked only the leak. `tutor`'s measurement of hints checked the form the way `api` would check it: exactly one sentence is a question, no more than two sentences, from 1 to 30 words, the letters of the hint's language — Cyrillic in a Russian one, where a Latin letter of the task statement, such as `x`, may stand too, and Latin in an English one.
  - The result on 34 test sheets, 204 hints per configuration: Opus 5.5 · `high` breaks the form in 25, all by the number of words, and 24 of them in English. Its English hint is 28.2 words on average, its Russian one 21.5, so the limit is by language: 30 words in Russian and 35 in English. Haiku 5.5 · `low` has 21 breaches, Haiku without thinking 65.
  - A hint that did not pass the form is the same as one that did not pass the leak: the learner reads the fallback text.
- **The rule of feedback by a rubric.** How feedback does not write the essay for the learner — the tutor never touches the learner's work — was left to the detailing. `tutor`'s measurement of essays checked feedback by a program: no more than three sentences and 60 words, a stretch in quotation marks of four words or more stands in the essay as it is written, the letters are Latin. Not one quote of others' words, and Opus exceeded the limit of 60 words in 3 feedbacks of 45 — all about an essay where three criteria are not met. So the limit is 80 words. Feedback that did not pass the rules is replaced by the phrase of `app` "no feedback this time", without a repeated call, and the marks of the criteria are recorded.
- **Grown-up mode** has neither the form check nor the leak check: its words tell the grown-up what the tutor did on the sheet, the solution among it, as asked behind the PIN, and their form is the prompt's.
- **Where the check is and whose code.** Both checks are done by `api`, before the text goes to the device, beside the leak check.
