- **The list of measures and who keeps them:**
  - the disclosure that the learner is talking to an AI, and educational materials on safe use — `app`, to all learners;
  - filters — the safety rules for minors in all prompts of `tutor` and the safety item in the eval sets; the safety system prompt by Anthropic's article enters only if Anthropic gives it. The article does not publish it: "For example, we may provide a child-safety system prompt, which organizations serving minors should implement as part of a comprehensive suite of safety measures" ([Guidelines for Organizations Serving Minors](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/9307344), updated 2026-03-16, read 2026-11-10);
  - monitoring — at the provider, and at the platform — an adult's report at the tutor's answer and escalation: the report goes to the operator, who reviews it within 3 days and, if a child is threatened with harm, acts by the escalation path below;
  - age verification — the method of parental consent and the age category;
  - COPPA and a statement about it — the privacy policy;
  - zero data retention at OpenAI for under 13 or under the age of digital consent — the fact `zero_data_retention`;
  - there is no inference of the learner's emotions anywhere: `tutor` does not call a model to judge the learner's feelings, and the verdict is given by a program, not by AI, so the platform does not automate "high-stakes actions … without human review".
- **The report** is the method `AttemptService.ReportProblem` of the contract `app` ↔ `api`, together with the consent: the attempt ID, which answer of the tutor and rung, the tutor's words as `app` showed them, a word of a closed set — incorrect, unclear, not for the age, harmful or dangerous, asks for or tells something personal, other — and a text of up to 1000 characters. The words are in the report because `api` does not store the correct answer words and the feedback on an essay. `api` stores the report in its database until the review and a year after, and the operator reads it with their command of `api`. The report outlives the deletion of the profile and the account until the end of the period — without the account, profile and attempt IDs, while the words and the text remain as written, so `app` asks not to write names in it; outliving the deletion is a proposal of the plan: the operator may have passed the report on. A year is the period for which a report to the CyberTipline preserves its contents, 18 U.S.C. §2258A(h)(1) as amended by the REPORT Act, Pub. L. 118-59, 2024: "shall be treated as a request to preserve the contents provided in the report for 1 year after the submission to the CyberTipline" ([LII](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/2258A), read 2026-11-10); one period for all reports, not a special one for those passed on.
- **The escalation path.** If the report shows that a child is threatened with harm, the operator reports to the CyberTipline what 18 U.S.C. §2258A requires, and when life is threatened — to the emergency services of the child's country what they need to avert it; the texts tell, in danger right now, to call the emergency service without waiting for the review. The review period is revisited by the public launch.
- **The providers' audits.** Both companies may check whether the platform carries out these measures, and suspend access: the list with the statuses is what the platform will show them.

— *Why:* both companies name "monitoring and reporting mechanisms", and OpenAI also "escalation paths for high-risk interactions": without its own report and escalation path the platform would have nothing to show at an audit, and nobody would see a child's admission of harm. The operator is so far one, the author, and a promise of 3 days they keep is better than a short one they break.

— *Rejected:*
- monitoring only at the provider; its own input filter and the platform reading the works — against the minimum of data;
- a report by letter to the operator at the address from the texts — the content of the work would go where the deletion of the account does not erase it, and a link outward would break the promise of no external links;
- keeping a report 90 days, and a year for those passed on — two periods, and which report is passed on is not seen at once; 3 years — longer than the review needs;
- requesting the child-safety system prompt together with the application for zero data retention; waiting for its publication.

— *Consequence:* `docs/privacy.md`; `docs/architecture.md`; `contracts/novatrail/api/v1/attempt.proto`; `docs/decisions.md`; `RUN.md`; `tutor`'s `docs/decisions.md`.

## Samples, eval sets and essays

**R124. The writing history in a sample from the samples page — the time and the course of the pen, with the pointer and what was erased — is biometric data. It occurs only in measurement samples from adults, with explicit consent under Art. 9(2)(a) GDPR that names it, is never published and serves nobody to identify the writer. The final geometry is personal data, but not biometrics, and the make-up of the sample file that the eval protocol sets does not change. There is no child's grade in the file: the band of grades is held by the record of the measurement organizer. An adult is one by the statement "I am 18 or older, and under the laws of where I live I may make this agreement". An adult withdraws measurement samples by a letter to the organizer and the operator, by the writer code or, if it is lost, by the name and the date of the form, and the organizer erases them within 30 days; the signed measurement form is kept for 5 years after all the samples under it are erased. Item (c) of the DCO, when item (a) is certified in the form, and the field `license` are fit.** The sources were read 2026-11-09 (sources 3.4).
- **Biometrics:**
  - GDPR Art. 4(14): "'biometric data' means personal data resulting from specific technical processing relating to the physical, physiological or behavioural characteristics of a natural person, which allow or confirm the unique identification of that natural person". Art. 9(1) prohibits the processing of "biometric data for the purpose of uniquely identifying a natural person", and photographs, by recital 51, are biometrics "only when processed through a specific technical means allowing the unique identification or authentication of a natural person";
  - WP29, WP193, 27 April 2012, §4.4.6: "While traditional signature recognition relies on the analysis of static or geometric characteristics of the visual image of the signature (how the signature looks like), signature biometrics instead refer to the analysis of dynamic characteristics of the signature (how the signature was made)", and among these characteristics — "the amount of pressure, the angle of writing, velocity and acceleration of the pen";
  - the ICO, "Biometric recognition" — by a copy of the Wayback Machine of 2026-09-25, the site answers 403, and the page is marked "under review" after the Data (Use and Access) Act: "Behavioural characteristics can include a person's handwriting, how they type", and "specific technical processing" is an operation "which makes it possible to uniquely identify them";
  - EDPB 3/2019, v2.0, para. 74: "processing of raw data … must imply a measurement of this characteristics";
  - COPPA, §312.2, personal information (10): "A biometric identifier that can be used for the automated or semi-automated recognition of an individual, such as fingerprints; handprints; retina patterns; iris patterns; genetic data, including a DNA sequence; voiceprints; gait patterns; facial templates; or faceprints". Handwriting is not in the list, but the measure is "can be used for", not the use;
  - the CCPA, Cal. Civ. Code 1798.140(c), by the text of the California Privacy Protection Agency, names as biometrics also "keystroke patterns or rhythms". BIPA, 740 ILCS 14/10, excludes "writing samples, written signatures", but this was read by a copy at FindLaw: ilga.gov did not open, and it was not checked against the primary source.
- **Claude's reading.** The writing history carries the very dynamics that WP193 calls signature biometrics. The ban of Art. 9 depends on the purpose, and the purpose of another's copy cannot be held, so the history is treated as biometrics. A sample file carries no pressure ([the contracts text](../contracts/README.md)), and the time and the course of the pen are still these dynamics. The final geometry is "how the signature looks like". But for a child it is personal information by the measure of COPPA all the same, so it is not published and is kept only for the period of child samples.
- **What follows from this:**
  - the measurement notice and the measurement form name the writing history and take explicit consent for it;
  - the runner of `tutor` and the measurement organizer do not compare writers by handwriting and link samples only by the writer code;
  - no development agent gets the writing history.
- **A child's grade.** The target for children's handwriting is measured by grades, and a first-grader's handwriting is different. There is no grade in the file: the file goes to the runner, and with admission to the AI providers as well. The band of grades — 1–2, 3–4 or 5–6 — the measurement organizer writes into their own record by the writer code, and it lives as long as the sample. Only they break the results down by bands.
- **"I am 18".** Majority does not come at 18 everywhere:
  - Alabama, §26-1-1(a) — at 19, but by (f) "an unemancipated minor who is 18 years old and of sound mind … may enter into a binding contract";
  - Nebraska, §43-2101(1) — at 19, but by (2)(a) from 18 one may "Enter into a binding contract";
  - Mississippi, §1-3-27 — at 21, but for contracts on personal property — at 18; this was read by a copy at FindLaw and was not checked;
  - in Scotland transactions are entered into from 16 (Age of Legal Capacity (Scotland) Act 1991, s.1).

  So the statement in the form and on the page is "I am 18 or older, and under the laws of where I live I may make this agreement". The weakness is not in the age, but in that the statement cannot be checked. A minor's contract can be disaffirmed: so by the sense of NY Gen. Oblig. Law §3-101(1), which forbids this only after 18. Against this the organizer accepts a form only from a person they have spoken with themselves.
- **DCO.**
  - Item (c) of DCO 1.1 — "The contribution was provided directly to me by some other person who certified (a), (b) or (c) and I have not modified it". It does not say where item (a) is certified, so a certification in the signed form holds it.
  - Item (a) — "under the open source license indicated in the file", and the field `license: "Apache-2.0"` of an eval-set sample is exactly this license in the file.
- **The order.** The form comes before the first sample, as the samples page of `canvas` has it: the data appear after the consent.
- **A name on the sheet.** In measurement samples and child samples it is looked for by the measurement organizer — by hand, without AI and agents, before the file goes to the runner, as in eval-set samples the eval-set organizer does it. A sample with a name is erased, and the person writes it anew.
- **The measurement notice** names the period — 2 years from the session, as for children's samples — and what remains after withdrawal: the AI providers' logs by their periods and the copy of the file on the device, which the person erases themselves. The runner's report that names the IDs of erased samples lies in the same place as they do, and is erased together with them; conclusions recorded without IDs — thresholds and targets in decisions — remain.
- **Withdrawal and the form.** A volunteer withdraws measurement samples by a letter to both the organizer and the operator, by the writer code, or by the name and the date of the form if they lost the code, and the organizer erases them within 30 days, as for children's samples. The signed measurement form — with the name, the signature and the date — is kept for 5 years after all the samples under it are erased, as the scan of the parent's form.

— *Why:* the supervisory authorities call precisely the writing history behavioural biometrics, and the final geometry holds everything eval needs without it. The grade is needed by the target, but not by the file, which goes further than the organizer. One withdrawal period for both purposes fits into the month of Art. 12(3) GDPR (sources 3.5), and the form is the proof of explicit consent to the writing history (Arts. 7(1), 17(3)(e)).

— *Rejected:*
- **both records are biometrics.** Then the final geometry too would need explicit consent under Art. 9, and eval-set samples are published forever, and the purposes of others' copies cannot be held;
- **neither** — diverges from WP193 on the dynamics of writing;
- **no grade anywhere** — the target by grades cannot be checked;
- **the grade in the file** — requires a change to the sample file of the eval protocol and of the samples page, and the grade goes with the file;
- **the date of birth in the form** — extra data, and it cannot be checked anyway;
- **checking a document** — a copy of a document for the sake of a license on a sample.

**R125. Child samples. The consent is a separate signed form of the parent before the first session. The period is 2 years from the session: a withdrawal by the writer code erases earlier, within 30 days, and the period can be extended only by a new form. The sample file and the scan of the form go to the measurement organizer into the operator's private Cloud Storage bucket in the project `infra`, `us-east4`, by an upload link valid for at most 12 hours from the session, which the organizer gives. Only they see them, and before the first child the bucket moves to a project of the operator's own, where CI of `infra` holds nothing. A child sample does not go to AI until the admission table admits to the provider the work of a child under 13 — the strictest category —, since there is no category in the file.**
- **The consent.** It is a separate signed form of the parent or guardian with the child's code; the organizer accepts it before the first session.
  - The form names:
    - what lies in the sample — the final geometry without the writing history, the crops and the markup from the child's words;
    - what for — to check the target for children's handwriting and to recheck models;
    - who sees it, the period and how to withdraw;
    - Apple's cloud — if Safari saves downloads to iCloud Drive;
    - and that the adult erases the file from the device once they have passed it to the organizer.
  - The basis is consent under Art. 6(1)(a) and Art. 8 GDPR, and for children under 13 also the verifiable parental consent under COPPA, by the same method as the parental consent to a child's profile: a signed form.
- **The period.**
  - COPPA, §312.10: "Personal information collected online from a child may not be retained indefinitely", and the written retention policy names "a timeframe for deletion" (sources 3.4). 2 years from the session cover the target before the beta and the rechecking of models after it. It can be extended only by a new form, with a new period.
  - Withdrawal: the parent names the code or the form, and the organizer within 30 days erases the samples of this code, their copies and the runner's reports that name their IDs.
  - The organizer's record with the band of grades is erased together with the samples of its code. The scan of the parent's form — the proof of consent — lives 5 years after all the samples under it are erased, as the minimal record of a child consent, and is erased then too.
  - Deletion by the period is done by the bucket's lifecycle rule, not by the organizer's memory. It counts from the upload, so the upload link is valid for at most 12 hours from the session: the period from the upload stays the period from the session.
- **The channel and the place.** It is the operator's private Cloud Storage bucket in the project `infra`, `us-east4`, the platform's data region. Cloud Storage is a service of Google Cloud, and by the Cloud Data Processing Addendum, para. 4.1, "Google is a processor", and Cloud Storage is in the list of the Google Cloud Services Summary, both "Last modified October 30, 2026" (sources 3.4).
  - The adult uploads the file and the scan of the form by the upload link that the organizer gives for the session, on a page that `infra`'s tool makes: a POST policy signed through IAM by `signBlob`, without a key, which only writes under the session's prefixes. A signature without a key lives at most 12 hours: "The max duration allowed is 12 hours. This limitation exists because the system-managed key used to sign the URL may not remain valid after 12 hours" (gcloud storage sign-url, read by `infra` 2026-11-13; sources 10.1 infra), so the link is valid for at most 12 hours from the session (Д238). Neither the platform's server nor GitHub sees the file.
  - Samples, forms and the organizer's records each lie under their own prefix. Access is only for the measurement organizer, without development agents; CI of `infra` loses its access only when the bucket moves to the operator's own project.
  - The same bucket holds the volunteers' forms of eval sets, under their own prefix; the scans of the parental consents that `app` uploads lie in a bucket of their own.
  - The organizer reads the file in the bucket or on their own device and puts no copies into other storage: the runner takes the file from the same place.
- **CI of `infra`.** Both buckets — this one and the bucket of the consents' scans — lie in the platform's project, where the configuration's service account `infra-config` holds `roles/firebase.admin`, with `storage.buckets.*` and `storage.objects.*` (sources 10.6 infra), so a job of CI could read, write and erase any object and change a bucket's policy, and a read is Data Access, which is off, so no log shows it. The door is one environment, `production-config`, where only `main` runs, after a review. The author accepts this while only adults' files lie there; before the first child sample or scan of a consent — before the first child — both buckets move to a project of the operator's own, where CI of `infra` holds nothing, and `api` writes the scans there by its variables (Д240).
- **To AI** a child sample does not go until the admission table admits to the provider the work of a child under 13 — and before the approval of zero data retention it does not admit it. The strictest category — because there is no child's category in the file, and the band of grades lies only in the organizer's record. The runner holds this by the field "who wrote", by a refusal for each sample `WRITER_CHILD`, until the provider is admitted. A sample is never given to development agents.
- **Hosting.** The session is run by a build of the page from a file. When the page moves to Firebase Hosting, the IP address of the session's device will go into the Hosting log for "a few months" — the notice and the form name this.

— *Why:* the period is what COPPA requires, and 2 years cover the target. A bucket under the Cloud DPA is the channel and the storage at once: a processor by agreement, the period set by code, and access with one person. The texts promise the person what the link does, and the child-sample form and the DPIA's measures promise one person's access; no child data exist yet, so moving the empty buckets then costs nothing.

— *Rejected:*
- **until the end of the beta and 12 more months** — there is no date of the end of the beta, and the retention policy needs a period;
- **5 years** — longer than eval needs;
- **hand to hand** — does not suit a volunteer from far away;
- **email** — attachments lie with the mail services of both sides, and the platform has no processor agreement with them;
- **a key of a service account** for the link, which allows 7 days;
- **"a day" as an upper bound** — the texts say the link "works for one day";
- **an upload screen of `canvas` now** — the page opened from a file goes to no network, and the screen waits for the move to Firebase Hosting;
- **the operator's own project now** — while only adults' files lie in the buckets, the platform's project serves them;
- **a narrower role of `infra-config`** — CI would still run jobs as any service account.

**R126. The volunteer's form of an eval set and its route. The form lives as long as at least one sample by it is in any published version of a module: it is the evidence of the license and of point (a) of the DCO. A form by which no sample was contributed is erased 12 months after it is signed. The form takes no consent to training an own reading model, and an essay is graded by two people, each on their own, a third deciding where they differed. The volunteer may withdraw a sample within 30 days: it leaves the next version of the module, and released versions keep it. The files and the scan of the form come to the operator's private bucket of samples by an upload link valid for at most 12 hours. A file that failed the check is erased at once; one that passed lies in the bucket until it is entered into the module's repository, and one not entered is erased with its form or 12 months after its upload, whichever comes first.** The sources were read 2026-11-09 (sources 3.4).
- **What is in the form** — to the list that `modules` sets for an eval set:
  - the text of DCO 1.1 word for word and the certification of point (a);
  - the statement "I am 18 or older, and under the laws of where I live I may make this agreement";
  - publication under Apache-2.0: a sample in a published version of a module is public forever, and by point (d) of the DCO "a record of the contribution … is maintained indefinitely"; a withdrawal takes it only out of the next version;
  - the runs of the sample at AI providers in CI of `modules`, with the names of the providers;
  - no consent to training an own reading model: the samples are for checking AI, and training would require a new version of the text set. The platform does not train its own model on the samples, but anyone may take the published ones;
  - samples without names and signatures, on made-up topics;
  - how an essay is marked: two people grade it, each on their own, and where they differed, a third decides; one mark per criterion is published;
  - the version of the text set and the form's retention period.
- **Where.** In the operator's private bucket of samples, under its own prefix, with access for the eval-set organizer. The record of the form names the SHA-256 digests of the samples contributed by it.
- **Retention period.**
  - The form and the record live as long as at least one sample by it is in a published version of a module — that is, indefinitely. The basis is GDPR Art. 17(3)(e): erasure does not apply while the data are needed "for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims". The form says so.
  - A form with no contributed samples is erased 12 months after it is signed.
- **Withdrawal.** The volunteer withdraws an eval-set sample by the name and the date of the form, and it is done within 30 days: a sample not contributed to the module's repository is erased, and one contributed leaves the next version of the module and its tests. Released versions keep it forever, as do others' copies under Apache-2.0.
- **Channel.** The volunteer uploads the files and the scan of the form by an upload link valid for at most 12 hours from the session, the same kind of link as for child samples. The platform's server and GitHub do not see them.
- **A file that failed the check** is erased at once with all its copies. The record of the form marks only that it was rejected, and the date, and the volunteer writes the sample anew.
- **A file that passed the check** lies in the operator's bucket until the organizer enters it into the module's repository, and then its copy in the bucket is erased: once entered it is public, and the copy adds nothing. The organizer enters a file only while its form still lives.
  - A file not entered is erased no later than its form: when a form under which no sample was contributed is erased, 12 months after it is signed, the organizer erases the files that came under it with it, and the bucket's lifecycle rule erases a file 12 months after its upload, whichever comes first.
  - The set `eval-set` version 2 — `eval-set-notice` and `volunteer-form` — and the policy `privacy-policy` version 4 say so: "erased when your form is, or 12 months after the upload, whichever comes first".
- **The writer and the organizer may be one person.** A module author writes their own samples by the volunteer's form, signs it themselves and accepts them themselves, by `modules`' own rule for an author's sample. Then they sign the commit of the sample under point (a) of DCO 1.1, not (c), and their name in the commit is their own signature. The `volunteer-form` in force does not exclude this case: "signing the commit … under point (c)" and "Nothing of you is in the commit" describe the organizer and a promise to another person, and an author who is the organizer knows this and accepts it.

— *Why:* the license is not withdrawn, and a dispute about it is possible at any moment, and without the form there would be nothing to show point (a) with. Consent to a purpose that does not exist is not "specific" (GDPR Art. 4(11)), and one mark does not catch an assessor's error. The upload comes after the signature, so a file could outlive its form, the one evidence of its license and of point (a) of the DCO, and then it can no longer be entered: a file with no purpose is kept against Art. 5(1)(e).

— *Rejected:*
- **5 years after the contribution** — a dispute about the license is possible later too, and by then the form would be gone;
- **a version of `volunteer-form` and of the set `eval-set` with a phrase for an author who is the organizer** — one more round of approval for a case the author knows themselves;
- **erasing the copy after entry without a rule** — the period would hang on the organizer's memory, while a period is kept by a rule, as for child samples;
- **no period for a file not entered** — against Art. 5(1)(e);
- **keeping the file 12 months from the upload whatever its form** — a file with no purpose;
- **a form living 12 months from the last upload and not from the signature** — the texts and the rule of `eval-set/forms/` of `infra` would change for a case that erasing with the form already closes.

— *Consequence:* `docs/privacy.md`; `docs/dpia.md`; `legal/`.

**R127. An essay is personal data of the learner and of those it names. A disclosure of self-harm is data about health. The platform does not look for such things. To a learner under 18, at work with a rubric and in `app`, where to turn is always shown: to an adult they trust, and to the helplines of their country. To an adult — "report a problem", and to the operator — the escalation path for reports, with a report under 18 U.S.C. §2258A if they learned of what this law names. `app` reminds the learner to keep names out of the work on the camera of a task from paper, before the photo, and in the adult's Help; no reminder stands before Check. Topics under 18 are made-up and general.** The sources were read 2026-11-09 (sources 3.4).
- **Personal data.** CJEU, C-434/16 Nowak, 20 December 2017:
  - para. 37 — "the content of those answers reflects the extent of the candidate's knowledge and competence in a given field and, in some cases, his intellect, thought processes, and judgment. In the case of a handwritten script, the answers contain, in addition, information as to his handwriting";
  - para. 42 — the examiner's comments also relate to the candidate;
  - para. 45 — "The same information may relate to a number of individuals".

  Therefore an essay and the marks of a rubric are the learner's data, and a person named in an essay is one more data subject. A disclosure of self-harm is data about health: by Art. 4(15) it is "personal data related to the physical or mental health", and the ICO counts among them "details about an individual's mental health" (by a Wayback Machine copy of 2026-10-17).
- **Topics.** To a learner under 18 a module gives made-up and general topics, and marks a topic about the learner's life as not for their category, by the task's `age_categories`.
- **The reminder.**
  - On the camera of a task from paper, under the viewfinder, before the photo is taken or picked, `app` reminds the learner to keep names out of it: a page may hold names the learner did not write — a worksheet's field "Name", a school, a teacher's notes.
  - The adult's Help says that the name is made up, so no real names go into the work, an essay's either.
  - No reminder stands before the submission of work that goes to an AI provider whole — before Check of a sheet, of an essay or of a task from paper —, nor over the field of a request about the page. The essays module has none in its statements either: it leaves the reminder to `app`.
  - The platform does not look for others' names in an essay, and does not store the text of an essay, but as a stored work, when storage on the server is turned on.
- **Disclosure of harm.**
  - **The platform has no duty to report.**
    - 18 U.S.C. §2258A tells a provider to report to NCMEC's CyberTipline "after obtaining actual knowledge" of child pornography, of child trafficking (§1591) and of enticement of a child (§2422(b)), and by (f) "Nothing in this section shall be construed to require a provider to— (1) monitor any user".
    - In 17 states and Puerto Rico "any person" is obliged to report (Child Welfare Information Gateway, "Current Through 05-31-2023"). That is a person who learned, not a program that nobody reads.
    - In England s.85 Crime and Policing Act 2026 is a duty of a person in a "relevant activity", and it is not in force yet ("Prospective"). When it will be brought in is not verified.
  - **The platform does not look for signs of harm.** That would be an inference about the learner's health and feelings (Art. 9), and the platform does not monitor the content of works. The ICO counts under Art. 9 an inference too, when "you intend to treat someone differently on the basis of inferred information".
  - **To a learner under 18**, at work with a rubric and in the section "Help" of `app`, which is open to them from any screen, there is always shown: "if something is wrong — tell an adult you trust", and the helplines of their country.
    - The helplines come as a name and a number, without links, so the privacy promise of "no external links" holds.
    - Samaritans: "At a minimum standard, all sites and platforms should provide basic signposting, including: Trusted helplines" and "All companies must review signposting regularly to ensure accuracy of contact numbers". Therefore the list by country that `app` keeps carries the date it was checked.
  - **To an adult** — "report a problem" at each answer of the tutor, and the operator handles the reports by the escalation path.
    - If from a report or otherwise the operator gained actual knowledge of what §2258A names, they report to the CyberTipline.
    - The ICO: "Data protection law doesn't prevent you from doing this" (A 10 step guide to sharing information to safeguard children, a Wayback Machine copy of 2026-10-15), and under a threat to life the basis is Art. 6(1)(d) and 9(2)(c).
- **Storage on the server.**
  - The text of the switch says that an essay may hold personal matters, including about health and about the family, and that nobody reads it. Its words are the legal text `storage-consent` [of the part `legal/`](../legal/README.md), with a version and a gist in the language of the screen, not a string of `app`: the version the person saw is written by the consent record.
  - Turning it on is explicit consent to what the essay discloses about health (Art. 9(2)(a)). It is given by whoever gives consent for this learner.

— *Why:* nobody will read a child's disclosure, so it is proportionate not to look for it, but to tell the child where to turn — the minimum that Samaritans name — and to keep a path for what a person learned. The camera's reminder stands where names come that the learner did not write, before the page goes whole; the words of the switch are a legal text, so that a consent names the version that was seen.

— *Rejected:*
- **detection and a report to an adult** — an inference about health and feelings (Art. 9), and if the harm comes from the adult themselves, the report would do harm;
- **nothing beyond the adult's report and the operator's escalation path** — below the minimum of Samaritans;
- **a reminder before each Check of work that goes to AI whole**, as `modules` proposed — the camera's reminder stands where names come that the learner did not write. What that leaves is the risk of names on the sheet or the page that go to the provider, medium in [docs/dpia.md](dpia.md), and `parent-consent` version 1, in force, says "the app reminds your child": its next version, or the reminder back, is a condition before the first child (Д288).

— *Consequence:* `docs/privacy.md`; `docs/dpia.md`; `legal/`; `run/DEBT.md`.


**R128. Firebase Hosting is fit for the build of `app` and the samples page: by the Firebase Data Processing and Security Terms Google is a processor for Hosting, and IP addresses for serving the site and for protection are "support for the internal operations" under COPPA. The link of Hosting with Cloud Logging is off. The retention period of Hosting — "a few months" — and the retention period of the audit — 400 days, which concerns the operator and CI, not an account owner or a learner — stand in the written retention policy and in the notice to the parent.** The sources were read 2026-11-09 (sources 3.4).
- **The agreement.**
  - Hosting works under the Google APIs Terms of Service, the Firebase Data Processing and Security Terms and the Firebase Paid Services Agreement ([Firebase Terms](https://firebase.google.com/terms), "Terms last modified: September 24, 2026").
  - DPST, §5.1.1: "Google is a processor of that Customer Personal Data", and by §14.1, on a conflict with the rest of the agreement, "these Terms will prevail" ([DPST](https://firebase.google.com/terms/data-processing-terms), "Terms last modified: August 21, 2024").
  - The Google APIs Terms, §1(i), take in the Controller-Controller Terms only "To the extent required by data protection laws". The list of Controller Services is "Google Maps APIs, Google Play, NotebookLM Plus for Workspace Service Data, Subscribe with Google, Waze APIs and SDKs, Waze Carpool, Google Beam" ([Services](https://business.safety.google/services/), "Last update: 27 April 2026"): Hosting is not in it.
  - The suspicion that Hosting comes under "controller to controller" terms was not confirmed.
- **COPPA.**
  - An IP address is personal information, item (7) of §312.2.
  - Serving the site and protection from abuse are "support for the internal operations": "(ii) Perform network communications; … (v) Protect the security or integrity of the user, website, or online service". The condition is that the information does not go "to contact a specific individual … to amass a profile on a specific individual, or for any other purpose".
  - Whoever does only this is not a "third party" (§312.2), and there is no disclosure.
  - The written assurances of §312.8(c) are the DPST and its Appendix 2 on security measures.
  - The weak spot is §7(a) of the Google APIs Terms: "Google may use submitted information in accordance with our privacy policies". The DPST prevails (§14.1), but how the FTC will read this is not verified.
- **Measures:**
  - The link of Hosting with Cloud Logging is off. The request log of Hosting carries `remoteIp` and the full URL of the request ([Hosting logs](https://firebase.google.com/docs/hosting/web-request-logs-and-metrics), "Last updated 2026-11-05 UTC"), and the link itself is turned on only by choice: "You can link your Firebase project to Cloud Logging".
  - The retention period of Hosting cannot be configured — "Hosting retains IP data for a few months" — and it stands in the written retention policy (§312.10) and in the notice to the parent together with the internal operations for which the IP address is taken (§312.4(d)(3)).
- **The Admin Activity audit** — 400 days, the period cannot be configured. This period stands in the same retention policy.
  - The callers are the operator and CI. Nothing in the project `novatrail` calls `SignUp`: the learners' users are created by the Google window, `SignInWithIdp`, which writes no Admin Activity, and of Identity Platform the audit holds only the three entries of the setup of sign-in, with the email and IP address of whoever set it up. So the 400 days concern the operator and CI, not an account owner or a learner, and the sentence of `privacy-policy` versions 1–3 that the first deployment checks this needs no new version.
  - This was checked on the project after the first deployment, over the audit from 2026-11-12; the entries of other services were not gone through. A new call of `api` to Identity Toolkit comes as a row «в реестр spec» before its release, and then this is checked again.
- **The retention policy (§312.10)** is assembled from the period of each kind of data that [docs/privacy.md](privacy.md) sets — among them those of stored works, of the consent record, of child samples, of the volunteers' forms and of this entry. The privacy policy carries it.
- **The samples page** may move to Hosting as a separate site. When, the author decides; the notice and the form name the retention period of the Hosting log.

— *Why:* the agreement makes Google a processor, and the log that Google keeps itself serves only the internal operations that COPPA names.

— *Rejected:*
- **Cloud Storage with Cloud CDN or Cloud Run** under the Cloud DPA — the logs and periods there are in our own hands, but it is longer and more expensive, revises `infra`'s choice of Hosting, and Google stays a processor there too;
- **Hosting only for `app`** — an iPad with the samples page still does not work.

— *Consequence:* `docs/privacy.md`; `legal/`.

## DPIA

**R129. The platform's DPIA is [docs/dpia.md](dpia.md), in English, by the ICO's template. It is reviewed by a task that changes what it rests on, and besides — before the beta, before the public launch and at least once a year. Parents and children are not asked, neither before the first child nor before the public launch; a council of experts on the rights and development of children is, before the public launch. No DPO is appointed, and the DPIA records why. The measures and the residual risks are accepted by the author. The DPIA is also the assessment of Connecticut, Colorado and Montana, and every version of it is kept in `spec`'s git history.** The sources were read 2026-11-09, and the DPIA lists them.
- **Place and language.** It is an internal record, not a text shown to people, so it lies among the documents of `docs/` and is written in English, as the other documents of `docs/`. The repository is public, so the DPIA is published: the ICO — "it is good practice to publish your DPIA", and WP248 — "controllers should consider publishing at least parts". It is given as it is, with its date and version, to the ICO at a consultation (Art. 36(3)(e)) and to an AI provider at a review of its measures for minors. Another document cites no section of it: it says in words what it needs from the DPIA.
- **Review.**
  - GDPR Art. 35(11): "at least when there is a change of the risk represented by processing operations". The ICO adds outside changes: "if a new security flaw is identified, or a new public concern is raised".
  - Therefore the DPIA is reviewed by a task that changes what it rests on: a kind of data or a retention period, a provider or a processor, an AI capability or an AI route, opening an age, a country or a function to children. Its «Сделано» names the review, and the log at the start of the DPIA — the version.
  - A problem report or a mail to the operator in which a family says that a measure does not work is a reason for a review too.
  - Besides — before the beta, before the public launch and at least once a year. No source sets a period: the yearly review is the platform's own rule.
- **The views of parents and children.** Art. 35(9) — "Where appropriate, the controller shall seek the views of data subjects", and the ICO's code, std 2, Step 3 — "seek and document the views of children and parents". Parents and children are not asked, neither before the first child nor before the public launch: Art. 35(9) asks for their views "where appropriate", and they are not needed here. The DPIA departs from std 2 and records why. A problem report or a mail to the operator does not replace asking: whether a child understands what they are told, nobody checks — risk 19 of the DPIA, medium, accepted by the author.
- **A council of experts** on the rights and development of children, which std 2 advises, — before the public launch.
- **DPO.** Not appointed: by the ICO, "Under the UK GDPR, you must appoint a DPO if" the core activity is "large scale" monitoring or processing of special categories on a "large scale", and the platform has no scale before the beta. This is a retelling of the ICO, and the text of Art. 37 is not checked. The ICO: "If you decide that you don't need to appoint a DPO … it's a good idea to record this decision". The decision is reviewed before the public launch.
- **Sign-off.** The measures and the residual risks are accepted by the author. If a high risk remains, the first child waits, and by Art. 36(1) the platform consults the ICO. Colorado also asks for the "names, positions, and signatures" of whoever approves (Rule 8.04(A)(13), sources 3.12): the DPIA names the author as whoever approves it, and the author signs the PDF of the version in force before the first child, and of each new version from then on; the versions in between need no signature. The operator keeps the PDFs as long as the DPIA itself.
- **The assessments of three states.** The DPIA is also the assessment of Connecticut, Colorado and Montana, element by element, and it is kept: every version stays in `spec`'s git history, and the operator neither deletes the repository nor rewrites that history as long as the platform is offered and for three years after the processing it assesses ends. CGS §42-529b(c)(2), C.R.S. 6-1-1309.5(2)(b) and MCA 30-14-2819(2)(b) ask for the longer of those two periods, and 4 CCR 904-3 Rule 8.05(E) asks to keep "prior versions" too, "in an electronic, transferable form" (read 2026-11-13, sources 3.12). Git keeps every version by itself, with its date, so the rule asks for nothing new but not to erase them.

— *Why:* the DPIA is read first of all by the author, and by the ICO and providers on request. A review by event catches changes that the platform makes itself, and a yearly one those that come from outside.

— *Rejected:*
- **`legal/dpia.md`** — `legal/` holds the texts shown to people, and the DPIA is an internal record;
- **both languages** — the two texts will diverge;
- **a review by event only** — outside changes would not trigger it;
- **every half year** — twice the work without a new argument;
- **a consultation of the parents of the first families before the first child**, and **a consultation before the public launch, together with the experts**;
- **a survey before the beta** — a study with its own data and texts;
- **a separate archive of the versions** — a second copy of what git already keeps.

— *Open:* a problem report by the learner themselves, not only by the adult of the account (П-26).

— *Consequence:* `docs/dpia.md`; `docs/privacy.md`.

## Legal texts

**R130. The platform's legal texts are a normative part of `spec`, [the part `legal/`](../legal/README.md): the policy, the terms, the consents, the text sets of the samples page and the volunteer's form. The part has a version of its own, an integer, and each text and set has its own versions 1, 2, 3…, each as a file of its own forever. A version's status is draft or in force, a version in force applies from its day, `in_force_since`, and it does not change by a byte. A text is Markdown in English, a version may have translations without force, and the passport `legal.yaml` carries the versions, statuses, days and the gist in the languages of the screen. The texts for `app` are given by `api` with the method `LegalService.GetLegalTexts`, the current version of each and the next, and `canvas` and the organizer take theirs from the release file `legal-<version>.tar.gz`.**
- **Versions.** `legal/VERSION` is the version of the layout, of the passport's schema and of the rules, as with the deployment configuration. A text and a set have their own numbers. Consent must be demonstrable after the text changes too — GDPR Art. 7(1): "the controller shall be able to demonstrate that the data subject has consented", — and a sample names the version of the set forever. Therefore each version is a file of its own `texts/<id>/<n>.md`, and it never leaves the part.
- **Status.** `draft` is edited freely and shown to nobody. `in_force` — with `in_force_since`, the day from which the version applies, a date in UTC from 00:00: the day the author approved it, or, for a text whose place is `app`, a later day, so that `app` shows a new version before it applies, as version 2 of the policy promises in «Changes to this policy». A set, a notice of the samples page and a form apply from the day they were approved: no screen shows them ahead. From the release that puts a version in force its file and the passport's record do not change by a byte — the rule `legal.in-force-unchanged` compares them with the part of the previous release, as published versions of modules are compared with the previous ones.
- **Current and next.** A reader reads the part on a day. The current version is the newest in force whose day has come, and the next one is the one that becomes current on the nearest day still to come; a consent names only the current one.
- **Format.** A text version is Markdown, CommonMark with GFM tables, in English — the English text is in force, — without HTML, pictures and links: `app` shows the texts as its own pages, without external links, and the form is printed. The gist of a version in `en` and `ru` lies in the passport beside the version and is approved together with it: the gist and the text will not diverge, and a copy gives its own.
- **Translations.** A text version may name the languages of the interface, other than English, into which it has a translation, by the field `translations`, and a translation is a file `texts/<id>/<n>.<tag>.md`, without force: English is in force, and a consent names the version. `GetLegalTexts` gives the translation into the language of the screen.
- **Rules** — [the part `legal/`](../legal/README.md): `legal.files`, `legal.versions`, `legal.set-texts`, `legal.markdown`, `legal.operator` and `legal.in-force-unchanged`; `legal.files`, `legal.markdown` and `legal.in-force-unchanged` hold translations too. `legal.set-texts` holds a set in force to texts that apply by its own day. `legal.operator` holds every part, a copy's folder and spec's own alike: the part has `privacy-policy` at the place `app` with a version whose day has come, and every version of it, a draft too, has a heading of the second level that reads exactly `Who we are`; a translation needs none, since the English text is the one in force. They are checked by `just legal-check` together with the schemas, examples and reading vectors, whose vector gets the day, `today`, and the next versions, `next`, and the folder of a self-hosting copy by `just -f spec/justfile legal-check-dir <folder>`, without the comparison with a release.
- **Types.** `types/legalv3`, in Go and TypeScript, by the generator of `tools/types`.
- **Who reads it.**
  - `api` — from the Go module of `spec`, `spec.Legal`, and a copy's `api` — from its operator's folder. It gives the texts with a place of `app` by the method `LegalService.GetLegalTexts`, and the next versions in `next_texts`: Connect GET without a token, as the methods of `PackageService`, because the policy is read before sign-in ([the contracts text](../contracts/README.md)). A consent names its text version by the request that gives it.
  - `canvas` puts the sets of its purposes into the build of the samples page from the release file of `spec` that `release-verify` accepted; a purpose is open only with the current set.
  - The organizer of an eval set and of a measurement takes the form from the same place.
- **Drafts.** The part opens with draft texts: their words are written afterwards, and the author approves them.
- **Line.** A new version of the part opens a line of `spec`'s releases: version 1 comes out with `v0.13.0`, with draft texts, and the words of the texts and their approval come out in the line 0.13 with the next releases; version 2, the translations, starts the line 0.15, and version 3, the day a version applies, the next version and `legal.operator`, starts the line 0.17.

— *Why:* a consent and a sample refer to a text forever, so a text must have a version that cannot be rewritten, and a place from which everyone who shows it takes it. The method of the contract comes with the part, not later with the consent contract. Connecticut's law requires a privacy notice in every language of the service (sources 3.9), and English stays the text in force. CGS §42-520(b)(3) sets no number of days for the notice of a change: "a reasonable opportunity … to withdraw consent" and "all reasonable electronic measures" (sources 3.11), so how far ahead a version comes is the author's choice with each version, not a rule of the part. By the part's own rules a change of its rules comes with a new `VERSION`, and `release-version` refuses a new rule ID within a line.

— *Rejected:*
- **a date as the version** — two versions of one day could not be told apart;
- **git's history only** — `api` and the organizer would not show a former version from one release;
- **three statuses** with "superseded" — a replacement would edit the old file, and "superseded" can be derived anyway;
- **all in YAML** — long legal texts in YAML are harder to read and edit;
- **the gist in the translations of `app`** — it would not follow the text version, and a copy would show the gist of the platform's texts;
- **an npm package** — the types package would carry legal texts;
- **a method in `AccountService` with a token** — the policy must be shown before sign-in;
- **the method later, together with the consent contract** — the plan's proposal;
- **templates with the operator's name** for a copy — another operator would promise what the platform does;
- **a translation as a separate text with its own ID** — `app` would guess by the name whose translation it is;
- **a field of the passport of its own for the day a version applies** — a change of the schema, so a new version of the part, for what one date can say; **the device's memory** — that is not "before"; **a letter** — the platform sends none;
- **the next version as a field of `LegalText`** — the current version and the next are two texts of one shape, and a text with a next version and no current one would have no place;
- **`legal.operator` only for a copy's folder** — one reader, one set of rules, and spec's own part meets it;
- **a day in the time zone of the person** — `api` serves everyone one answer, and an hour's lifetime of the answer already moves the moment by up to an hour;
- **a least number of days in the part** — the law sets none.

— *Consequence:* `legal/`; `contracts/README.md`; `types/legalv3/`.

**R131. The platform's operator is in the United States: ALT EdTech LLC, the author's company, formed in Texas. Its name, postal address, telephone and email — the company's, not the author's — and with them the law and court of the terms of use are written into the drafts of the texts. The privacy policy is one for all learners: with the notice to the parent under COPPA §312.4(d) and the written retention policy of §312.10. Consent to storing works on the server is the legal text `storage-consent`. Representatives in the EU and in the United Kingdom under Art. 27 of the GDPR and of the UK GDPR the operator appoints before the first learner from there, and until then `api` accepts no learners, and the organizer of the samples page no volunteers, from the countries of the EU, the EEA and the United Kingdom. What the laws of US states ask of the platform is fulfilled for all learners from the United States.** The sources were read 2026-11-09 (sources 3.5).
- **Where the operator is.** The GDPR covers learners from the EU with an operator in the United States too — Art. 3(2): "the processing of personal data of data subjects who are in the Union by a controller or processor not established in the Union, where the processing activities are related to: (a) the offering of goods or services, irrespective of whether a payment of the data subject is required". Then Art. 27(1): "Where Article 3(2) applies, the controller or the processor shall designate in writing a representative in the Union". The exception of 27(2)(a) is processing "which is occasional, does not include, on a large scale, processing of special categories of data … and is unlikely to result in a risk". The platform's processing is constant, the data are children's, and an essay may disclose health, so the exception does not fit it — Claude's reading. The UK GDPR has the same Arts. 3(2) and 27(1), with a representative "in the United Kingdom" ([legislation.gov.uk](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eur/2016/679/article/27), the revision of 2026-09-30).
- **Contacts.** COPPA §312.4(d)(1): "The name, address, telephone number, and email address of all operators collecting or maintaining personal information from children"; GDPR Art. 13(1)(a) — "the identity and the contact details of the controller". They are the company's data, not the author's, so they are written into the drafts, not at the approval of a version. The email is written as code: `legal.markdown` rejects a bare address, which GFM makes into a link ([the part `legal/`](../legal/README.md)).
- **One policy.** §312.4(d) names what the notice on the website says, and §312.10 — "The operator must provide its written data retention policy addressing personal information collected from children in the notice on the website or online service provided in accordance with § 312.4(d)". Therefore version 1 of the policy already speaks of children, with the retention periods of all kinds of data, and of the samples of the samples page too, and a child's profile will not require a new version. The parental consent and the texts for the child are texts of their own.
- **Storage consent is a text of the part.** Turning storage on is explicit consent under Art. 9(2)(a), since an essay may disclose health, and consent must be demonstrable (Art. 7(1)): the version of the words the person saw is written into the consent record, as with the other consents. For a teenager who gives consent themselves, the learner turns it on themselves, in their own profile.
- **The version a consent names** is named by the request that gives the consent — `LegalTextRef` from `GetLegalTexts`: `CreateAccount` — `privacy-policy` and `terms-of-use`, `RequestChildConsent` and `RestateAge` — `parent-consent`, `GiveOwnConsent` — `teen-consent`, `SetWorkStorage` — `storage-consent`; a version that is not current gets `CAUSE_TEXT_NOT_CURRENT`.
- **Representatives.** Until they are appointed, the policy says that the platform does not accept learners from the EU, the EEA and the United Kingdom, and a version that names them will come as a new one (Д165). As with learners, the organizer of the samples page takes no forms from volunteers who live there until representatives there are named. The appointment is the author's step: it costs money.
- **Transfer to the United States** — what each agreement says (Art. 13(1)(f)):
  - Google — [Cloud Data Processing Addendum](https://cloud.google.com/terms/data-processing-addendum), "Last modified October 30, 2026", Appendix 3, §4.1: with an "Alternative Transfer Solution" the transfer goes by it, otherwise — by the SCCs; [Alternative Transfer Solution](https://cloud.google.com/terms/alternative-transfer-solution), "Last modified September 29, 2026": "Google LLC has certified to the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework" and "to the UK Extension to the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework". Firebase Auth goes under the terms of Google Cloud ([Firebase Terms](https://firebase.google.com/terms), "Terms last modified: September 24, 2026"), and Hosting — under the [DPST](https://firebase.google.com/terms/data-processing-terms), §10.6: "The Data Privacy Framework will apply to any Restricted European Transfer to a certified Google entity in the US". The fallback SCCs of both are Module 2 with the UK Addendum;
  - Neon — the Product Specific Schedule refers to the DPA of Databricks ([Databricks DPA v3](https://www.databricks.com/legal/dpa), 2023-07-21), §8.1: "such transfer shall be governed by the Standard Contractual Clauses", Annex B — Module 2 and the UK Addendum; by §8.2 an "alternative transfer mechanism" applies instead of them, and Databricks, Inc. with Neon, LLC is in the Data Privacy Framework list, EU and UK Extension, "Active" (the API of [dataprivacyframework.gov](https://www.dataprivacyframework.gov/list), read 2026-11-09);
  - OpenAI — [DPA](https://openai.com/policies/data-processing-addendum), "Updated: December 1, 2025", a Wayback Machine copy of 2026-10-28: §4.1 — the data of the EEA are processed by OpenAI Ireland Limited, which transfers them outside the EEA "on the basis of agreements containing SCCs"; §4.2 — the data of the United Kingdom "with the SCCs as amended by the UK Addendum";
  - Anthropic — [DPA](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/data-processing-addendum), "Effective Feb 24, 2025", §I.1: "the terms of the SCCs Module Two (controller to processor) and/or Module Three (processor to processor) … are hereby incorporated by reference", and Appendix 3 B is the UK Addendum.

  Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic is in the Data Privacy Framework list.
- **The United Kingdom's regulator.** In the UK GDPR since 2026-09-30 stands "the Commission" — an amendment under the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (Art. 27(4)), — and what the regulator is now called is not verified. Therefore the policy names the right to complain in the words of Art. 77(1) — "in particular in the Member State of his or her habitual residence, place of work or place of the alleged infringement" — without the regulator's name.
- **The laws of US states.** The platform knows the learner's country, not the state, so what of the states' laws concerns it is fulfilled for all learners from the United States.

— *Why:* an operator in the United States makes COPPA its law, and the GDPR and the UK GDPR the laws for learners from there, with a representative; one policy, and the law calls it complete only when it has children and retention periods in it.

— *Rejected:*
- **the section on children as a version 2, with the texts for the family** — the version in force would have to be replaced before the first child;
- **the words of the switch as a string of `app`** — nothing to demonstrate which version of the words the person saw;
- **representatives now** — paying before the first learner from there; **not opening the EU and the United Kingdom** — would close markets without a review;
- **the states — before the public launch** or **without an analysis**.

— *Consequence:* `legal/`; `docs/privacy.md`; `docs/dpia.md`; `run/DEBT.md`.

**R132. The texts for the family: the parental consent form asks for the consent request code, the parent's name, a signature and a date, and does not ask for the child's name; to the learner — two texts: `child-notice` under 13 and `teen-notice` from 13 to 18, and to one who gives consent themselves — also `teen-consent`; consent withdrawal deletes the learner's profile with all its data, as profile deletion does, and the minimal record of the consent remains — of a teenager's own consent too; an adult withdraws the parental consent by `DeleteProfile`, and the learner withdraws their own by `WithdrawOwnConsent`, by their own learning request, and exports before it themselves — `ExportProfile` with `ACTION_LEARNING` at their profile; storage of works for a learner who gives consent themselves is turned on by the learner themselves; a problem report is handled by the operator within 3 days.**
- **The form.** COPPA §312.5(b)(2)(i) — "a consent form to be signed by the parent" (sources 3.3). The operator has nobody to attribute a signature without a name to, and the parent's name is an adult's data in a scan that lies in the operator's closed bucket for the same period as the minimal record of the consent. The child's name is not in the form: it names the request code that `app` shows.
- **Two texts to the learner.** The ICO's code, std 4: "Provide additional specific 'bite-sized' explanations", and the table by ages tells for the younger ones "full privacy information … in a format suitable for parents" beside the text for the child, and for teenagers — "full information in a format suitable for parents to sit alongside the child focused information" (a Wayback Machine copy of 2026-09-26, the site answers 403; sources 3.5). The platform does not store ages in years, so it does not have the ICO's bands — 0–5, 6–9, 10–12, 13–15, 16–17 —, and the boundary 13 is the boundary of its categories. The text under 13 is in short phrases, the tutor voices it; the text for 13–17 is about the same, in more detail, and with who decides about the data. The English text is in force, and the gist in the language of the screen is, for a child who reads in Russian, the only thing they will read, so the gist of these texts says everything.
- **Withdrawal.** GDPR Art. 7(3) — "It shall be as easy to withdraw as to give consent" (sources 3.3); COPPA §312.6(a)(2) — the parent's right "to refuse to permit the operator's further use or future online collection … and to direct the operator to delete", and §312.6(c) allows stopping the service to the child after such a refusal (sources 3.5). A withdrawal without deletion would keep the child's data without a basis, so a withdrawal is the same as profile deletion, and the export comes before it. In the contract an adult withdraws the parental consent by `DeleteProfile`, and the learner withdraws their own by `WithdrawOwnConsent`, by their own learning request; the export before the withdrawal a learner who gave consent themselves makes themselves — `ExportProfile` with `ACTION_LEARNING` at their profile.
- **The review period** is 3 days, and in danger right now the texts tell to call the country's emergency service.

— *Why:* through the form, the texts and the withdrawal, the parent and the learner get what the rules of consent and the ICO's code promise, without new data, except the parent's name on the form. The right to portability (GDPR, Art. 20) is the learner's who gave consent themselves, and they hold it by the same interface as the withdrawal.

— *Rejected:*
- **the form** — only a signature and a date; also "parent or guardian" as a separate field — the form says "parent or legal guardian" anyway;
- **the texts to the learner** — one for all under 18; five by the ICO's bands;
- **withdrawal** — to stop the profile and keep the data for a period for the export; only an adult exports — a teenager, withdrawing consent, would lose their data without an export;
- **storage for a teenager** — the owner turns it on, the teenager confirms; no storage for them;
- **the review period** — 24 hours; 7 days.

— *Open:* `app` shows the learner their texts, `teen-consent` and the storage switch, and withdrawal as the step of profile deletion, the export first (Д168); `api` names the escalation path of a problem report in the operator's review — now only the 3-day period (Д169).

— *Consequence:* `legal/`; `docs/privacy.md`; `docs/dpia.md`; `run/DEBT.md`.

**R133. The text sets of the samples page and the volunteer's form: the notice and the form of each purpose say one thing; the measurement names Anthropic as the provider, and the eval set — Anthropic and OpenAI, and a change of providers is a new version of the set; each form asks for a name, a signature, a date and the version of the text set, the measurement form — also the writer code, and the parent's form — the writer code of the child; the volunteer's form carries DCO 1.1 word for word; the texts — notices and forms — name both ways by which the page is opened: a file from GitHub and a site on Firebase Hosting.**
- **Providers** are those at which the samples run: the measurement — on Claude models, as `tutor`'s measurement sets, the eval set in CI of `modules` — on models from the list of admitted ones, at OpenAI and Anthropic, with the platform's key for eval. A consent names the providers, so a new provider is a new version of the set, and `tutor` or `modules` says so with a row «в реестр spec».
- **Forms.** A signature without a name cannot be attributed to anyone, as on the parental consent form. The statement is "I am 18 or older, and under the laws of where I live I may make this agreement". The parent's form has the writer code of the child, which the adult got in advance; the band of grades is only in the organizer's record, not in the form: the form lives longer than the samples.
- **Writing history** in the texts is the time and the course of the pen, without pressure: a sample file carries no pressure ([the contracts text](../contracts/README.md)), though the rule of samples names pressure in the writing history that is biometric data.
- **The writer code** an adult also writes into the measurement form, as a parent writes the child's code: by it samples are withdrawn and the form's retention period is counted, and the page does not remember the code. Each form carries also the version of the text set that the page showed.
- **DCO 1.1** — word for word, as a block of code, so that the line breaks and the letters of the points stay as in the [primary source](https://developercertificate.org/) (read 2026-11-09); the volunteer certifies point (a) and understands point (d).
- **IP address.** Now the page is opened from a build file downloaded from the release of `canvas` on GitHub, and GitHub sees the IP address of whoever downloaded it; on Hosting the log keeps the device's IP address "a few months" (sources 4.4). The texts name both, and the move of the page does not require a new version of the set.
- **Retention periods** — as the rules of samples and forms set them: measurement samples and children's samples — 2 years from the session, withdrawal — 30 days, the measurement and parent's forms — 5 years after the samples, the volunteer's form — while its samples are published, and without them — 12 months.

— *Why:* the notice on the page and the form that the organizer accepts say one thing, and the form names everything to which consent is given — and nothing beyond that.

— *Rejected:* consent to model training now; one assessor of an essay or two without a third; withdrawal of a measurement "as soon as possible", without a period; only the route through GitHub — a move to Hosting would require a new version of each set; the measurement form is erased together with the samples — there would be nothing to demonstrate the consent to biometrics with.

— *Open:* `tutor`'s measurement notice and form name Anthropic as the provider, and `tutor` files a row «в реестр spec» before a run on a new provider (Д171).

— *Consequence:* `legal/`; `docs/privacy.md`; `docs/dpia.md`; `run/DEBT.md`.

**R134. The age of digital consent by country is a normative part, `consent-age/`: by country — the age, the day from which it applies, the law and its provision, a quote in the original, the primary source and the date it was read; in the table — the 27 countries of the EU, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, the United Kingdom and the United States; a country outside the table — 18; a record is not rewritten, and a new age is a new record; when a country's age went up, a learner who gave consent themselves states their age anew.** The laws were read 2026-11-10 (sources 3.6).
- **A part of its own**, the way of `deployment/` and `legal/`: a version of its own, a schema, rules, vectors, the check `just consent-age-check`, the release file `consent-age-<VERSION>.tar.gz` from the line 0.14, a Go module — `spec.ConsentAge` — and the types `consentagev1` ([the part's text](../consent-age/README.md)). Not a section of `admission/`: the admission table gets no country, and a new input would be its major.
- **Countries** — the EU and the EEA, where the age is given by Art. 8(1) of the GDPR or by the country's law that lowered it; the United Kingdom — the UK GDPR, 13; the United States — COPPA, 16 CFR §312.2, "under the age of 13", and the laws of the states are weighed apart from the table. The legal analysis named no other countries, and a market outside them is not chosen.
- **Outside the table — 18:** consent for a learner under 18 is given by a parent, and the category `from_consent_to_18` is empty. The platform does not know a law that nobody has read. An error in this direction is a parent's consent for a teenager who could have given their own, not a teenager's own consent where the law requires a parent's. A rule "13, unless the country's law says otherwise" a program cannot check.
- **Category** — by the age in years and the country on the day when the age is stated: under 13 — `under_13`, below the country's age — `from_13_to_consent`, below 18 — `from_consent_to_18`, otherwise — `adult`. An age in the table is from 13 to 18: under 13 consent is given by a parent everywhere (COPPA; Art. 8(1) of the GDPR).
- **History.** A country's record is not rewritten: it has `from` — the day from which the age applies, and a law passed with a deferred entry into force is a record with a day ahead, and a bill is not a record. The table starts with the ages in force on 2026-11-10, when it was read: what was before, the record's note names. The words of a record — the law, the provision, the quote, the source, the date read, the note — can be corrected, and the age and the day cannot: the rule `consent-age.ages-kept` holds them against the release before.
- **The age went up.** `api` stores the category, the day and the country's age by which the category was given — from 13 to 18, a property of the law, not of the learner, — and not the age in years. For a profile `from_consent_to_18` whose country now requires a higher age than that one, `api` asks before the next work to state the age anew. The age is stored, not only the day: a law found late — a record with a day in the past — would otherwise change what this day gave, and there would be no question. A lowered age waits for the yearly confirmation: the former category is stricter. Storing the country's age is a proposal of the plan, by a finding of the review.
- **Country codes** — the 249 codes that ISO 3166-1 assigns officially, as an enumeration of the schema: a code that ISO only reserves — `UK`, `EL` — the schema rejects, and `api` and `app` take the same enumeration. The enumeration is by Debian's iso-codes project ([`data/iso_3166-1.json`](https://salsa.debian.org/iso-codes-team/iso-codes/-/blob/d055275324963c9bce5882eaaa93024cf2bf7ed0/data/iso_3166-1.json), commit d055275 of 2023-02-22, read 2026-11-10); a new code is a new version of the part.
- **To close a country** the table cannot: it is about the law, the same for all copies. A country is closed by the list of countries of the operator of `api`: the EU, the EEA and the United Kingdom — until representatives there.

— *Why:* the category decides who gives consent, and `api` must compute it by a program, from primary sources, with a date — the rule "unless the law says otherwise" cannot be computed.

— *Rejected:* a section of `admission/` — the admission function takes no country as an input; more Russian-speaking countries — the market is not chosen, and Russia also has 242-FZ on storing citizens' data in Russia, and that is a question of whether one may go there at all; 13 outside the table — a teenager of 13–17 from a country whose law requires a parent would consent themselves; 16 — the same for countries where the boundary is above 16; a country outside the table closed to children — the refusal `CAUSE_COUNTRY_NOT_ACCEPTED` closes a country to everyone, and a new one would be needed; waiting for the yearly confirmation when the age went up — for up to a year a teenager would work on their own consent where the law already requires a parent.

— *Consequence:* `consent-age/`; `tools/consent-age/`; `spec.go`; `types/consentagev1/`; `.github/workflows/release.yml`; `docs/decisions.md`; `docs/privacy.md`; `docs/concepts.md`; `docs/dpia.md`.

**R135. The export format is a normative part, `export/`: an export file is a ZIP of JSON files — the manifest of `app`, the part of `api` byte for byte, `api.zip`, per profile a file of what the device holds, each stored work as `GetWork` gives it, and each page from the learner's paper; one form for the export of a profile and of an account; the evidence log, the model's state and the observation are the JSON of their protobuf messages, and their `.proto` files are in the export; records — by the part's JSON Schema; the version is an integer, and a new one opens a line of `spec`.** Normative — [the part's text](../export/README.md).
- **The container is a ZIP**: any system opens it without a program of its own, and `app` puts the part of `api` as a separate file, as the method gave it, without parsing it. Inside `api.zip` — `account.json` in an account export, `profiles/<id>.json` and `proto/`; beside it, the manifest, the device's files, the stored works and the pages from paper ([the part's text](../export/README.md)).
- **Protobuf is JSON of the same value**, by the protobuf JSON mapping with the field names as in `.proto`, as `buf convert` does, and the `.proto` of the version of `learner-model` that computed it and `novatrail/observation/v1/observation.proto` lie in the export: the export says what each field means, and the same bytes can be assembled from it again. A history of writing and a context of submission go in as the JSON values their bytes hold. The one kind of bytes in the export is an image, in base64 — a stored work's picture, a page's photo and a task's crop —, since an image has no JSON of its own.
- **Records** — the profile with its hint mode, consents — who gave each, the owner, a parent or the learner, the request code, the state of the form, the text versions as a list —, attempts, observations, submissions with a rubric, lesson runs, engine choices, evidence, the state, counters, whether storage of works is on, the records of storage consent, the problem reports and what the device holds — by the part's schemas, by the columns «в выгрузку» of the data in `api`'s and `app`'s `docs/architecture.md`; without secrets and service data, without the minimal consent record and the scan of the form.
- **Stored works** — `api.zip`'s profile file names each as `ListWorks` does: the attempt, the kind — handwriting, an essay or a drawing —, when `api` kept it and the size, without its bytes. `app` writes each from `GetWork` as a file of its own: the IDs of the profile and the attempt, the kind, when kept, the history and the contexts and the picture. The rule `export.works` holds a profile to one work for each attempt, each work it names to its file and each such file to a work it names, by the profile, the attempt, the kind and the instant it was kept. A work that `GetWork` gives with another time, or does not give, makes `app` begin the export again, at most three times in a row; if the third finds a work changed or gone as well, it hands over no file and tells the owner that the works are changing on another device and to try again later. When storage on the server is on, a work may lie both at `api` and on the device; the export puts both, and a reader recognizes them by the attempt ID. The text of an essay is stored nowhere.
- **Pages from paper** — the server keeps none, so `app` writes each page from the device as a file of its own: when it was taken, the photo, the frames of the tasks with who drew each, the AI or the learner, and each picked task's attempt, its frame, its crop, its history of writing, the place of its tracing paper and its submissions. `api.zip`'s profile file holds the open attempts of tasks from paper as `paper_attempts` — what `api` keeps of each while it is open: the counts and the rungs —, without the model's hidden solution and answer. They are no evidence and no part of the evidence log. The rule `export.paper` holds each page to a profile the part of `api` holds and to the IDs its path names, each task to one of the page's frames, and an attempt to one task of one page of the profile.
- **IDs as paths.** The ID of a profile, an attempt or a page that names a file is one part of a path, `file_id`: letters, digits, `-`, `_` and `.`, never `.` or `..`, which the UUIDs of `api` fit. No two profiles of an export, and no two stored works or pages of a profile, have IDs that are one once `A`–`Z` are read as small: the rule `export.case` refuses such an export and names the files of each, and [the contracts text](../contracts/README.md) holds `api` to IDs that differ in more than letter case.
- **The evidence log.** A record of an attempt names it by `attempt_id`, and the adult's correction of a module's level (`level_set_by_adult`) by `correction_id`, with the package of the module's current version as its `package_digest`; no `wrong_key` version filters a correction out. In the reading mode `single` a record's `observation` is the one reader's.
- **One form for two scopes**: a profile export is one profile without the account, an account export is the account and all its profiles; the rules of [the part's text](../export/README.md) hold this.
- **The version** — the integer `export/VERSION` and the field `format` of each JSON file of the export; the manifest's `api_format` and the contract's `export_format_version` are the same integer as a string. A new field, a new kind of record or of file or a new rule is a new version of the part and a new line of `spec` (`tools/release/export-line.mjs`); a schema's annotations — `title`, `description`, `$comment` and `examples` — and the examples and vectors change within a version. Each version has its types, `types/exportv<version>` and `@altnovatrail/spec/exportv<version>`, from its line on, and the lines before keep theirs. An export of an earlier version is read by that version, as its `export-<version>.tar.gz` holds it, which no release changes; a reader of one version refuses another by the schema. [The part's text](../export/README.md) names each version and its line.
- **A build of `app` older than the part of `api`**: one that gets an `export_format_version` its build does not write builds no file and offers to reload, as on `unimplemented`. `api` goes out first with a new version, so the build that meets it is the older one.

— *Why:* the export is the account owner's right (GDPR Arts. 15 and 20; sources 3.3), and any program must read it, without the platform's library, and `api` and `app` must write it by one norm.
